hanzi: 一代人有一代人的僵尸肉
pinyin: yí dài rén yǒu yí dài rén de jiāngshī ròu
literal: one generation + has + one generation's + zombie meat
meaning: A wry generational joke about freezer-hoarding: every generation has its own 'zombie meat' — food frozen so long it's practically undead — whether that's a parent's decades-old cured pork wrapped like a brick, or a younger person's forgotten oat milk and meal-prep containers. Used to point out that hoarding habits just take different forms across generations, not that any generation is exempt.
meaning_zh: 网络热梗，调侃两代人冰箱里都藏着'僵尸肉'——冻了太久、几乎'成精'的食物。老一辈可能是腌成砖头一样的腊肉、放了几年的排骨；年轻一代则是囤积却忘记喝的燕麦奶、吃了一半的预制菜。意思是'断舍离'这件事人人都懂但人人都做不到，只是每代人囤积的东西不一样。
example: 别笑我妈的腊肉了，你冰箱里那盒过期酸奶不也是你这代人的僵尸肉。
example_pinyin: Bié xiào wǒ mā de làròu le, nǐ bīngxiāng lǐ nà hé guòqī suānnǎi bù yě shì nǐ zhè dài rén de jiāngshī ròu.
example_translation: Don't laugh at my mum's cured pork — that expired yogurt in your fridge is your generation's zombie meat too.
context: The phrase surfaced in July 2026 alongside a wave of social posts and news pieces comparing what different generations let go bad in their freezers — a parent's meat frozen for years next to a twenty-something's abandoned oat milk and takeout leftovers. It works as gentle intergenerational ribbing rather than real criticism: the joke isn't that older people hoard and younger people don't, it's that everyone has a version of the same habit.

sources.note: 中华网娱乐：一代人有一代人的僵尸肉（2026-07-02）

meaning: A grandma's soothing 'now, now, say no more' — used to wave away criticism of someone you dote on, or to declare you're not going to argue the point. Carries a strong flavour of blind favouritism, and is often used jokingly about yourself or a pampered pet or child.
meaning_zh: 网络流行语，意思接近“好了好了，别说了”，原是奶奶护着孙子、不让大人数落他的口头禅。常带点护短、偏心的意味，多用来调侃自己或别人一味偏袒某个对象。
example: 只要我家猫开心，家具坏了不讲不讲。
example_pinyin: Zhǐyào wǒ jiā māo kāixīn, jiājù huài le bù jiǎng bù jiǎng.
example_translation: As long as my cat is happy, I don't care that the furniture's wrecked — not gonna get into it.
context: From the 《孙孙吃汤饭》 family skits by Douyin creator 杨大牛, performed in Wuhu (Anhui) dialect. The grandma — forever chasing her grandson with a bowl of soup-rice (汤饭) — waves her hand and says '不讲不讲' whenever the parents start scolding him; viewers joke that she usually says it only after stirring up the row herself. The line went viral around early 2026 as shorthand for doting, shield-the-favourite behaviour.

meaning: A trash-talk meme image/caption used to mock someone whose composure has cracked — 'you're already so worked up you're crying.' Usually paired with a garish AI-generated alien face and flung at an opponent or a friend mid-argument or mid-game.
meaning_zh: 一个嘲讽梗图/配文，用来讥讽对方心态崩了——“你已经急得哭出来了”。常配一张五颜六色的AI外星人头像，在对线或游戏里甩给对手、损友。
example: 别死磕了，你已急哭。
example_pinyin: Bié sǐkē le, nǐ yǐ jí kū.
example_translation: Give it up — you're already crying with frustration.
context: Two gaming memes collided. '你已急哭' was a taunt used by a Naruto mobile-game streamer and his chat (later punned as '你已疾苦'), while an AI-generated alien image — made with the 豆包 app and first seen in comment sections in November 2025 — circulated among *Call of Duty Mobile* players as an 'alien aim' compliment and profile picture. Somebody fused the caption with the alien, and by January 2026 the multicoloured versions were everywhere as a way to tilt opponents.

hanzi: 从从容容游刃有余，匆匆忙忙连滚带爬
meaning: A reusable contrast template — "it should have been composed and effortless, but instead it's frantic and undignified" — for describing any plan or day that fell apart into chaos.
meaning_zh: 一句可以随意套用的对比句式——"本该从容不迫、游刃有余，结果却是手忙脚乱、狼狈不堪"——用来形容任何计划或日子崩成一团糟的状态。
example: 这周的deadline，本来应该从从容容游刃有余，现在是匆匆忙忙连滚带爬。
example_pinyin: Zhè zhōu de deadline, běnlái yīnggāi cóngcóngróngróng yóurènyǒuyú, xiànzài shì cōngcōngmángmáng liángǔndàipá.
example_translation: This week's deadline was supposed to be calm and easy — instead it's a frantic scramble.
context: The line comes from an old clip of Taiwanese politician 王世坚 (Wang Shih-chien) questioning officials in the Taipei City Council, years before he became a legislator. In early October 2025 mainland musician 王搏 cut the clip's outbursts — including '你哭什么哭啊，没出息' ('what are you crying for, you're hopeless') — to an electronic beat, and the result, nicknamed 《没出息》, went viral on both sides of the Strait. The phrase then detached from politics and became a template netizens paste over their own disasters — exam cramming, the 17th draft of a PPT, a failed diet.

sources.note: 百度百科：没出息（网络热词）
扬子晚报：微观察——“本来应该从从容容、游刃有余”，神曲《没出息》为啥火遍两岸

meaning: A wobbling, sunglasses-and-necktie 3D penguin GIF that netizens caption over any moment they want to frame as "composed despite the chaos" — the joke is committing hard to fake dignity while visibly stumbling through it.
meaning_zh: 一只戴墨镜、系领带、摇摇晃晃却一脸自信的3D企鹅动图。网友喜欢把它配在任何"明明很狼狈却硬装淡定"的场合，笑点就在于那份认真扮演的滑稽感。
example: 老板突然点名让我发言，我表面高雅企鹅，内心慌得一批。
example_pinyin: Lǎobǎn tūrán diǎnmíng ràng wǒ fāyán, wǒ biǎomiàn gāoyǎ qǐ'é, nèixīn huāng de yī pī.
example_translation: My boss suddenly called on me to speak — on the outside I was the elegant penguin, on the inside I was panicking.
context: The 3D penguin images were uploaded to the stock site Shutterstock in 2014 by an artist called 3Dalia, and later sat in Chinese asset libraries under the file name 'William Tell Penguin'. In late 2024 netizens dug it out of a free asset library and made AI dance clips of its wobbling strut; around Mid-Autumn 2025 a version set to '明月几时有' (the classic 但愿人长久) took off, and by November 2025 the '高雅人士' (posh person) penguin was everywhere. Its clumsy walk paired with sunglasses and a tie reads as someone leaving a fancy function trying to look dignified, so netizens caption it over their own moments of 'barely holding it together but performing composure'.

sources.note: 澎湃新闻：最近爆火的“高雅人士”企鹅表情包，究竟什么来头？
腾讯新闻：火爆全网的高雅人士企鹅，到底什么来头？

hanzi: 世界破破烂烂，小猫越补越烂
pinyin: shìjiè pòpòlànlàn, xiǎomāo yuè bǔ yuè làn
meaning: A twist on the earlier saying '世界破破烂烂，总有人在缝缝补补' ('the world's a mess, but someone's always patching it up'). This cat-owner version jokes that instead of fixing anything, your beloved cat just keeps wrecking the house — shredding curtains, knocking things over — and somehow you can't even be mad, because it's too cute. Used affectionately to describe a pet (or person) whose chaos you've simply made peace with.
meaning_zh: 改编自更早的网络用语'世界破破烂烂，总有人在缝缝补补'。养猫版说的是：猫咪不但不'缝补'，反而不断'拆家'——抓破窗帘、打翻东西，但主人因为太爱它，根本骂不出口。常用来形容对宠物（或某人）造成的麻烦已经全盘接受、甚至觉得可爱的心态。
example: 我家猫又把窗帘抓烂了，真是世界破破烂烂，小猫越补越烂。
example_pinyin: Wǒ jiā māo yòu bǎ chuānglián zhuā làn le, zhēnshi shìjiè pòpòlànlàn, xiǎomāo yuè bǔ yuè làn.
example_translation: My cat shredded the curtains again — truly, the world's falling apart and my cat's only making it worse.
context: The original phrase '这个世界破破烂烂，总有人在缝缝补补' is a feel-good internet line praising the quiet people who keep things together. Cat owners flipped it for pet content around spring 2024: instead of a patient mender, the cat is a gleeful destroyer, and the joke is the owner's helpless devotion despite the damage.

sources.note: 腾讯新闻：世界破破烂烂，小猫咪越补越烂……
网易：世界破破烂烂，小猫越补越烂

meaning: To blindly copy someone else's style or success without understanding what actually made it work, ending up looking worse than before you tried. From the Zhuangzi parable: the plain-looking Dongshi saw that the famous beauty Xishi looked charming even while clutching her chest and frowning in pain, so she copied the frown herself — only to look ridiculous rather than beautiful.
meaning_zh: 比喻盲目模仿别人，却不明白对方好看/成功的真正原因，结果适得其反、更加丑陋可笑。出自《庄子》寓言：丑女东施看到美女西施因病捂胸皱眉的样子很动人，便刻意模仿，结果反而吓跑了邻里。
example: 别人减肥成功是靠控制饮食，你天天喝代餐粉却照吃夜宵，真是东施效颦。
example_pinyin: Biérén jiǎnféi chénggōng shì kào kòngzhì yǐnshí, nǐ tiāntiān hē dàicānfěn què zhào chī yèxiāo, zhēnshi dōngshī xiàopín.
example_translation: Other people lost weight by actually controlling their diet — you drink meal-replacement powder but still eat late-night snacks; that's just a clumsy copy that misses the point.
context: A classical chengyu that never left everyday use, and it's especially alive in comment sections today: netizens reach for it whenever a brand, influencer, or celebrity copies a viral trend (a dance, a marketing stunt, a rival's look) without grasping why the original worked, and the copy flops or looks awkward instead.

sources.note: 百度百科：东施效颦（汉语成语）
汉典：东施效颦的解释

pinyin: yǐ dào gōngwèi, xiāoxi miǎo huí
literal: already at workstation, messages answered instantly
meaning: A tongue-in-cheek note to friends: 'I'm at my desk, so I'll reply instantly.' The joke is that rapid replies during office hours mean you're slacking off, not working hard — and the moment you clock off you vanish completely.
meaning_zh: 打工人之间心照不宣的摸鱼暗号：上班坐到工位上，聊天消息就能秒回——因为正在摸鱼；一旦回复中断，多半是领导派活了；而下班后反而“人间蒸发”。主打上班秒回、下班失联的反差。
example: 九点一到我就给闺蜜发：已到工位，消息秒回！下班以后可就找不到我了。
example_pinyin: Jiǔ diǎn yí dào wǒ jiù gěi guīmì fā: yǐ dào gōngwèi, xiāoxi miǎo huí! Xiàbān yǐhòu kě jiù zhǎo bu dào wǒ le.
example_translation: The moment it hits nine I text my best friend: 'At my desk — instant replies guaranteed!' After work, though, good luck finding me.
context: A 2026 Weibo trend (#已到工位消息秒回#): workers posted their 'office hours' for chatting — instant replies from 9 to 6, a lunchtime nap break, last orders just before clocking off — turning the desk into a hub for gossip with friends. The humour lies in the reversal: being reachable at work is proof of slacking, and being unreachable afterwards is the real luxury.

sources.note: 新浪新闻（微博）：#已到工位消息秒回# 是当代打工人心照不宣的摸鱼暗号（2026-07-01）

meaning: A mad-libs template phrase — "[X] basic, [Y] not basic" — used to point out a jarring, funny contrast between two things that are supposed to match (e.g. a plain top with a wild bottom, a modest salary with wild spending). Expanded from a fashion tip into an all-purpose "unexpectedly extra" joke format.
meaning_zh: 一种句式流行语，格式为"XX基础，XX不基础"，用来调侃两件本该匹配的事物之间出人意料的反差和不协调，比如"上衣基础，下装不基础"。后来被网友套用到生活各领域，表达"意料之外的离谱反差"。
example: 别看他工资基础，消费可一点不基础。
example_pinyin: Bié kàn tā gōngzī jīchǔ, xiāofèi kě yìdiǎn bù jīchǔ.
example_translation: Don't be fooled by his modest salary — his spending is anything but modest.
context: Originated from a fashion blogger's styling tip: "上身基础，下身就不基础" (basic top, not-basic bottom) — pairing a plain blazer with wild, colour-clashing pieces below for contrast. Netizens loved the mismatched-but-it-works effect and started applying the "X basic, Y not basic" template everywhere — salary vs spending, a calm mind vs an insane exam question, and so on. It was named one of 2025's top ten internet buzzwords.

sources.note: 央视网时尚：上身基础，下身就不基础
腾讯新闻：上身基础，下身就不基础

literal: I will resign, stay home, and study [it]
meaning: A mock-serious catchphrase used when something someone said or did is so profound, absurd, or relatable that the only fitting response is joking about quitting your job to devote your life to studying it. Netizens slot in whatever sparked the reaction after 研究 ("study").
meaning_zh: 网络热梗句式，字面是"我要辞职回家专门研究这段话/这件事"，用来夸张地表达某句话或某件事让人深受触动、觉得意味深长，值得反复回味、深入研究。常用于评论区玩梗跟风。
example: 他这段话说得太通透了，我将辞职在家研究他。
example_pinyin: Tā zhè duàn huà shuō de tài tōngtòu le, wǒ jiāng cízhí zàijiā yánjiū tā.
example_translation: What he said was so enlightened, I'm going to quit my job and study him full-time.
context: Sparked in February 2026 when singer 苏醒 (Su Xing), on the variety show 《快乐老友记》, gave an unexpectedly wise riff on self-acceptance — allowing yourself to be imperfect and make mistakes as part of being genuinely you. Netizens turned his sincerity into self-deprecating comedy: "我将辞职在家研究苏醒" (I'll quit my job to study Su Xing) went viral, and the template spread to any statement or person netizens find weirdly profound or funny.

sources.note: 网易新闻：“我将辞职在家研究苏醒这段话”走红，解锁自嘲式通透

meaning: An all-purpose superlative of praise — "absolutely incredible," "off the charts," "smashed it" — used for anything impressively good, from a meal to a performance to someone's whole vibe. Grittier and more dialect-flavoured than yyds.
meaning_zh: 万能夸赞类网络热词，意思是"厉害到极点、好到极致"，可以用来形容任何令人惊艳的人、事、物，比起"yyds"更接地气、更有方言味。
example: 这场演出真的夯爆了，全场都在尖叫。
example_pinyin: Zhè chǎng yǎnchū zhēn de hāng bào le, quán chǎng dōu zài jiānjiào.
example_translation: That show absolutely smashed it — the whole crowd was screaming.
context: '夯' (normally meaning to ram earth, as in 夯实基础) picked up the sense 'hot, popular' via Minnan usage, and young netizens adopted it as the top rung of a five-tier ranking they use to rate anything: 夯 (top-tier) > 顶级 > 人上人 > NPC > 拉完了 (terrible). Adding '爆了' pushes it to the extreme. It broke into the mainstream when it flooded the on-screen comments of CCTV's New Year's Eve gala and then turned up in state-media headlines, cementing it as early 2026's go-to compliment.

sources.note: 百度百科：夯爆了
红网时刻：“夯爆了”刷屏，年轻人不止是玩梗狂欢

meaning: Self-deprecating/critical term for oneself or others as an exploited, overworked labourer — treated like a beast of burden by one's job. Sharper and more bitter than 打工人 (fellow worker), implying real resentment at being worked to the bone for someone else's benefit.
meaning_zh: 指被工作压榨、像牲口一样被使唤的打工人，多用于自嘲或吐槽职场剥削，语气比“打工人”更愤懑、更强调被压榨感。
example: 加班到十一点，我真的是纯纯的城市牛马。
example_pinyin: Jiābān dào shíyī diǎn, wǒ zhēn de shì chúnchún de chéngshì niúmǎ.
example_translation: Working overtime until 11pm, I really am just a pure city ox-and-horse.
context: Already common online by 2024, 牛马 is widely seen as a harsher successor to 打工人 (2020): where 打工人 is wry and cheerful, 牛马 stresses being exploited and fed up, and it often appears alongside 摆烂 and 躺平. The self-mocking '纯纯牛马' ('a pure beast of burden') is a common intensifier, and by 2026 it has largely become the go-to word for describing overwork.

sources.note: 百度百科：牛马（网络流行语）
维基百科：牛马

meaning: A sarcastic comment-section stock phrase: pretending to be outraged that someone withheld some "crucial" piece of information, when the information is actually completely obvious or irrelevant. Used to needle low-effort or redundant comments.
meaning_zh: 评论区常用的反讽公式梗，字面是“这么重要的事你怎么不早说”，实际是调侃对方说了句废话或人尽皆知的信息，带着一种配合演出的幽默感。
example: 评论说“多喝热水对身体好”，底下回复：我去，不早说。
example_pinyin: Pínglùn shuō “duō hē rè shuǐ duì shēntǐ hǎo”, dǐxià huífù: wǒ qù, bù zǎo shuō.
example_translation: A comment says "drinking more hot water is good for you" — the reply underneath: "Whoa, you didn't say so earlier."
context: The phrase traces back to a screenshot of a village group chat: a village head posted a notice about funeral arrangements worded ambiguously, and a villager named 周军 replied with the deadpan “我去，不早说”, as if he'd just received life-changing news. Screenshotted and passed around, it became the standard reply netizens now paste under obvious or filler comments — a way of "playing along" with a joke rather than genuinely complaining.

sources.note: 东方财富·财富号：“我去，不早说”网络流行梗释义
百度贴吧·热梗百科：我去，不早说

pinyin: zhēn méi kòng péi nǐ nào le
literal: [I] really don't have time to play around with you
meaning: A dismissive kiss-off line — "I genuinely don't have time for this nonsense" — deployed by netizens, often mock-quoting a celebrity, to shut down drama, gossip, or a pointless argument.
meaning_zh: 用来表达“我没空搭理你这些无聊事”的怼人金句，网友常“引用”明星语气来终结八卦、争论或无意义的纠缠。
example: 又来问我有没有对象，真没空陪你闹了。
example_pinyin: Yòu lái wèn wǒ yǒu méiyǒu duìxiàng, zhēn méi kòng péi nǐ nào le.
example_translation: Asking me if I have a partner again — I really don't have time for this nonsense.
context: Widely attributed to actress 赵丽颖: in April 2025 the line set off a wave of online speculation, with netizens playing detective over who or what she meant. It has since detached from her and gets pasted under petty online squabbles, nagging relatives or last-minute work requests as a theatrical way of refusing to engage.

sources.note: 搜狐：赵丽颖“我真没空陪你闹啦”，这背后故事有点“上头”

meaning: A viral 2026 meme: a photo of a real opossum caught standing upright indoors, hands folded behind its back, staring blankly out a window. Netizens — especially office workers (打工人) — adopted it as a mascot because an opossum's signature defence is to freeze and 'play dead' rather than flee, which mirrors how it feels to face deadlines and bosses: outwardly composed, inwardly already checked out.
meaning_zh: 2026年爆红的表情包，源自一张海外网友抓拍的照片：一只负鼠溜进屋内，被发现后背手站立、呆望窗外。因为负鼠天性是遇到危险就'装死'僵住而不是逃跑，打工人借此自嘲面对工作、消息和老板时'精神已经进入负鼠模式'——表面淡定，内心早已放弃思考。
example: 老板又在群里@我了，我已经进入负鼠模式了。
example_pinyin: Lǎobǎn yòu zài qún lǐ @ wǒ le, wǒ yǐjīng jìnrù fùshǔ móshì le.
example_translation: The boss @-mentioned me in the group chat again — I've already switched to possum mode.
context: Originated from a candid overseas photo of an opossum that had wandered indoors, standing by a window with its paws seemingly folded behind its back, staring out at the blue sky. It took over Chinese chat apps in late May 2026 as office workers projected their own blank-minded exhaustion onto it, and captioned versions multiplied. The fit is apt: opossums are famous for 'playing dead' when threatened — just as you can't literally collapse at your desk, but spiritually you already have.

sources.note: 百度百科：负鼠表情包
羊城晚报金羊网：2026年最火表情包出现了，是一种比“躺平”更彻底的姿态
京报网（科普中国）：“背手负鼠”火了，网友到处寻图！它到底什么来头？（2026-05-31）

literal: cow / comes — homophone for 牛市来 (bull market's here)
meaning: The title of a crude, home-made 3D animated film that flopped on release and then went viral for exactly that reason: its janky animation made it a shared 'abstract cinema' joke, and because 牛来 can be read as 牛市来 ('the bull market's coming'), stock investors bought tickets as a lucky charm.
meaning_zh: 一部由母子二人耗时五年手工制作的国产3D动画电影，上映后票房惨淡，却因画面粗糙、“抽象”出圈，网友纷纷“见证历史”；片名又被解读为“牛市来了”，不少股民买票讨彩头，成为全网玩梗的现象级话题。
example: 为了讨个好彩头，他专门买票去看了《牛来》。
example_pinyin: Wèile tǎo ge hǎo cǎitóu, tā zhuānmén mǎi piào qù kànle 《Niú Lái》.
example_translation: To get a bit of good luck, he specially bought a ticket to go watch 'Niu Lai'.
context: 《牛来》 is an 86-minute 3D animated film made over five years by director 信雨萌 and his mother 孙丽芳, whose company had started life as a decoration firm. It opened on 5 August 2026 with almost no publicity and took just ¥7,705 in its first ten days. Its rough CG then went viral on social media, cinemas added screenings as people went to 'witness history', and commentators linked the title to the A-share market as a 'bull market's coming' omen. By the end of its run it had grossed about ¥64 million.

sources.note: 维基百科：牛来（制作、票房与“与中国大陆股市联动”）

meaning: A workplace self-deprecating label for someone stuck at the '45-degree angle' between 0° (fully 躺平, lying flat) and 90° (fully 内卷, grinding) — too worn out to hustle hard, too anxious to give up entirely.
meaning_zh: 职场自嘲词，用几何角度打比方：0°是完全躺平，90°是拼命内卷，“夹角打工人”就是卡在中间的45°——卷不动也躺不平，进退两难。
example: 别问我卷不卷，我就是个夹角打工人，卡在中间动不了。
example_pinyin: Bié wèn wǒ juǎn bu juǎn, wǒ jiùshì ge jiājiǎo dǎgōngrén, kǎ zài zhōngjiān dòng bu liǎo.
example_translation: Don't ask me whether I'm grinding or not — I'm a 45-degree worker, stuck in the middle and unable to move either way.
context: In use online since at least October 2023, when it was described as a new buzzword for people who can neither fully lie flat nor go all out. It reframes the 内卷 (grinding) vs 躺平 (lying flat) binary as a geometry joke: most workers aren't at either extreme but stuck at the angle in between. By 2025 even management writing had picked it up — a 清华管理评论 essay used it for undervalued behind-the-scenes staff who can't settle into lying flat yet lack a foothold to climb.

sources.note: 网易：躺不平，卷不赢，你是否也是这样的“夹角打工人”？（2023-10-17）
虎嗅网（转载清华管理评论）：职场人如何摆脱“夹角打工人”的宿命（2025-08-21）

meaning: Describes the anxious, low-key, trying-not-to-be-noticed vibe of doing something on the quiet — like you're sneaking around, even though you're not doing anything wrong. Not an insult: young people use it self-deprecatingly for things like secretly working out, dressing down so as not to draw attention, or quietly grinding at something without telling anyone.
meaning_zh: 形容一个人做事小心翼翼、不想被人注意到，像小偷一样偷偷摸摸的心理状态；并非贬义，而是年轻人自嘲社交焦虑、低调行事的说法，比如偷偷健身、偷偷努力却不想被人发现。
example: 她悄悄减肥成功了，还跟我说："你最近偷感是不是也很重？"
example_pinyin: Tā qiāoqiāo jiǎnféi chénggōng le, hái gēn wǒ shuō: "Nǐ zuìjìn tōugǎn shì bu shì yě hěn zhòng?"
example_translation: She lost weight on the sly, and even said to me, "Have you been on that same sneaky low-key grind lately?"
context: Took off on social platforms in 2024, first describing the awkward, trying-not-to-be-noticed manner of someone dodging the camera or doing something nervously — like a guilty thief, but without the guilt. In December 2024 《语言文字周报》 named 偷感（很重） one of its top ten internet buzzwords of the year, and spin-offs like 超绝偷感 ('ultra sneaky vibe') followed. It remains a common way for young people to joke about wanting to keep a low profile.

sources.note: 百度百科词条「偷感很重」
腾讯新闻：《啥是「偷感、红温」，这些网络流行语你会用吗》

meaning: A 1996 interview line by Tianjin goalkeeper Shi Lianzhi — that he was training to get his body back to 'peak condition' — resurfaced in 2026 and went viral. Athletes and netizens now recite the exact phrase (in his Tianjin accent) as a self-hyping catchphrase before anything stressful, regardless of whether they're anywhere close to their actual best.
meaning_zh: 源自1996年原天津足球队门将施连志接受采访时用天津话说的一句话：“这一段时间主要是训练，把我的身体恢复到最佳状态。”2026年被翻出后突然爆火。很多运动员和网友模仿他的语气和用词，把这句话当成自我打气的口头禅——不管实际状态如何，先喊出来提提精神。
example: 明天面试，先喊一句“把我的身体恢复到最佳状态”壮壮胆。
example_pinyin: Míngtiān miànshì, xiān hǎn yī jù "bǎ wǒ de shēntǐ huīfù dào zuì jiā zhuàngtài" zhuàngzhuang dǎn.
example_translation: Interview's tomorrow — let me shout "getting my body back to peak condition" first, just to hype myself up.
context: Origin: a 1996 interview with former Tianjin goalkeeper Shi Lianzhi (施连志), delivered in broad Tianjin dialect. Thirty years later, in 2026, the clip resurfaced on short-video platforms, and Chinese Super League players such as 高天意 and 朱辰杰, plus Tianjin basketball player 赖俊豪, recreated the line in their own interviews, turning it into a widely recognised self-encouragement catchphrase.

sources.note: 光明网：为嘛三十年前的“最佳状态”旧梗又火了

meaning: Originally a niche streetwear-industry title for a brand's creative lead, a translation of the Japanese "ディレクター" (director), probably via Hong Kong fashion magazines. In 2025 small business owners in every field adopted it as a self-important-sounding stand-in for "boss/owner", from cafés to fried-chicken stalls. It spread so widely that it's now used half-mockingly: calling yourself 主理人 signals main-character energy for what might just be a noodle stand.
meaning_zh: 原本是潮牌圈的专业称呼，指品牌的创意负责人，源自日语"ディレクター"（director），大概率经香港潮流杂志翻译而来。2025年起被餐饮、零售等各行各业的小店主纷纷拿来自称，取代"老板"，用得泛滥后反而显得有点自我拔高、不接地气，入选刘兴亮2025年"哈哈榜"十大网络流行语。
example: 楼下那家炸鸡店老板现在管自己叫“主理人”了。
example_pinyin: Lóuxià nà jiā zhájī diàn lǎobǎn xiànzài guǎn zìjǐ jiào "zhǔlǐrén" le.
example_translation: The owner of that fried-chicken place downstairs now calls himself the "zhǔlǐrén."
context: Traced to the Japanese streetwear title ディレクター. In the 1990s Ura-Harajuku scene, a brand's founder was its ディレクター, and Hong Kong fashion magazine editors most likely rendered the word as 主理人. For years it stayed tied to streetwear and celebrity brands. In 2025 it generalised explosively, from street-stall "炸鸡主理人" to social-media "生活主理人". Tech commentator Liu Xingliang ranked it #2 in his annual "哈哈榜" top-10 buzzwords of 2025, published on Tencent News, describing it as a devalued, over-generalised title.

meaning: Chinese nickname for American livestreamer iShowSpeed (Darren Watkins Jr.), coined because his manic, exaggerated on-camera reactions resemble the hyperactivity of hyperthyroid disease. Now also used more generally to tease anyone acting wildly over-the-top in front of a camera.
meaning_zh: 中国网友给美国主播iShowSpeed（达伦·沃特金斯）起的外号，因为他直播时夸张亢奋的反应像甲状腺功能亢进（甲亢）发作；现在也被用来调侃任何在镜头前情绪特别激动、上蹿下跳的人。
example: 他一看到自己抽到SSR就开始满屋子跑，跟甲亢哥附体一样。
example_pinyin: Tā yí kàndào zìjǐ chōudào SSR jiù kāishǐ mǎn wū pǎo, gēn Jiǎkàng Gē fùtǐ yíyàng.
example_translation: The moment he pulled an SSR he started running around the room like he'd been possessed by Jiǎkàng Gē.
context: The nickname refers to his permanently manic, hyper-excited on-camera persona, which looks like a hyperthyroid flare-up. Chinese fans already knew him for a mishearing gag around 大张伟's song 《阳光彩虹小白马》, which they sang at him in the street. He broke through in China with his livestreamed China tour in April 2025. In the first half of 2026 he dropped his Huawei tri-fold phone into the sea during a jet-ski livestream, and netizens memed it everywhere. During the 2026 World Cup, 退钱哥 He Sheng shouting "梅西是GOAT" at him on camera also went viral.

meaning: Nickname for Chinese football fan He Sheng, who shouted "Refund!" into a reporter's live TV microphone in 2016 after the men's national team lost at home to Syria. Now used as a stock reaction for furious, disappointed fans who feel they deserve their money back.
meaning_zh: 中国球迷何胜的外号。2016年国足在西安主场0比1负于叙利亚后，记者在直播中把话筒递给他，他喊出"对得起我们吗？退钱！"，瞬间走红；现在常被用来调侃任何觉得自己"看了场寂寞"、想讨回票钱的失望观众。
example: 这场比赛踢得也太拉了，我都想学退钱哥喊一句"退钱"了。
example_pinyin: Zhè chǎng bǐsài tī de yě tài lā le, wǒ dōu xiǎng xué Tuìqián Gē hǎn yī jù "tuì qián" le.
example_translation: This match was so bad I wanted to channel Refund Bro and yell "Refund!"
context: On 6 October 2016, in a World Cup qualifier, China lost 0–1 to Syria at Xi'an's Zhuque Stadium. Outside the ground a reporter, broadcasting live, handed her microphone to He Sheng, a fan from Leshan, Sichuan, who yelled "对得起我们吗？退钱！" — a clip netizens nicknamed "朱雀门事变". During the 2026 World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico (which China again failed to reach), he went at his own expense and watched 20 matches, and a clip of him yelling "梅西是GOAT" at the streamer 甲亢哥 (IShowSpeed) went viral, giving the old meme another round.

meaning: A joke about how manic Chinese university back-to-school weeks have become — nonstop reunion dinners, hotpot, BBQ, milk tea runs and club-recruitment treats — so packed with eating that it looks less like term starting and more like a wedding banquet.
meaning_zh: 调侃现在大学开学场面太热闹，新生报到、老同学重逢、社团招新全变成了聚餐局，火锅、烧烤、日料、奶茶轮番上阵，热闹得分不清到底是开学还是办酒席。
example: 我们宿舍这两天天天有饭局，真是应了那句"开学即开席"。
example_pinyin: Wǒmen sùshè zhè liǎng tiān tiāntiān yǒu fànjú, zhēnshi yìngle nà jù "kāixué jí kāixí".
example_translation: Our dorm's had a group dinner every single day this week — living proof that "term starting is basically a banquet starting."
context: 2026年9月开学季，微博话题#这到底是开学还是开席#火了，网友晒出各校迎新现场：锣鼓横幅、摊位福利、聚餐接龙，调侃大学新生"第一天约饭，第二天吃席，第三天已经找不到空闲的肚子了"。

meaning: A joking phrase for when an AI service like ChatGPT goes down or glitches en masse — especially funny when it happens right as the company is busy hyping how powerful the model is.
meaning_zh: 调侃ChatGPT等AI服务突然大面积宕机、卡顿或报错的说法，常用在厂商刚吹完模型多强、结果服务反而先崩了的场合，形成反差笑点。
example: 官方刚宣布进入AGI时代，结果GPT炸了，网友：这就是传说中的AGI（艰难）时代吧。
example_pinyin: Guānfāng gāng xuānbù jìnrù AGI shídài, jiéguǒ GPT zhà le, wǎngyǒu: zhè jiùshì chuánshuō zhōng de AGI (jiānnán) shídài ba.
example_translation: They'd just announced we'd entered the AGI era, and then GPT crashed — netizens joked, "guess this is the legendary Age of Great Inconvenience."
context: 2026年9月3日OpenAI发布GPT-6（"Astra"），总裁Greg Brockman宣称"我们可能已经实现AGI"；当晚ChatGPT、Claude、Grok等却同时出现大面积异常，中文AI社区网友纷纷刷"GPT炸了""我的GPT要挺住啊"，调侃AGI宣言和服务器崩溃同时发生的反差。

meaning: Borrowed from zoo husbandry, where "enrichment" means improving a captive animal's surroundings to keep it physically and mentally healthy. Young people now apply it to themselves: deliberately adding fresh stimulation to a dull, repetitive, screen-bound routine (a new hobby, a different commute, a low-cost offline outing), as if giving themselves the care a zookeeper gives an animal. "人你该丰容了" ("human, time for some enrichment") is the stock nudge.
meaning_zh: 原是动物园的动物养护理念，指从生活环境入手提升动物的身心健康。年轻人借用这个词自嘲地形容给自己单调重复、被屏幕占满的生活"加料"——学点新技能、换条通勤路线、来一次低成本的线下体验，对抗班味和精神内耗，就像饲养员给动物做丰容一样。"人你该丰容了"是常见的提醒句式。
example: 周末去公园遛了一圈，给自己丰容一下，不然真要班味上脑了。
example_pinyin: Zhōumò qù gōngyuán liù le yī quān, gěi zìjǐ fēngróng yīxià, bùrán zhēn yào bānwèi shàngnǎo le.
example_translation: I took a walk in the park this weekend to enrich myself a bit — otherwise the office funk was really going to my head.
context: 丰容 ("enrichment") comes from zoo animal care: improving the living environment to support animals' physical and mental health. In 2026 it surfaced in youth culture as "人类丰容" (human enrichment). Beijing Youth Daily covered it as one of the year's youth social trends: rejecting a life alienated by the digital world and reconnecting with the real one through cheap, restorative offline experiences. The catchphrase "人你该丰容了" became a gentle reminder to break out of a two-points-and-a-line routine.

meaning: A good-luck exclamation — "may fortune come!" — that exploded via the viral rap song 《八方来财》 ("Fortune from all directions") by Guangdong rapper 揽佬. People now chant or type it before an exam, an interview or a gacha pull, hoping for luck.
meaning_zh: 源自广东说唱歌手揽佬的洗脑神曲《八方来财》，"来财，来"的歌词朗朗上口，网友把它当祈福口头禅——考试前、面试前、抽卡前喊一句"来财"，图个好运。2025年入选国家语言资源监测与研究中心年度十大网络流行语。
example: 明天面试，来财来财，祝我上岸！
example_pinyin: Míngtiān miànshì, lái cái lái cái, zhù wǒ shàng'àn!
example_translation: Interview tomorrow — come fortune, come fortune, wish me luck landing it!
context: 《八方来财》 was released by Guangdong rapper 揽佬 in August 2024 in a Memphis-rap style. Spread by DJ remixes and short-video dances built around a beckoning "come, fortune" gesture, it went viral in early 2025 and passed 10 billion plays within months. In December 2025 the National Language Resources Monitoring and Research Centre named 来财 one of the year's ten top internet buzzwords.

literal: old man + toy with/tease + naughty + child
meaning: Describes a veteran or expert effortlessly toying with a far weaker opponent in a game, match, or esports round — a vivider, more mock-classical replacement for the older, blunter gaming slang "炸鱼" (netting fish, i.e. stomping newbies). Used self-deprecatingly by the loser or admiringly by onlookers.
meaning_zh: 形容高手对新手形成碾压级的实力差距，轻松愉快地“戏耍”对手，多见于游戏、棋类、电竞解说和体育比赛场景，是“炸鱼”一词更生动、更有画面感的新说法，带调侃意味。
example: 这局大神带我这个萌新，纯纯老叟戏顽童。
example_pinyin: Zhè jú dàshén dài wǒ zhège méngxīn, chúnchún lǎosǒu xì wántóng.
example_translation: That pro carried me, a total noob, this round — a pure case of the old man toying with the kid.
context: A line from the Chinese live-action drama 《棋魂》 (an adaptation of the Go manga Hikaru no Go): "这分明就是老叟戏顽童". In summer 2026 柯洁 won a "王中王" title, the drama got a second wind, and clips and remix videos of the line spread everywhere. Gamers then adopted it as a more genteel, wittier stand-in for "炸鱼" (a strong player stomping newbies). In this framing, a respected elder is just playfully sparring with a youngster, so there's no guilt involved.

meaning: "Digital hoarding syndrome" — compulsively bookmarking, favouriting, or downloading articles, tutorials, and games and never actually opening them, like a hamster stuffing its cheeks with food it never eats. Often driven by FOMO and the illusion that "saved = learned".
meaning_zh: 形容像仓鼠囤粮一样疯狂收藏文章、教程、游戏等数字内容却从不打开、不消费的行为——“收藏即学会”的错觉，本质是一种数字囤积症，常源于错失恐惧症（FOMO）。
example: 我收藏夹里三千篇干货一篇没看完，典型电子仓鼠症晚期。
example_pinyin: Wǒ shōucángjiā lǐ sānqiān piān gānhuò yī piān méi kàn wán, diǎnxíng diànzǐ cāngshǔzhèng wǎnqī.
example_translation: I've got three thousand "must-read" articles saved and haven't finished a single one — textbook late-stage digital hoarding syndrome.
context: Grew out of years of "数字囤积/电子囤积症" (digital hoarding) discourse — Steam gamers' "喜加一" habit of grabbing every free game and never playing it is often cited as a sub-case — and crystallised recently into the punchier "电子仓鼠(症)" label, now a stock self-deprecating tag for anyone whose bookmarks folder outpaces their reading.

meaning: Being physically at your desk but mentally checked out — doing the bare minimum because your mind has already "clocked off", even though your body is still at work. An extension of the older 摸鱼 (fish-slacking) idea, but about mental disengagement rather than sneaking in side activities.
meaning_zh: 指人身体还在工位上，但精神已经"下班"了，只完成最低限度的工作量。是"摸鱼"概念在心理层面的延伸，强调的是内心的抽离而非偷偷摸鱼。
example: 开完那个没完没了的会，我整个人精神下班了，剩下的工作全靠惯性。
example_pinyin: Kāiwán nà ge méiwánméiliǎo de huì, wǒ zhěnggè rén jīngshén xiàbān le, shèngxià de gōngzuò quán kào guànxìng.
example_translation: After that endless meeting I mentally clocked out — the rest of my work is just running on autopilot.
context: One of Digitaling's top 30 internet buzzwords for H1 2026. It captures a burnout-adjacent mood among office workers who no longer bother hiding their disengagement — a step beyond 摸鱼 (covert slacking) into open, low-effort presenteeism.

meaning: "Hold it together" — telling yourself (or someone else) to keep a straight face and not crack up laughing or break down crying, in the face of something absurd, cringe, or overwhelming.
meaning_zh: 形容在离谱、搞笑或令人崩溃的场面前，努力忍住不笑或不崩溃。是老梗"蚌埠住了"（绷不住了）的反向用法——从"绷不住"变成一句要绷住的自我提醒。
example: 他一本正经地念错了自己的名字，我们全场绷住没笑出声。
example_pinyin: Tā yī běnzhèngjīng de niàn cuò le zìjǐ de míngzi, wǒmen quánchǎng bēngzhù méi xiào chū shēng.
example_translation: He solemnly mispronounced his own name, and somehow the whole room held it together without laughing.
context: A 2026 offshoot of the older pun "蚌埠住了" (Bengbu city + 绷不住了 "can't hold it together"), which broke out of 抗压背锅吧-style forums and 二创 comment sections around 2020. "绷住" flips the collapsed version back into an imperative, and has spawned its own mini-vocabulary: 难绷 (hard to hold it together), 老绷家 (a chronic can't-keep-a-straight-face type), 轻松绷住 (holding it together with ease).

literal: green plum (from 青梅竹马, childhood sweethearts) + ox and horse (from 牛马, an overworked employee)
meaning: Your first-job comrades: the colleagues you started out with, clueless together, who bonded with you through onboarding, meetings, overtime and getting told off, before everyone scattered to different companies. A mashup of 青梅竹马 (childhood sweethearts, literally "green plums and bamboo horse") and 牛马 (ox-and-horse, slang for an exploited, overworked employee). Earlier names for the same bond were 初代同事 and 职场发小.
meaning_zh: 指第一份工作时一起入职、一起从校园菜鸟熬成职场"牛马"的同事，戏称为"职场发小"。化用成语"青梅竹马"，把纯真的儿时情谊置换成职场共患难的战友情。
example: 我俩是当年一起被公司骗进来的青梅牛马，现在虽然各奔东西，但还是每周吐槽老板。
example_pinyin: Wǒ liǎ shì dāngnián yīqǐ bèi gōngsī piàn jìnlái de qīngméi niúmǎ, xiànzài suīrán gè bèn dōngxī, dànshì háishì měi zhōu tǔcáo lǎobǎn.
example_translation: The two of us are first-job comrades who got suckered into the same company together — we've scattered to different jobs since, but we still trade boss complaints every week.
context: One of Digitaling's top 30 internet buzzwords for H1 2026. It reworks the classic 成语 青梅竹马 to name the nostalgic bond with the first cohort of coworkers who suffered through entry-level grunt work alongside you.

meaning: A self-deprecating-but-proud label workers use for themselves, blue-collar and white-collar alike — resigned to the daily grind but refusing to feel ashamed of it. It largely replaced the earlier, more defeated '社畜' (corporate livestock, borrowed from Japanese): darkly funny, but with a stubborn dignity underneath.
meaning_zh: 打工人是劳动者对自己的一种自嘲又带点骄傲的称呼——认清了打工的辛苦和现实，却依然苦中作乐、不卑不亢。不论体力劳动者还是白领，只要在'打工'，都可以自称打工人。
example: 早安，打工人！新的一天又要开始搬砖了。
example_pinyin: Zǎo'ān, dǎgōngrén! Xīn de yì tiān yòu yào kāishǐ bānzhuān le.
example_translation: Morning, fellow worker! Another day of grinding begins.
context: Broke out in October 2020 from short videos by streamer 抽象带篮子, whose catchphrase '早安，打工人' turned into a nationwide meme almost overnight. It's still the default way Chinese social media refers to anyone with a job, and gave rise to a whole family of compounds already in this deck (脆皮打工人, 打工人人传人, 青梅牛马).

meaning: To stop trying to fix a bad situation and just let it get worse — a step past 躺平 (lying flat, doing the minimum) into deliberately doing nothing and accepting the fallout. Roughly: 佛系 (not caring) < 躺平 (giving up effort) < 摆烂 (actively giving up).
meaning_zh: 事情已经没法往好的方向发展了，索性不再采取措施补救，任由它继续往坏的方向走，比'躺平'程度更深一层：佛系—躺平—摆烂，一个比一个'放弃'。
example: 反正这个季度目标肯定完不成了，摆烂了，不改PPT了。
example_pinyin: Fǎnzhèng zhège jìdù mùbiāo kěndìng wán bù chéng le, bǎilàn le, bù gǎi PPT le.
example_translation: This quarter's target isn't happening anyway — I'm done trying, not touching the slide deck again.
context: Borrowed from NBA commentary, where a team out of playoff contention 摆烂 (tanks) — loses on purpose to secure a better draft pick next year. Chinese esports fans adopted it around 2021 for teams that give up mid-match, then it spread to everyday life for anyone consciously abandoning a losing effort instead of struggling on.

meaning: A humblebragging style: dressing up a boast as a complaint or an offhand remark, often via a fake self-deprecating question you then answer yourself, or by quoting someone else's praise of you. Now also a verb — 'you're so 凡尔赛' calls someone out for doing it.
meaning_zh: 在社交平台上用看似平淡、甚至带点抱怨的语气，不经意间炫耀自己的优越条件——'先抑后扬、明贬暗褒'，有时自问自答，或借他人之口夸自己，简称'凡学'。
example: 老公非要送我这个爱马仕，我说真的用不着，他还生气了，愁死我了。
example_pinyin: Lǎogōng fēi yào sòng wǒ zhège Àimǎshì, wǒ shuō zhēn de yòngbuzháo, tā hái shēngqì le, chóu sǐ wǒ le.
example_translation: My husband insisted on buying me this Hermès bag — I told him I really didn't need it and now he's upset. What a headache.
context: Named in 2020 after 《凡尔赛玫瑰》(The Rose of Versailles), a Japanese manga about the extravagant French aristocracy. Weibo blogger 小奶球 systematised the format — self-deprecating opener, backhanded reveal, borrowed third-person praise — into a genre nicknamed '凡学', and it's remained one of the most durable labels for a specific flavour of social-media boasting.

meaning: To ruin something good by adding an unnecessary extra touch. A stock comment-section putdown for over-engineering, a needless sequel or update, or a plot twist that spoils a perfectly good story.
meaning_zh: 比喻做了多余的事，反而把原本好好的东西弄糟了。网友常用来吐槽画蛇添足式的改版、续集或剧情反转。
example: 这次改版本来挺好的，非要加个新手引导弹窗，纯属画蛇添足。
example_pinyin: Zhè cì gǎibǎn běnlái tǐng hǎo de, fēi yào jiā ge xīnshǒu yǐndǎo dàn chuāng, chúnshǔ huàshétiānzú.
example_translation: This update was fine as it was — they just had to add a tutorial popup. Completely unnecessary.
context: From a Warring States-era story in 《战国策》: several men raced to finish drawing a snake first to win a jug of wine; the winner, with time to spare, kept going and added feet to his snake — and lost the bet, since a snake has no feet. Still a common way to call out anything that was fine until someone 'improved' it.

meaning: Shorthand for the Jiangsu Province City Football League (江苏省城市足球联赛), a mixed pro/amateur tournament between Jiangsu's 13 cities that turned into a nationwide sensation in 2025. "苏超" now stands for the whole cultural phenomenon — the matches, the city-rivalry trash talk, the memes — not just the sport itself.
meaning_zh: "江苏省城市足球联赛"的简称，2025年爆红的全民现象级赛事。江苏13个地级市组队踢球，票价低、直播免费，把地域间互怼的"散装江苏"文化变成了全国津津乐道的网络热梗，"苏超"也从赛事名称变成了这场全民狂欢的代称。
example: 这周末苏超又开赛了，南京和常州这对老对手又要在评论区打起来了。
example_pinyin: Zhè zhōumò Sū Chāo yòu kāisài le, Nánjīng hé Chángzhōu zhè duì lǎo duìshǒu yòu yào zài pínglùnqū dǎ qǐlái le.
example_translation: Su Chao kicks off again this weekend — Nanjing and Changzhou, old rivals, are about to go at it in the comments again.
context: Officially the 江苏省城市足球联赛, launched in 2025 as a low-stakes tournament mixing professional and amateur players from Jiangsu's 13 cities. It went viral not for the football but for the memes: cities roasting each other's history and stereotypes ("散装江苏", Jiangsu's running joke about its own lack of unity), Changzhou's early losing streak spawning a bit where netizens jokingly "remove strokes" from the city's name, and local government social-media accounts joining the trash-talk themselves. Named one of 2025's top ten catchphrases by language magazine 《咬文嚼字》.

meaning: "Embodied intelligence": AI with a physical body — a humanoid robot, say — that learns by sensing and acting in the real world, as opposed to "disembodied" AI like a chatbot that only processes text. It's become the go-to term whenever people talk about humanoid robots, robot dogs, or the current robotics boom.
meaning_zh: 指拥有物理身体、能通过与真实环境互动来感知、学习和行动的人工智能（比如人形机器人），区别于像DeepSeek、豆包这类只能处理文字、没有实体的"离身智能"。2025年被写入政府工作报告，成为讨论机器人和AI产业时绕不开的关键词。
example: 现在满大街都在聊具身智能，人形机器人送外卖都算不上新闻了。
example_pinyin: Xiànzài mǎn dàjiē dōu zài liáo jùshēn zhìnéng, rénxíng jīqìrén sòng wàimài dōu suàn bu shàng xīnwén le.
example_translation: Everyone's talking about embodied intelligence these days — a humanoid robot delivering takeout isn't even news anymore.
context: A robotics research term, not originally netizen slang, that broke into everyday conversation in 2025 as viral humanoid-robot demos multiplied and the phrase was written into China's government work report as a priority future industry alongside biomanufacturing and quantum tech. Named one of 2025's top ten catchphrases by 《咬文嚼字》, marking the year "robots with bodies" became ordinary dinner-table conversation rather than science fiction.

meaning: "Digital nomad" — someone who works entirely online and isn't tied to a fixed office, so they work from wherever: a different city, a café, a co-living space abroad. Names the lifestyle of chasing geographic freedom instead of a desk.
meaning_zh: 指完全依靠互联网远程赚取收入、不受固定办公地点束缚的人群，常在不同城市甚至国家之间流动办公，追求工作与生活的动态平衡，是一种类似"游牧民"的生活状态。
example: 他辞职去大理当数字游民了，白天写代码，晚上去洱海边发呆。
example_pinyin: Tā cízhí qù Dàlǐ dāng shùzì yóumín le, báitiān xiě dàimǎ, wǎnshàng qù Ěrhǎi biān fādāi.
example_translation: He quit his job to become a digital nomad in Dali — coding by day, staring at the lake by night.
context: Translated from the English "digital nomad" (a term coined in the 1990s), but only became everyday Chinese vocabulary as remote work normalised post-2020 and nomad hubs sprang up in places like Dali and Chiang Mai. Named one of 2025's top ten catchphrases by 《咬文嚼字》, cited as reflecting how AI-era work is decoupling from fixed offices and hours.

meaning: A metaphor for graduates who feel too "educated" to take a manual or low-status job, but whose degree doesn't get them a well-paid white-collar one either — stuck refusing to "take off the long gown" of their credentials even as it holds them back. Used both sympathetically (describing the real bind) and as self-deprecating humour by young jobseekers themselves.
meaning_zh: 源自鲁迅小说《孔乙己》，比喻当代年轻人把学历当作身份象征，即使找不到匹配学历的工作，也放不下面子去做体力活或"低端"工作，像穷酸秀才孔乙己脱不下那件象征读书人身份的长衫一样。常用于讨论就业焦虑，也被年轻人自嘲使用。
example: 读了四年新闻系，现在送外卖，总觉得脱不下这件孔乙己的长衫。
example_pinyin: Dúle sì nián xīnwén xì, xiànzài sòng wàimài, zǒng juéde tuō bù xià zhè jiàn Kǒng Yǐjǐ de chángshān.
example_translation: Four years of journalism school, and now I'm delivering takeout — I can't quite bring myself to take off this Kong Yiji long gown.
context: In early 2023 a netizen line went viral on Weibo as "孔乙己文学": "学历不仅是敲门砖，也是下不来的高台，更是孔乙己脱不下的长衫" ("a degree is not just a stepping stone but a pedestal I can't climb down from, Kong Yiji's gown I can't take off"). In March 2023 an 央视网 (CCTV) commentary told young people to take off the gown and loosen this 'shackle on the heart'. Young jobseekers pushed back hard, saying it blamed them for a tight labour market rather than the market itself. Kong Yiji, from Lu Xun's 1919 short story, is a failed scholar too proud to give up his gown even in poverty. Still a standard reference three years on whenever Chinese media or netizens discuss graduate underemployment.

meaning: The resolution to 种草 (having a craving "planted" in you): either finally buying the thing and satisfying the itch, or deciding it's not worth it and killing the desire outright. Context tells you which — "拔草了" after gushing about a product means "bought it"; after a bad review, it means "talked myself out of it".
meaning_zh: “种草”的收尾动作：要么终于买了，把心里种下的购买欲“拔”掉（欲望被满足），要么发现东西没那么好，直接打消购买念头（欲望被消除）。具体是哪种要看上下文——种草时满心期待说“拔草了”通常是买到手了，看了差评后说“拔草了”则是决定不买了。
example: 看了三个测评之后，我把这个空气炸锅拔草了，不买了。
example_pinyin: Kànle sān gè cèpíng zhīhòu, wǒ bǎ zhège kōngqì zháguō bácǎo le, bù mǎi le.
example_translation: After watching three reviews, I've talked myself out of that air fryer — not buying it.
context: The mirror image of 种草 ("planting grass", catching a purchase urge), born in the same beauty-forum-turned-Xiaohongshu recommendation culture. Because 拔草 covers both "bought it, itch scratched" and "decided against it, itch gone", it only makes sense read alongside whatever came before — which is exactly how netizens use the pair as shorthand for the whole arc of an online purchase decision.

sources.note: 搜狐《网络种草是什么意思？网络拔草是什么梗？种草和拔草有什么区别》
知乎问答《拔草的意思？》

meaning: To recommend something with real enthusiasm — a show, a snack, an idol, an app — the way an Amway salesperson pitches a product. "给你安利一下" (let me recommend you something) is the standard opener before someone gushes about their latest obsession.
meaning_zh: 指热情、真诚地向别人推荐某样东西（剧、零食、爱豆、app等），带有安利传销式推销的那种“逢人就安利”劲头。“给你安利一下”是网友开始安利前的经典开场白。
example: 求安利！最近有什么好嗑的剧吗？
example_pinyin: Qiú ānlì! Zuìjìn yǒu shénme hǎo kē de jù ma?
example_translation: Recommendations wanted! Any good dramas to binge lately?
context: Borrowed from 安利 (Amway), the American direct-sales company whose door-to-door, friend-recruits-friend pitching style became a byword for enthusiastic, slightly relentless recommending. Chinese internet forums adopted it in the 2010s as a neutral-to-affectionate verb — "安利" someone something is a compliment to both the recommender's taste and the thing itself, unlike the pushiness of the original MLM sense.

sources.note: 金投网《"安利"是什么意思-网络流行语》
中国日报双语新闻《每日一词：安利》

meaning: A warning to steer clear of a bad product, restaurant, hotel, or experience — the opposite of 种草/安利. A "避雷帖" (avoid-the-mine post) shares a disappointing purchase so others don't fall into the same trap.
meaning_zh: 提醒别人不要踩坑，是“种草”“安利”的反义词。“避雷帖”就是分享自己踩雷（买到/遇到不好的东西）的经历，帮别人避开同样的坑。
example: 这家民宿真的要避雷，图片和实物完全对不上。
example_pinyin: Zhè jiā mínsù zhēn de yào bìléi, túpiàn hé shíwù wánquán duì bú shàng.
example_translation: Steer clear of this homestay — nothing like the photos.
context: Grew up alongside 种草 as its counterweight on review-heavy platforms like Xiaohongshu and Dianping, giving shoppers a way to warn each other off a "雷" (landmine/dud) rather than just praise good finds. It's since become such a fixture of consumer-review culture that commentators now note its overuse — some 避雷帖 have drifted from genuine warnings into outrage bait or, ironically, a tactic for extracting freebies from brands.

sources.note: 腾讯新闻《曾经能帮大忙的避雷贴，如今却活成了网友最讨厌的样子》
澎湃新闻·湃客《全网都是的“避雷帖”，藏着多少坑？》

meaning: Self-mocking shorthand for compulsive online shopping — "chopping off your own hand" so you can't click "buy" again. Someone who overspends on shopping festivals like 双十一 (Double Eleven) is a member of the 剁手党 ("hand-chopping party").
meaning_zh: 自嘲式网购失控用语——网购剁手，意思是把自己乱买东西的手“剁掉”，好让自己不能再乱买。热衷网购、尤其是在双十一等购物节疯狂下单的人被称为“剁手党”。
example: 双十一购物车清空了，感觉自己又要剁手了。
example_pinyin: Shuāng shíyī gòuwùchē qīngkōng le, gǎnjué zìjǐ yòu yào duòshǒu le.
example_translation: Cleared out my Double Eleven cart — feels like I'm about to go broke shopping again.
context: Often traced to Jin Yong's novel 《射雕英雄传》, where the beggar-hero 洪七公 cuts off his own finger to break a bad habit; netizens repurposed the image for shopaholics as Chinese e-commerce and shopping festivals like 双十一 (Singles' Day) took off in the early 2010s. "剁手党" made 《咬文嚼字》's 2015 top-ten catchphrases list and has stayed durable ever since as the standard self-deprecating label for post-spree regret.

澎湃新闻《剁手党、网红入选“十大流行语”，“然并卵”为什么落选？》

literal: lemon + spirit/demon (a lemon that has become a sprite)
meaning: Someone eaten up with envy — 'sour' like a lemon at others' looks, money, relationships or luck. Once a jibe at others, it's now mostly used self-deprecatingly: 'I'm such a lemon' = I'm jealous (but in a joking, admiring way). Spawns 我酸了 ('I've gone sour') and 酸了酸了.
meaning_zh: 形容爱嫉妒、看到别人好就心里“酸溜溜”的人。最初用来嘲讽别人，后来贬义淡化，多用于自嘲，表达对别人外貌、财富、感情等方面的羡慕，常与“我酸了”连用。
example: 看到室友的男朋友又送花，我这个柠檬精酸了一整晚。
example_pinyin: Kàndào shìyǒu de nánpéngyou yòu sòng huā, wǒ zhège níngméng jīng suānle yī zhěng wǎn.
example_translation: Seeing my flatmate's boyfriend bring her flowers again, lemon-sprite me stayed sour all evening.
context: Chinese has long used 吃醋 / 酸 ('eating vinegar', 'sour') for jealousy; 柠檬精 updates the metaphor. It started in esports fan circles, then exploded in January 2019 via a Weibo post listing 'the four essences of humankind: 鸽子精 (the flake), 柠檬精, 复读机 (the parrot) and 真香怪 (the U-turner)'. Lemon emoji 🍋 and 'lemon tree' memes followed, and it was named one of the 国家语言资源监测与研究中心's top ten internet terms of 2019. Its survival owes to the shift from insult to cheerful self-mockery.

sources.note: 百度百科：柠檬精（网络流行语）词条
搜狐：“柠檬精”流行语解码——羡慕与自嘲心理

literal: electronic + pickled mustard tuber (the cheap relish eaten with rice)
meaning: The video, drama or clip you put on to eat a meal with — background viewing that 'helps the rice go down', the way zhacai does. Typical examples: film-recap channels, mukbangs, carpet-cleaning videos, or rewatching 甄嬛传 / 武林外传 for the hundredth time.
meaning_zh: 指吃饭时看的视频、剧集或文章，像榨菜一样“下饭”。常见的有影视解说、吃播、洗地毯视频、反复重温的经典剧（如《甄嬛传》《武林外传》）等，不找个合适的看就吃不香。
example: 外卖到了，快帮我找个电子榨菜，没视频我吃不下饭。
example_pinyin: Wàimài dào le, kuài bāng wǒ zhǎo gè diànzǐ zhàcài, méi shìpín wǒ chī bù xià fàn.
example_translation: The takeaway's here — quick, find me something to watch; I can't eat without a video on.
context: 榨菜 is the humble salty pickle that makes plain rice palatable, so '电子' + 榨菜 names the screen equivalent. The term spread through 2022 among young people eating alone at desks or in flats, and became a talking point about solo dining and attention (media pieces asked whether an 'efficiency tyranny' makes people unable to just eat). It was named one of the ten buzzwords (年度十大流行语) of 汉语盘点2022, announced in December 2022 by the National Language Resources Monitoring and Research Centre, the Commercial Press and Guangming Online — sitting on the list alongside 党的二十大 and 中国式现代化.

meaning: A love-obsessed mindset: someone who, once in a relationship, puts the partner above everything — career, friends, self-respect — and will make any sacrifice or excuse for them. Used as a criticism, a warning to friends ('don't be so 恋爱脑'), or self-mockingly.
meaning_zh: 一种“爱情至上”的思维模式，指一谈恋爱就把全部精力和心思放在对方身上，为了感情不惜放弃事业、朋友甚至底线的人。多用于批评或劝诫，也可用来自嘲。
example: 他为了女朋友连offer都不要了，真是恋爱脑晚期。
example_pinyin: Tā wèile nǚpéngyou lián offer dōu bù yào le, zhēn shì liàn'ài nǎo wǎnqī.
example_translation: He turned down a job offer for his girlfriend — terminal case of love-brain.
context: Took off around 2019–2022 on Weibo, Douyin and 小红书, where the hashtag has hundreds of millions of reads and Douyin videos on it tens of billions of views. It became the go-to label in drama fandom (heroines who give up everything for the male lead) and in relationship advice, and spawned a whole 'anti-恋爱脑' genre: warnings, 'cure your love-brain' courses and even businesses built on it. It sits in the same family as 边界感 and 情绪价值 — young people auditing what a relationship should cost them.

meaning: All theory, no practice — talking a great game from books or plans but unable to deliver when it counts. Used of armchair experts, untested plans, and people who've never actually done the thing.
meaning_zh: 在纸面上谈论用兵打仗，比喻空谈理论，不能解决实际问题，或只会照搬书本、不懂变通。
example: 评论区一堆人纸上谈兵，真让他们上场估计第一轮就被淘汰。
example_pinyin: Pínglùnqū yī duī rén zhǐ shàng tán bīng, zhēn ràng tāmen shàngchǎng gūjì dì-yī lún jiù bèi táotài.
example_translation: The comments are full of armchair generals — put them on the pitch and they'd be out in round one.
context: From the story of Zhao Kuo (赵括) in 《史记·廉颇蔺相如列传》: son of the famous Zhao general Zhao She, he could out-argue even his father on military texts, but when he replaced Lian Po as commander he followed the books rigidly and led Zhao to catastrophic defeat by Qin at Changping (260 BC). Sima Qian never wrote the four characters themselves — the chengyu crystallised much later, around the Ming–Qing. Online it's a stock put-down for comment-section experts (键盘侠), 'strategy' threads and 攻略 that collapse on contact with reality, often paired with 实践出真知.

meaning: Introvert / extrovert, borrowed from MBTI letters. A lighter, jokier way to describe your social energy and boundaries than the plain words 内向/外向 — used for self-labelling ('I'm a hardcore i人, don't make me talk at the party'), matchmaking-style small talk, and memes about i人 hiding and e人 dragging them out.
meaning_zh: 源自MBTI人格测试：i人指内向型的人，e人指外向型的人。比“内向”“外向”更轻松俏皮，常用来给自己贴标签、说明社交边界，或调侃i人怕社交、e人热情过头。
example: 我是纯纯的i人，聚会让我坐角落就行，别让我自我介绍。
example_pinyin: Wǒ shì chúnchún de i rén, jùhuì ràng wǒ zuò jiǎoluò jiù xíng, bié ràng wǒ zìwǒ jièshào.
example_translation: I'm a total introvert — just let me sit in the corner at the party, don't make me introduce myself.
context: MBTI personality tests swept Korean and then Chinese social media around 2022, and the first letter (I/E) broke out of the test into everyday speech. By 2023 '你是i人还是e人？' had become a standard icebreaker, and it spawned a whole genre of memes (i人 hiding in lifts to avoid neighbours, e人 befriending the delivery rider). Mainstream outlets from The Paper to the Ministry of Education's student site have written it up. It endures because it names a real, constantly needed distinction in a playful, low-stakes way, and it combines productively (i人狂喜, e人社交, 装e的i人).

meaning: Used when someone swears they'll never do or like something, then happily does exactly that — a sweet, self-mocking U-turn. Unlike 打脸 (humiliating face-slap), 真香 stresses that the reversal turned out to be enjoyable. Often extended as 真香定律 ('the law of 真香').
meaning_zh: 形容一个人先信誓旦旦说绝不做某事，后来却自己打脸、做了相反的事，而且还很享受。比“打脸”更强调态度反转后的愉悦感，也叫“真香定律”。
example: 说好再也不买盲盒了，结果新系列一出……真香。
example_pinyin: Shuō hǎo zài yě bù mǎi mánghé le, jiéguǒ xīn xìliè yì chū……zhēn xiāng.
example_translation: I swore I'd never buy another blind box, then the new series came out… so worth it, honestly.
context: From Hunan TV's reality show 《变形记》 (2014): city teenager 王境泽, sent to live with a rural family, declared he'd rather starve to death than eat a single thing of theirs — and was filmed hours later tucking into fried rice saying 'mm, 真香'. The clip went viral as a meme around 2018 and has since detached from its origin: it now covers any cheerful reversal, from products to people to games. Banyuetan (半月谈) wrote about it as a lasting cultural shorthand, and it's one of the most durable memes of the late-2010s internet.

literal: social + fear (short for 社交恐惧症)
meaning: Originally short for social anxiety disorder, but online it's a casual, self-deprecating label for disliking or dreading social interaction — making phone calls, greeting neighbours, forced small talk at gatherings. Often less about fear than about refusing pointless socialising. Its opposite is 社牛 (social butterfly).
meaning_zh: “社交恐惧症”的简称，原是心理学名词。网络上泛化为年轻人对自己害怕、逃避社交状态的调侃，比如不敢打电话、怕在电梯遇到熟人，也常表示不愿进行无效社交。反义为“社牛”。
example: 作为资深社恐，外卖我都备注“放门口，别敲门”。
example_pinyin: Zuòwéi zīshēn shèkǒng, wàimài wǒ dōu bèizhù “fàng ménkǒu, bié qiāo mén”.
example_translation: As a seasoned social-phobe, I always add a note on my takeaway orders: 'leave it at the door, don't knock'.
context: The clinical term 社交恐惧症 got shortened and turned into a lifestyle label on Weibo and Douban from the late 2010s, peaking around 2021–22 when state media (Guangming Daily, People's Daily Health, China News) ran pieces asking 'are you really 社恐?' and warning that it had become a catch-all excuse. It paired off with 社牛 and 社死 (already in the deck) into a whole 社X family, and sits naturally alongside i人. Durable because it names an everyday feeling in a word everyone recognises.

literal: a man of Qi worries (that) the sky (will fall)
meaning: Needless, groundless worry; fretting over things that will never happen. Online it's a gentle put-down for overthinking or catastrophising, and a self-aware tag for anxious 内耗 spirals.
meaning_zh: 比喻不必要的、毫无根据的忧虑。网上常用来劝人别想太多，或自嘲自己过度焦虑、精神内耗。
example: 还没面试就担心试用期被开，你这纯属杞人忧天。
example_pinyin: Hái méi miànshì jiù dānxīn shìyòngqī bèi kāi, nǐ zhè chúnshǔ qǐ rén yōu tiān.
example_translation: You haven't even had the interview and you're already worried about being sacked in probation — that's pure needless worrying.
context: From the Daoist text 《列子·天瑞》: a man from the state of Qi was so afraid the sky would collapse and the earth give way that he couldn't eat or sleep, until a friend explained the sky is just accumulated air and the earth just packed soil. In comment sections it pairs naturally with modern anxiety vocabulary like 内耗 and 精神状态 — someone posts a worst-case spiral and replies say 杞人忧天 or 别杞人忧天了. Occasionally used positively to defend foresight ('this isn't 杞人忧天, it's 忧患意识').

meaning: To watch a scandal or drama unfold as a bystander without getting involved — the online equivalent of grabbing popcorn. The spectator is a 吃瓜群众 ('melon-eating masses'), and the gossip itself becomes the 瓜: 有瓜 (there's gossip), 大瓜 (a huge scandal), 瓜保熟吗? (is this gossip legit?).
meaning_zh: 指在网上围观热点事件、八卦或他人纠纷，只看热闹、不发表意见也不参与，类似英语里的“吃爆米花看戏”。围观者叫“吃瓜群众”，八卦本身则被称为“瓜”，如“有大瓜”“这瓜保熟吗”。
example: 他俩又在评论区吵起来了，我先搬个小板凳吃瓜。
example_pinyin: Tā liǎ yòu zài pínglùnqū chǎo qǐlái le, wǒ xiān bān gè xiǎo bǎndèng chī guā.
example_translation: Those two are at it again in the comments — I'm pulling up a stool to watch the drama.
context: Grew out of forum culture, where a post would fill up with onlookers chatting idly beneath it; people began calling them 不明真相的吃瓜群众 ('the melon-eating masses who don't know the truth'), a riff on the stock news phrase 不明真相的群众. The 瓜 was originally melon seeds (瓜子), the classic snack of theatre audiences, but the emoji and memes soon turned it into watermelon. 吃瓜群众 made 《咬文嚼字》's top-ten buzzwords for 2016 and the Ministry of Education's 2016 top-ten internet terms, and a decade on it's thoroughly mainstream — every celebrity scandal on Weibo hot search is 'a melon'.

meaning: Zen-like and unbothered: not competing, not striving, taking whatever comes. Attaches to anything — 佛系青年 (chilled-out youth), 佛系追星 (a fan who doesn't fight in fandom wars), 佛系考研 (sitting a postgrad exam without stressing). Can be a sincere life stance or a self-mocking cover for having given up.
meaning_zh: 形容一种不争不抢、不苛求、看淡一切、随遇而安的生活态度，“都行、可以、没关系”。常作前缀构词，如“佛系青年”“佛系追星”“佛系养娃”，既可真心表示心态平和，也常带自嘲意味。
example: 这次比赛我就佛系参加，拿不拿奖都无所谓。
example_pinyin: Zhè cì bǐsài wǒ jiù fóxì cānjiā, ná bù ná jiǎng dōu wúsuǒwèi.
example_translation: I'm doing this competition the zen way — prize or no prize, I don't mind.
context: Borrowed from a 2014 Japanese magazine feature on 佛系男子 ("Buddha-type men" who prefer their own company to dating). The Chinese version exploded in December 2017 when an article about 佛系青年 swept WeChat Moments, and it made 《咬文嚼字》's top-ten buzzwords for 2018. It's the older sibling of 躺平 and 摆烂: commentators read all three as young people's response to exhausting competition, but 佛系 is the gentlest of the three — serene rather than defeated.

literal: down · head (opposite of 上头, 'going to your head')
meaning: A total turn-off; the moment someone or something kills the mood and your enthusiasm drains away. Most often used of cringe behaviour in dating — a 下头男 / 下头女 is someone whose words or actions instantly put you off — but works for any buzzkill.
meaning_zh: 指某人或某事让人扫兴、反感、瞬间失去好感，情绪从兴奋“降温”。是“上头”（令人兴奋、着迷）的反义词。常用于约会、感情场景，如“下头男”“太下头了”。
example: 约会时他一直在炫自己的车，真的好下头。
example_pinyin: Yuēhuì shí tā yīzhí zài xuàn zìjǐ de chē, zhēn de hǎo xiàtóu.
example_translation: He kept showing off about his car the whole date — such a turn-off.
context: Formed by simple analogy from 上头, the slang for being hooked or giddy (like alcohol going to your head): if 上头 is the rush, 下头 is the comedown. A linguistics paper traces the slang sense to actor Li Xian (李现), who on 20 November 2019 posted an Instagram photo of himself in a deliberately goofy pair of glasses, calling himself a '下头' boy — playing against the 上头 craze his fans had built around him that summer. It took off in dating talk, spawning 下头男 and endless '下头行为大赏' lists of red-flag behaviour. Now an everyday word for 'ick'.

meaning: A situation that invites suspicion, where it's wise to steer clear even if you're innocent. Used to say someone should avoid the appearance of impropriety — e.g. an official, a judge, or a celebrity seen in compromising circumstances.
meaning_zh: 比喻容易引起嫌疑的场合或处境。提醒人即使清白，也应主动避嫌，不要置身于容易被人误会的环境中。
example: 他是评委，又跟选手单独吃饭，瓜田李下，难免被人议论。
example_pinyin: Tā shì píngwěi, yòu gēn xuǎnshǒu dāndú chīfàn, guātián-lǐxià, nánmiǎn bèi rén yìlùn.
example_translation: He's a judge and he went to dinner alone with a contestant — that's asking for suspicion, so of course people are talking.
context: From the ancient ballad 《君子行》 (often attributed to Cao Zhi): 瓜田不纳履，李下不整冠 — 'in a melon field, don't stoop to fix your shoe; under a plum tree, don't raise your hand to straighten your hat', lest you look like a thief. Online it pairs naturally with 吃瓜: when a scandal breaks, comment sections split between the 吃瓜群众 and those scolding the person involved for not knowing to 避嫌 in a 瓜田李下 situation.

meaning: A compulsive contrarian: someone who contradicts whatever you say just to argue, ignoring facts. Used to call out nitpickers in comment sections.
meaning_zh: 指无论别人说什么都要唱反调、为了抬杠而抬杠的人，不关心事实对错，只图反驳的快感。贬义。
example: 别理他，他就是个杠精，你说天是蓝的他都要反驳。
example_pinyin: Bié lǐ tā, tā jiù shì gè gàngjīng, nǐ shuō tiān shì lán de tā dōu yào fǎnbó.
example_translation: Ignore him — he's a born contrarian; say the sky is blue and he'll argue.
context: From 抬杠 (to bicker) plus 精 (as in a demon that has 'become a spirit'). The word was around by 2017, but it took off in April 2018 with a viral comic in which a girl confesses her feelings to a contrarian and asks to meet his mother — he says that's the one thing he can't allow, because '杠精不配拥有母亲' (contrarians don't deserve mothers). Named one of 《咬文嚼字》's ten buzzwords of 2018 and on the national language centre's top-ten internet terms list that year; now a permanent fixture of comment-section fights.

meaning: Someone who is used by others as a tool — always on call, doing the favours and the grunt work, but never treated as an equal. Often self-deprecating ('I'm just the office tool').
meaning_zh: 指对他人随叫随到、任劳任怨地付出，却始终得不到平等对待、只被当作工具使唤的人。常用于自嘲。
example: 每次搬家都叫我，我就是他们的工具人。
example_pinyin: Měi cì bānjiā dōu jiào wǒ, wǒ jiù shì tāmen de gōngjùrén.
example_translation: They call me every time they move house — I'm just their human tool.
context: Spread to the mainland from Taiwanese internet usage, originally describing the 'backup' admirer a woman calls on for favours with no romance in return; gamers also used it for the teammate who draws fire so others can score. Broadened to workplaces and friendships, and named one of 《青年文摘》's ten internet buzzwords of 2020 alongside 打工人.

literal: 笑死我了 laugh-die-me-(particle), pinyin initials
meaning: 'I'm dying of laughter' — the Chinese LOL/LMAO, typed as the initials of 笑死我了.
meaning_zh: “笑死我了”的拼音首字母缩写，表示某事非常好笑，相当于英文的LOL。
example: 他那个表情包xswl，我截图了。
example_pinyin: Tā nàge biǎoqíngbāo xiàosǐwǒle, wǒ jiétú le.
example_translation: That meme of his — LMAO, I screenshotted it.
context: One of the pinyin-initial abbreviations that grew out of fan-circle (饭圈) chat around 2018, where abbreviations let fans talk quickly and a little cryptically. Along with yyds and dbq it became standard 00后 shorthand, covered by mainstream outlets as youth 'code', and is still everywhere in danmu and comments.

literal: point at a deer, call it a horse
meaning: To deliberately call black white; to twist the facts and force others to go along with it. Online, used for blatant gaslighting or spin.
meaning_zh: 比喻故意颠倒黑白、混淆是非，并逼迫别人附和。网上常用来讽刺睁眼说瞎话、强行洗白。
example: 证据都摆在这儿了，他还在指鹿为马。
example_pinyin: Zhèngjù dōu bǎi zài zhèr le, tā hái zài zhǐ lù wéi mǎ.
example_translation: The evidence is right here and he's still calling a deer a horse.
context: From 《史记·秦始皇本纪》: the eunuch Zhao Gao presented a deer to the Second Emperor of Qin as a horse, then quietly punished the courtiers who said 'deer' — a loyalty test to see who dared contradict him. Netizens reach for it when a brand, official or influencer insists on an obviously false version of events, and it pairs naturally with modern words like PUA and 洗白.

meaning: A young person from a small town or county who got into a good university by grinding through exams, but who feels they lack the connections, confidence and wider horizons of big-city peers. Used self-mockingly, and about a whole class of strivers.
meaning_zh: 指出身小城镇、埋头苦读、擅长应试，但缺乏视野、人脉和资源的青年学子。多用于自嘲，也用来讨论寒门学子的处境。
example: 我就是个小镇做题家，除了考试什么都不会。
example_pinyin: Wǒ jiù shì gè xiǎozhèn zuòtíjiā, chúle kǎoshì shénme dōu bú huì.
example_translation: I'm just a small-town exam grinder — apart from taking tests, I can't do anything.
context: Born in 2020 in the Douban group 985废物引进计划 ('985 losers' recruitment programme'), where students at China's elite 985 universities described themselves as failures once they found exam skills didn't translate into social capital. 做题家 ('question-solving expert') became 小镇做题家, and it ended up on the 2022 list of top ten internet buzzwords. People's Daily and others weighed in, arguing whether it was self-pity or a fair critique of how unequal opportunity is — which is exactly why it has lasted.

meaning: To break out of a niche: a person, work, brand or subculture gets noticed and accepted by the general public far beyond its original fanbase. Close cousin of 出圈.
meaning_zh: 指某人、某作品或某种文化突破原本的小圈子，被更广泛的大众接受和认可。由饭圈用语“出圈”演变而来。
example: 这部国产动画彻底破圈了，连我爸妈都在看。
example_pinyin: Zhè bù guóchǎn dònghuà chèdǐ pòquān le, lián wǒ bàmā dōu zài kàn.
example_translation: This Chinese animated film has totally broken out of its niche — even my parents are watching it.
context: Grew out of 出圈, a fandom term from around 2018 for an idol becoming known beyond their fans. From 2020 onwards 破圈 spread into mainstream media and marketing-speak, where it now describes anything going mainstream — a Bilibili creator, a regional dish, a traditional craft. Very productive: 破圈之作, 破圈传播, 实现破圈.

literal: 'run' (pun on the English word; normally 'moist / to enrich')
meaning: To get out: emigrate, or leave a bad situation for good. 润学 ('run-ology') is the half-joking study of how to move abroad.
meaning_zh: 取英文 run 的谐音，指跑路、离开，尤指移民出国。由此衍生出“润学”，指研究如何出国移民的学问。
example: 工作太卷了，他已经在研究怎么润了。
example_pinyin: Gōngzuò tài juǎn le, tā yǐjīng zài yánjiū zěnme rùn le.
example_translation: Work is such a rat race that he's already researching how to get out of the country.
context: 润 is pronounced rùn, which sounds like English 'run'. Online dictionaries recorded it in 2021 as a playful word for 'leave, bolt', and its first Weibo uses in both senses (just leaving, and leaving the country) date from early January 2022. It then exploded in spring 2022 during the Shanghai lockdown, when searches about emigrating surged and 润学 ('run-ology') became a buzzword. It is sensitive in some contexts, but everyone understands it, and it still turns up in lighter uses like 我润了 ('I'm out of here').

meaning: To cheer someone on, show loud support for or endorse a person or thing. Often 为…打call ('cheer for …').
meaning_zh: 源自日本偶像演唱会的应援方式，指为某人或某事加油、支持、点赞。常见用法“为……打call”。
example: 为今天加班的所有打工人打call！
example_pinyin: Wèi jīntiān jiābān de suǒyǒu dǎgōngrén dǎ call!
example_translation: Here's a shout-out to every worker pulling overtime today!
context: Comes from Japanese idol culture, where fans at live shows perform 'calls': rhythmic chants, jumps and glow-stick waving. Chinese otaku borrowed it, added 打 to match fan verbs like 打榜/打歌, and in 2017 it went mainstream and was named one of 《咬文嚼字》's top ten buzzwords of the year. It now works for any enthusiastic support, from brands to friends.

literal: go up + shore → reach dry land
meaning: To finally pass a gruelling competitive exam — above all the civil-service exam (考公) or postgraduate entrance exam (考研) — and land a stable place; by extension, to reach any hard-won goal and be 'safe' (paying off debts, losing weight, getting into a relationship).
meaning_zh: 指通过考公、考编、考研等竞争激烈的考试，成功被录取、进入体制或理想院校；后泛指经过努力终于达成目标、脱离困境，如还清债务、减肥成功、脱单等。
example: 熬了三年，他终于考公上岸了。
example_pinyin: Áo le sān nián, tā zhōngyú kǎo gōng shàng àn le.
example_translation: After slogging away for three years, he finally passed the civil-service exam and made it ashore.
context: The image plays off 下海 ('going into the sea'), the 1980s–90s phrase for quitting a state job to try your luck in business. If the market is the sea, then the secure 'iron rice bowl' of the state system is dry land — so passing the exam to get in is 'climbing ashore'. As youth unemployment rose and exam applications hit records, 上岸 became the standard word in exam-prep circles on Xiaohongshu, Bilibili and WeChat, spawning set phrases like 考研上岸 and the joke '上岸第一剑，先斩意中人' (first thing after making it ashore: dump the person you were with). It has since generalised to any goal reached after a long struggle.

sources.note: 百度百科：上岸（网络用语）词条
腾讯新闻评论：《“上岸”，是“站点”而非终点》

literal: do / fix up + a turn, an act
meaning: To pull off a stunt or bit purely for entertainment value — doing something wacky, creative or absurd to get a laugh. As a noun (整活儿) it's the stunt itself; 整个活 = 'let's do a bit'.
meaning_zh: 指为了节目效果故意搞点花样、做出出人意料或搞笑的举动；也可作名词，指这种表演或花活儿。常说“整个活”“又在整活”。
example: 毕业典礼上，他穿着恐龙服上台拨穗，全场都笑疯了，太会整活了。
example_pinyin: Bìyè diǎnlǐ shang, tā chuānzhe kǒnglóng fú shàng tái bō suì, quán chǎng dōu xiào fēng le, tài huì zhěng huó le.
example_translation: At graduation he went up to have his tassel turned wearing a dinosaur costume — the whole hall was in stitches. What a showman.
context: From north-eastern (东北) speech, where 整 is an all-purpose verb ('do, make, get'). North-eastern short-video and livestream creators would announce '给大家整个活儿!' ('let me do a little act for you all!') before a stunt; it spread across Kuaishou, Douyin and Bilibili as the standard label for anything done for laughs. Commenters now praise creators with '会整活' and groan at stale bits with '整活失败'.

meaning: 'Miles ahead' — originally Huawei's boast, now used half-proudly, half-mockingly to hype anything as unbeatable, or to tease over-the-top marketing claims.
meaning_zh: 原为华为余承东在发布会上的口头禅，形容产品远超同行；网友借来既表达对国产科技的自豪，也用来调侃夸张的宣传话术，或戏称任何东西“遥遥领先”。
example: 我这次期末成绩在宿舍里遥遥领先——毕竟其他人都挂科了。
example_pinyin: Wǒ zhè cì qīmò chéngjì zài sùshè lǐ yáoyáo lǐngxiān — bìjìng qítā rén dōu guà kē le.
example_translation: My exam results were miles ahead of everyone in the dorm — mind you, everyone else failed.
context: Huawei executive Richard Yu (余承东) used 遥遥领先 repeatedly at the Mate 40 launch in October 2020 to describe how far Huawei's phones led rivals, and kept repeating it at later launches. When Huawei opened its Mate 60 Pro 'pioneer programme' in August 2023, netizens seized on the phrase — part pride in domestic tech, part parody of launch-event bluster. It made 《语言文字周报》's ten internet buzzwords of 2023 and is still the default jokey caption for any bold 'we're the best' claim.

meaning: Playing the zither to an ox — wasting your words on someone who can't or won't understand; also used to criticise a speaker for not considering their audience.
meaning_zh: 比喻对不懂道理的人讲道理、对不懂风雅的人谈风雅，白费口舌；也用来讥讽说话不看对象。
example: 跟杠精讲逻辑，简直是对牛弹琴。
example_pinyin: Gēn gàngjīng jiǎng luójí, jiǎnzhí shì duì niú tán qín.
example_translation: Trying to reason with a troll is like playing the zither to an ox.
context: From the Han-dynasty 《理惑论》 attributed to 牟融: the musician 公明仪 played a refined tune to an ox, which kept grazing; only when he imitated mosquitoes and a calf's lowing did it prick up its ears. The original moral was arguably about adapting to your audience, but today it's mostly a put-down. Online it's a staple of comment-section fights, where people sign off from pointless arguments with '不跟你对牛弹琴了', and it pairs naturally with deck words like 杠精 and 已读乱回.

sources.note: 百度百科：对牛弹琴（汉语成语）
汉典：对牛弹琴 词语解释

meaning: To grip someone's attention so completely they can't look away or move on — usually said of a song, a video, a face or a snack that has you hooked ('I got hard-controlled by this for an hour'). Can also mean to dominate a situation.
meaning_zh: 原指游戏中让对方角色无法操作的强制控制效果，现泛指某事物对人有极强的吸引力，让人移不开视线、停不下来，常用被动式“被……硬控了”；也可表示主导、掌控某个局面。
example: 这首歌把我硬控了一整个下午，单曲循环停不下来。
example_pinyin: Zhè shǒu gē bǎ wǒ yìng kòng le yī zhěng gè xiàwǔ, dānqǔ xúnhuán tíng bù xiàlái.
example_translation: This song had me completely hooked all afternoon — I couldn't stop putting it on repeat.
context: Gamer jargon from MOBA titles like League of Legends and Honor of Kings (王者荣耀), where 'hard control' means stuns, freezes and knock-ups that leave your opponent's character unable to act. In 2024 it broke out of gaming into everyday chat: people were '硬控' by short dramas, cute pets, a dish, an athlete. It made 《咬文嚼字》's 2024 Top Ten Buzzwords and even placed fifth in a ranking of Taiwan's top ten internet buzzwords of 2024 compiled by 網路溫度計 (DailyView) — a classic example of game slang crossing over.

meaning: When someone you admired — originally a celebrity idol — is exposed by a scandal and their image collapses. Fans say their idol has 'collapsed the house'; now applied to any streamer, brand or public figure whose reputation caves in.
meaning_zh: 比喻偶像因负面新闻、丑闻或隐瞒恋情等被曝光，在粉丝心中的美好形象轰然倒塌；后扩展到网红、主播、品牌等任何口碑突然崩塌的人或事物。
example: 我追了五年的爱豆昨晚塌房了，我直接脱粉。
example_pinyin: Wǒ zhuī le wǔ nián de àidòu zuówǎn tā fáng le, wǒ zhíjiē tuō fěn.
example_translation: The idol I'd followed for five years had a scandal blow up last night — I've quit the fandom on the spot.
context: Fan-circle (饭圈) slang that became ubiquitous in the early 2020s, as one 'gentle, devoted' male star after another was brought down by scandal — fans list pianist Li Yundi, Kris Wu (吴亦凡), actor Li Yifeng (detained by police in September 2022) and, in 2023, Cai Xukun. Fans picture their idol as a 'house' (房子) they've built their devotion in; when it collapses, the fan is left in the rubble. It has since spread well beyond idols to influencers and brands.

sources.note: 百度百科：塌房（网络流行语）词条
The World of Chinese: Netizen takes on fallen celebs (塌房 after Li Yifeng's detention, Sept 2022)

literal: little kid + big brother / big sister
meaning: A kid with skills or composure way beyond their years — the child who out-plays, out-performs or out-cools the adults. Respectful and affectionate: calling a child 'big brother/sister' acknowledges they've earned it.
meaning_zh: 指在某方面拥有过人本领或超强心理素质的孩子。用“哥”“姐”称呼小孩，带有佩服和调侃意味，表示对方虽年纪小，实力却让大人自愧不如。
example: 这个小孩姐打乒乓球比我们全办公室的人都厉害。
example_pinyin: Zhège xiǎohái jiě dǎ pīngpāngqiú bǐ wǒmen quán bàngōngshì de rén dōu lìhai.
example_translation: This little girl plays table tennis better than our entire office put together.
context: Spread through Douyin clips of children doing remarkable things, then exploded during the 2024 Paris Olympics, when China's very young athletes performed with startling poise — 《咬文嚼字》 cited an 11-year-old building 'rockets' and a 14-year-old girl setting an Olympic record. 《咬文嚼字》 put it in its 2024 Top Ten Buzzwords. It's productive: any precocious child can be a 小孩哥, from a chess prodigy to a kid who calmly handles a crisis.

sources.note: 新华网：《咬文嚼字》2024年十大流行语，“小孩哥/小孩姐”入选
北京日报：《咬文嚼字》主编黄安靖谈2024年十大流行语

literal: cut off a stanza, take the meaning
meaning: To quote out of context — pluck a line from what someone said and twist it to mean something they didn't. A go-to accusation in online arguments.
meaning_zh: 不顾全篇文章或谈话的完整内容，孤立地截取其中一段一句来理解或引用，使意思与原意不符。网上常用来指责别人截图、剪辑或片面引用，歪曲原意。
example: 你只截了半句话就开骂，这不是断章取义吗？
example_pinyin: Nǐ zhǐ jié le bàn jù huà jiù kāi mà, zhè bú shì duàn zhāng qǔ yì ma?
example_translation: You screenshotted half a sentence and started ranting — isn't that taking it out of context?
context: From the 《左传·襄公二十八年》: in the State of Qi, the official 卢蒲癸 married a woman of his own clan, which custom forbade. Challenged, he shrugged it off with 'when people recite the Odes they cut out a stanza (赋诗断章) and take what suits them' — openly admitting to cherry-picking. Today it's everywhere in comment sections, alongside 截图党 and 恶意剪辑: whenever a celebrity's interview clip or a netizen's post goes viral stripped of its context, someone will reply 断章取义.

sources.note: 百度百科：断章取义（汉语成语）
汉典：“断章取义”释义及出处

literal: chicken(-blood) + kid — short for 给娃打鸡血, 'inject the kid with chicken blood'
meaning: To push a child relentlessly — cramming them with tutoring, extra classes and competitions to get ahead; also the hothoused child or the parenting style itself. Can be a verb (鸡娃), a noun (鸡娃家长, 'tiger parents') and is usually wry or critical.
meaning_zh: 指父母给孩子“打鸡血”，不停地给孩子安排补习班、兴趣班和竞赛，逼孩子拼命学习、超前培养的教育方式；也可指被这样培养的孩子。多带调侃或批评色彩。
example: 隔壁三岁就开始学奥数了，这也太鸡娃了吧。
example_pinyin: Gébì sān suì jiù kāishǐ xué àoshù le, zhè yě tài jīwá le ba.
example_translation: The kid next door started Olympiad maths at three — talk about hothousing.
context: From 打鸡血 ('to inject chicken blood'), a slang phrase for getting someone hyped up, itself from a discredited 1960s health fad. Parents who 'inject' their kids became 鸡娃, with a pun on 激娃 ('stir up the kid'). It grew out of Beijing parenting forums — the archetype is the 海淀妈妈, the highly educated Haidian-district mum running a military-grade tutoring schedule — and went mainstream in 2021 with the TV drama 《小舍得》 and the national 'double reduction' (双减) crackdown on private tutoring. 《咬文嚼字》 named it one of 2021's top ten buzzwords, alongside 躺平 and 破防. It spawned 鸡娃群 (parent chat groups swapping tips), 牛蛙 (the high-achieving kid) and its opposite 佛系养娃.
