meaning: Someone who stays clear-eyed and grounded in a world of hype and temptation — not swept away by fame, romance or flattery, knows exactly what they want. Mostly high praise (a celebrity's level-headed interview answer, a friend's no-nonsense take on a bad relationship), sometimes self-applied with a wink.
meaning_zh: 形容面对纷繁复杂、充满诱惑的世界，始终保持清醒理性、不迷失自我、清楚自己定位的人或态度。多用于称赞，例如明星采访里的冷静发言、朋友对感情问题的理性看法，也可用来自嘲或自夸。
example: 她说“男人靠不住，搞钱最重要”，真是人间清醒。
example_pinyin: Tā shuō “nánrén kào bú zhù, gǎo qián zuì zhòngyào”, zhēn shì rénjiān qīngxǐng.
context: Took off around 2020–21 in entertainment commentary, where fans and media used it to praise stars whose interviews showed they hadn't let fame go to their heads; by August 2021 Shenzhen Daily was explaining it to English-language readers. It quickly spread to 'clear-headed' heroines in dramas, 情感 advice posts and everyday life: a 人间清醒 friend is the one who tells you to dump him. Often used as a label — 人间清醒语录 ('sayings of the clear-headed'), 人间清醒女孩 — and is a staple of 小红书 and Weibo captions.
example_translation: She said 'men are unreliable, making money is what matters' — so clear-headed.

sources.note: 百度百科「人间清醒」：网络流行词，指面对纷繁世界保持清醒的处世态度
知乎问题「什么是人间清醒？」
Shenzhen Daily 'Catch Phrase': 人间清醒 (2021-08-31)

meaning: Digital comfort content that soothes your mood the way a painkiller soothes a headache — cute animal clips, Chiikawa memes, a favourite variety show, a song on loop. Said of whatever you reach for to get through a bad day: 'this is my 电子布洛芬'.
meaning_zh: 比喻能缓解精神压力、治愈坏情绪的数字内容，如萌宠视频、二次元表情包、综艺片段、歌曲等，作用就像布洛芬止痛一样。常说“这是我的电子布洛芬”。
example: 上班太累了，回家刷了半小时小猫视频，电子布洛芬起效了。
example_pinyin: Shàngbān tài lèi le, huí jiā shuā le bàn xiǎoshí xiǎomāo shìpín, diànzǐ bùluòfēn qǐxiào le.
example_translation: Work was exhausting; half an hour of kitten videos at home and the digital painkiller kicked in.
context: Emerged around late 2022–2023 — ibuprofen (布洛芬) was a household word in China after the December 2022 COVID wave emptied pharmacy shelves of it. Fitting the 电子X pattern (电子榨菜, 电子宠物), it named the screen-based things young people use to self-soothe. It exploded in 2024 when the Japanese manga 《Chiikawa》 (吉伊卡哇) went viral in China and fans called its small, put-upon characters their 电子布洛芬; media such as 澎湃新闻 and 青年记者 have since written it up as a lens on youth stress and 'healing' culture. It still appears on 2026 lists of emotional-self-care buzzwords.

sources.note: 百度百科「电子布洛芬」：网络流行语，指用于缓解心理压力的数字内容
澎湃新闻·思想市场：年轻人在表情包中寻找“电子布洛芬”

literal: one word + hard to + exhaust — 'one sentence can't cover it'
meaning: It's a long (and not happy) story; too complicated or awkward to sum up. Online it has become a polite-but-damning verdict: calling a film, a meal or someone's outfit 一言难尽 means 'it was bad, and I'd rather not elaborate'.
meaning_zh: 形容事情曲折复杂，不是一句话能说清楚的，多用于不愉快的事。网络上常用作委婉的差评：说一部剧、一顿饭或某人的穿搭“一言难尽”，意思是“很糟糕，懒得细说”。
example: 这部剧的结局……怎么说呢，一言难尽。
example_pinyin: Zhè bù jù de jiéjú…… zěnme shuō ne, yī yán nán jìn.
example_translation: The ending of this show… how to put it — words fail me.
context: A classic idiom found in Yuan-dynasty drama — 李直夫's zaju 《虎头牌》 has a character sigh 我一言难尽 — and has always been used for troubles too tangled to explain. On Weibo, Douban and 小红书 it has taken on a sharper edge as the go-to diplomatic put-down: reviews titled 一言难尽, 'the acting was 一言难尽', often with a pause or ellipsis for comic effect. It works because it lets the reader fill in how bad it was.

literal: 爷 (this old man / me) + 青 (youth) + 回 (returns) — short for 爷的青春回来了
meaning: 'My youth is back!' — a burst of nostalgic delight when something from your childhood or teens returns: a classic cartoon reboot, an old band reuniting, a retired player back on stage. Its mirror image is 爷青结 ('my youth is over'), said when something beloved ends or shuts down.
meaning_zh: “爷的青春回来了”的缩写。看到童年或青春时期熟悉的人、动画、游戏、影视剧等重新回归或复出时，表达惊喜与怀旧之情。反义说法是“爷青结”（爷的青春结束了），用于心爱的事物落幕、停更或关停时。
example: 《喜羊羊》出新电影了？爷青回！
example_pinyin: 《Xǐ Yángyáng》 chū xīn diànyǐng le? Yé qīng huí!
example_translation: There's a new Pleasant Goat film? My childhood is back!
context: Its exact origin is disputed: it is usually linked to the LPL (League of Legends Pro League) esports fandom via its mirror image 爷青结, though some credit Bilibili anime comments. The cocky 爷 ('grandpa', used as a swaggering 'me') gives it a jokey tone. In 2020 it showed up more than five million times in Bilibili bullet comments and was named that year's most popular danmaku. It's still the standard bullet-comment reaction whenever a 90s/00s favourite comes back, and 爷青结 is what people post when one ends.

literal: 双 (double) + 标 (standard) — short for 双重标准
meaning: Double standards — judging the same kind of behaviour differently depending on who does it, especially being strict with others and lenient with yourself (or your side). Used as an accusation: '你好双标' ('you're such a hypocrite'). Someone who does it all the time gets called 双标狗.
meaning_zh: “双重标准”的缩写。对同一性质的事情用不同的标准评判，尤指对别人严、对自己宽，或对自己喜欢的一方宽容、对另一方苛刻。常用于批评，如“你好双标”；经常这样的人被调侃为“双标狗”。
example: 你迟到就是堵车，我迟到就是不重视你？太双标了吧。
example_pinyin: Nǐ chídào jiù shì dǔchē, wǒ chídào jiù shì bù zhòngshì nǐ? Tài shuāngbiāo le ba.
example_translation: When you're late it's the traffic, but when I'm late it means I don't care about you? That's such a double standard.
context: A plain clipping of 双重标准 that became one of the internet's go-to accusations. It's all over comment sections, couple arguments, fan wars (fans excusing their idol for things they'd slam a rival for), and online nationalism debates about foreign media. China Daily included it in its 一课译词 vocabulary series as 'double standard', and it's now fully mainstream. It's short and accusatory, so people fire it off as a one-word comeback.

sources.note: China Daily 一课译词：双标 (double standard)

meaning: To hustle for money, to get the bag. Young people use it openly and with self-mocking pride as a life motto ('搞钱要紧' 'making money comes first'), covering anything from the day job to side hustles, street stalls and online shops. It's less about greed than about money as the one thing that reliably eases anxiety.
meaning_zh: 想方设法赚钱。年轻人公开、带点自嘲地把“搞钱”当人生信条（如“搞钱要紧”“只想搞钱”），包括本职工作、副业、摆摊、开网店等。重点不在拜金，而在于把存款增长当作缓解焦虑、获得掌控感的方式。
example: 恋爱先放一放，今年的目标只有一个：搞钱。
example_pinyin: Liàn'ài xiān fàng yī fàng, jīnnián de mùbiāo zhǐ yǒu yī gè: gǎo qián.
example_translation: Romance can wait. This year I've only got one goal: making money.
context: 搞 is the all-purpose Chinese verb for 'get it done', and paired with 钱 it became a slogan for a generation that publicly talks 躺平 but privately grinds. It took off from the late 2010s, with '搞钱女孩' and '搞钱使我快乐' trending on Weibo and Xiaohongshu. Brands and media (SocialBeta, 数英) have run whole features on 'where this generation 搞钱'. It's often paired with 恋爱脑 jokes: 'a man only slows down how fast I make money.'

sources.note: SocialBeta：这届年轻人，到底在哪里搞钱？
数英：这届年轻人都在哪里搞钱？
虎嗅：搞钱至上？

literal: 社(交) social + 牛(逼症) 'awesome-itis' — short for 社交牛逼症
meaning: Someone with zero social fear — happy to chat to strangers, perform in public or do embarrassing things without a flicker of shame. The cheeky opposite of 社恐 (social anxiety). Said with a mix of admiration and teasing, and often used self-mockingly ('I'm 社恐 at work but 社牛 with my friends').
meaning_zh: “社交牛逼症”的简称，指在社交场合毫无心理压力、敢于和陌生人搭话、在公共场合放飞自我的人或状态，与“社恐”相对。语气里既有羡慕也有调侃，也常用来自嘲。时而社恐时而社牛的人则被称为“社交牛杂症”。
example: 他在地铁上跟陌生人合唱，真是社牛本牛。
example_pinyin: Tā zài dìtiě shang gēn mòshēngrén héchàng, zhēn shì shè niú běn niú.
example_translation: He sang a duet with a stranger on the underground — a social daredevil if ever there was one.
context: 社交牛逼症 took off in summer 2021 as the mirror image of 社恐 (social phobia). Its comic poster boy was the veteran internet prankster 焦双喜 ('双喜哥', whose skits star a character called 马牛逼), famous for stunts like lecturing a man for farting on the underground or dancing in an alien costume outside a top university, all with total composure. Clipped to 社牛 it became everyday vocabulary, spawning 社交牛杂症 for people who flip between the two, and it now sits alongside i人/e人 in how young Chinese talk about their social batteries. Xinhua even ran a piece on the 社恐/社牛/牛杂症 vocabulary in October 2021.

sources.note: 百度百科：社交牛逼症（网络流行语）词条，含来源与释义
新华网：《“社恐”“天花板”“牛杂症”……社交名词这么多，终极奥秘是什么》
数英：“社交牛逼症”源于古早网红焦双喜（双喜哥），马牛逼为其视频主人公

literal: 拿 take hold + 捏 pinch — to have something pinched between your fingers
meaning: To have someone or something completely under control; to nail it effortlessly. You can 拿捏 a task (totally sorted), a skill ('XX这块拿捏得死死的' — I've got XX absolutely nailed) or a person (have them wrapped round your little finger). Brims with confident, slightly smug energy, and often comes with a pinching-fingers gesture or sticker.
meaning_zh: 原义为把握、掌握分寸，网络流行义为“完全掌控、轻松搞定”。可以拿捏事（某事稳了），也可以拿捏人（把某人吃得死死的）。常见句式“XX这块拿捏得死死的”“拿捏了”，常配一个捏手指的手势表情包，带着自信甚至得意的语气。
example: 期末考试？这次我拿捏了。
example_pinyin: Qīmò kǎoshì? Zhè cì wǒ ná niē le.
example_translation: End-of-term exams? I've got this one nailed.
context: An ordinary verb ('to judge, get the measure of') that went viral around 2021–22, helped along by a pinching-gesture meme and the phrase 拿捏得死死的. It became productive — people 拿捏 their bosses, their pets, their diets — and was named one of 《咬文嚼字》's top ten buzzwords of 2022, alongside 雪糕刺客. Linguists have since written papers on its 'semantic generalisation', a good sign it's here to stay.

sources.note: 南方网：《咬文嚼字》发布2022十大流行语，拿捏、雪糕刺客等入选
汉斯出版社论文：《“拿捏”的语义泛化及流行研究》
腾讯新闻·观观有梗：拿捏

literal: 干 do / knock back + 饭 rice, a meal + 人 person
meaning: A self-styled devoted eater — someone for whom mealtimes are the highlight of the day and who attacks food with gusto. Mostly self-deprecating: 'useless at everything, first in line for lunch'. 干饭 on its own means simply to eat (with enthusiasm), as in 干饭了！ 'grub's up!'.
meaning_zh: 指奋力吃饭、把吃饭当头等大事的人，多为自嘲，意思接近“干啥啥不行，干饭第一名”。“干饭”本身即“吃饭”，带着一口气吃完的豪爽劲儿，常见“干饭了！”“干饭人，干饭魂，干饭都是人上人”。
example: 十二点一到，办公室的干饭人全都冲向食堂了。
example_pinyin: Shí'èr diǎn yí dào, bàngōngshì de gàn fàn rén quán dōu chōng xiàng shítáng le.
example_translation: The moment it hit twelve, every food-lover in the office stampeded to the canteen.
context: 干饭 is Sichuan–Chongqing dialect for eating, with a 'down it in one' heartiness. In late 2020 a rustic Douyin creator (诗书达礼之山人) went viral by opening every clip with '干饭了，干饭了！', holding up his bowl while his chickens pecked at it. Coined on the same pattern as 打工人 and 工具人, 干饭人 spread everywhere — 干饭人，干饭魂 became a slogan, brands and even companies registered the name — and it has settled into ordinary chat as a jokey way to say you live for your next meal.

sources.note: 百度百科：干饭人（网络流行语）词条
21英语网：“干饭人”的梗是怎么来的
网易：网络热词“干饭人”被注册成公司，起源如何

meaning: Someone who plays dirty or unexpectedly: a sneaky player who lurks in odd corners to ambush others. Off the gaming server, it means anyone who doesn't play by the rules, pulls a fast one, or is quietly scheming. Often used teasingly between friends.
meaning_zh: 原指游戏里不跟队友正面作战、专躲在暗处偷袭的玩家；引申为不按套路出牌、暗中使坏或搞小动作的人，朋友间常带调侃意味。
example: 说好一起减肥，你半夜偷偷点炸鸡，真是个老六！
example_pinyin: Shuō hǎo yìqǐ jiǎnféi, nǐ bànyè tōutōu diǎn zhájī, zhēn shì gè lǎo liù!
example_translation: We agreed to diet together and you secretly ordered fried chicken at midnight. You sneaky so-and-so!
context: Usually traced to Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, where 老六 was the player who split off from the team to lurk in odd corners and ambush opponents (why 'six' is disputed). It spread to every online shooter as a label for sneaky ambushers, then broke out of gaming entirely: '服了你个老六' made 《语言文字周报》's top ten internet buzzwords of 2022. Now it's everyday banter for anyone who blindsides you, cheats on a group agreement, or schemes behind the scenes. The phrase '你个老六' is half insult, half grudging respect.

sources.note: 萌娘百科「老六」词条：源自CSGO自由人战术，后泛指偷袭、不按套路的人
澎湃新闻：《语言文字周报》2022年十大网络流行语，含“服了你个老六”

meaning: A lingering sense of regret or heartache you can't let go of. Most often used about a drama, novel or game whose ending denied a character or couple their happy outcome, and also about missed chances in real life. It can be a noun ('my 意难平', the character/plot I can't get over) or a verb phrase ('I'm still 意难平').
meaning_zh: 心里的遗憾或不甘久久难以平复。多用于影视剧、小说、游戏中结局不圆满、让人放不下的角色或剧情，也可指现实中的错过与遗憾；既可作名词（"我的意难平"），也可作谓语。
example: 这部剧男女主最后没在一起，成了我这辈子的意难平。
example_pinyin: Zhè bù jù nánnǚzhǔ zuìhòu méi zài yìqǐ, chéngle wǒ zhè bèizi de yì nán píng.
example_translation: The two leads in this drama never ended up together. I'll never get over it.
context: The phrase comes from 《红楼梦》: the song 《终身误》 has Baoyu, married to Baochai while still pining for Daiyu, sigh 纵然是举案齐眉，到底意难平 ('even if we treat each other with perfect courtesy, my heart can't be at peace'). Fandoms on Weibo, Douban and Bilibili picked it up in the late 2010s to tag tragic endings, dead favourites and 'BE' (bad-ending) couples. Its mournful literary flavour made it stick: it now appears in mainstream entertainment coverage and drifts into real life for the one that got away or the exam you narrowly failed. A favourite character is often lovingly called 'my 意难平'.

sources.note: 搜狐：到底意难平——《红楼梦》《终身误》“纵然是举案齐眉，到底意难平”出处
网易：女生说“意难平”，是什么意思？（含义与用法）
腾讯新闻·大众日报：那些意难平的BE美学（影视结局遗憾）

meaning: When someone's own past words or actions come back to hit them. Think of an old post resurfacing to contradict them, or criticism they once dished out now applying to themselves. Netizens use it for the ironic 'what goes around comes around' moment, often in the set phrase 回旋镖正中眉心 ('the boomerang hit square between the eyes').
meaning_zh: 比喻一个人过去说过的话、做过的事最终反过来打在自己身上，前后对比形成讽刺，类似"自作自受""打脸"。常说"回旋镖正中眉心"。
example: 他去年还嘲笑别人买房被套，今年自己也被套了——回旋镖正中眉心。
example_pinyin: Tā qùnián hái cháoxiào biérén mǎi fáng bèi tào, jīnnián zìjǐ yě bèi tào le — huíxuánbiāo zhèng zhòng méixīn.
example_translation: Last year he mocked people for getting stuck with property they couldn't sell; this year it's happened to him. The boomerang hit him right between the eyes.
context: The image is simple: you throw it, and it flies back at you. It took off on Weibo and Bilibili around 2022–23 as netizens dug up celebrities', influencers' and officials' old statements that clashed with what they were saying or doing now. It also gets used for hypocrisy (double standards that eventually bite back). It's productive: you can 'throw a boomerang at yourself' (给自己扔回旋镖), and it's widely used outside its original pile-on context, including self-deprecatingly.

sources.note: 萌娘百科「回旋镖」词条：网络用语中指言行最终返落到自己身上

meaning: The very best, the upper limit of a category: 'the GOAT', 'top tier'. Attached to a field to crown its best example: 颜值天花板 (peak good looks), 演技天花板 (the best acting there is), 国产剧天花板 (the best Chinese drama). It's so common in sales patter that regulators treat it as a borderline superlative.
meaning_zh: 比喻某一领域的最高水平、顶配，相当于"天花板级别、无人能超越"。常见搭配如"颜值天花板""演技天花板""国产剧天花板"。
example: 这家店的小笼包绝对是上海小笼包的天花板。
example_pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn de xiǎolóngbāo juéduì shì Shànghǎi xiǎolóngbāo de tiānhuābǎn.
example_translation: This place's xiaolongbao are hands-down the best in Shanghai.
context: The word normally just means a room's ceiling, and its older figurative sense was a limit you can't break through, as in the glass ceiling. Online the image flipped: the ceiling is the highest point anything can reach, so the best thing in a category *is* the ceiling. It exploded across Weibo, Douyin and fan culture, is fully productive with any noun ('X天花板'), and 《咬文嚼字》 put it on its 2022 top ten buzzwords. It's so common in hype copy that a livestreamer was fined for calling a product the 天花板 and 扛把子 of its category; regulators said no rule bans the word outright but called it a borderline (擦边球) superlative.

sources.note: Moya Chinese dictionary — 天花板: ceiling; slang for 'the best in a field'

南方网：《咬文嚼字》发布2022十大流行语，“天花板”入选

meaning: 'Corporate livestock' — a self-mocking label for an overworked office worker who obeys the boss and has no life outside the job.
meaning_zh: 由日语「会社」和「家畜」组合而成，指像家畜一样被公司驱使、加班成常态、毫无个人生活的上班族，多用于自嘲。
example: 今天又加班到十点，社畜的命就是这样。
example_pinyin: Jīntiān yòu jiābān dào shí diǎn, shèchù de mìng jiù shì zhèyàng.
example_translation: Overtime till ten again today — that's the life of a corporate drone.
context: Borrowed from Japanese 社畜 (shachiku), which got a big boost from the 2018 Japanese drama 《无法成为野兽的我们》 with its downtrodden office-worker heroine. It landed in China the same period as the backlash against the 996 work schedule, and white-collar workers adopted it as a wry self-description. Calling yourself livestock is an insult turned into self-deprecation; it is an older sibling of 打工人 and 牛马, and remains in everyday use.

sources.note: Sixth Tone — young Chinese bemoan the rat race with memes, explains 社畜
The World of Chinese, Street Talk 'Cattle Class' on 社畜

meaning: A sarcastic 'thanks a lot' that means 'I'm speechless / fed up'; used to complain about something absurd or annoying without swearing.
meaning_zh: 表面是「会感谢你」，实则阴阳怪气地表达无语和不满，是「我TM谢谢你」的不带脏字版；「谢」还双关「凋谢」，形容被离谱的事弄得像花一样枯萎。
example: 刚到楼下外卖就被人拿走了，我真的会谢。
example_pinyin: Gāng dào lóu xià wàimài jiù bèi rén ná zǒu le, wǒ zhēn de huì xiè.
example_translation: Someone nicked my takeaway the second it arrived downstairs — honestly, thanks a lot.
context: A clean, no-swearing offshoot of 我TM谢谢你 that spread on 小红书 and then across platforms. 《语言文字周报》 listed '栓Q（我真的会谢）' among its 2022 top ten internet buzzwords, putting it in the same family as 栓Q: 'thanks' that isn't thanks at all. The pun on 谢 (to wither, as in 花谢了) adds the image of someone wilting from sheer exasperation.

sources.note: 萌娘百科「我TM谢谢你」词条，含「我真的会谢」变体与出处
澎湃新闻：《语言文字周报》2022年十大网络流行语，含“栓Q（我真的会谢）”

meaning: 'Guys, can anyone relate?!' — an opener used to rant or share something outrageous, inviting fellow netizens to commiserate.
meaning_zh: 网络上的吐槽开场白，把能理解自己的网友称为「家人」，用来分享离谱遭遇或只有同道中人才懂的感受，寻求共鸣。
example: 家人们谁懂啊，开会开了三个小时，最后说下次再议。
example_pinyin: Jiārénmen shéi dǒng a, kāihuì kāi le sān gè xiǎoshí, zuìhòu shuō xià cì zài yì.
example_translation: Guys, can anyone relate? A three-hour meeting, and at the end they said 'let's discuss it next time'.
context: 家人们 ('family') became the standard way livestreamers and short-video creators address their audience, and the logic stuck: whoever gets me is family. 家人们谁懂啊 grew into a ubiquitous opener on Douyin, 小红书 and Bilibili for venting about a bad date, a nightmare colleague, or anything only like-minded people would understand. It is formulaic enough that brands now borrow it in marketing (Bilibili built a campaign around the 'people who get you are family' idea).

sources.note: 数英网 — B站营销案例，引用「家人们，谁懂啊？」及「懂我的人就是家人」的逻辑

meaning: To have exhausted one's limited bag of tricks, exposing how little was there; said of someone who has run out of moves.
meaning_zh: 比喻仅有的一点本领已经用完，再也无计可施，露出了虚弱的本质，含贬义。
example: 他又开始翻旧账了，看来是黔驴技穷了。
example_pinyin: Tā yòu kāishǐ fān jiùzhàng le, kànlái shì qián lǘ jì qióng le.
example_translation: He's dragging up old grudges again — looks like he's run out of tricks.
context: From Tang writer 柳宗元's fable 《三戒·黔之驴》: there were no donkeys in Guizhou (黔) until someone brought one in. A tiger, awed by its size, at first thought it divine, but after seeing that all it could do was bray and kick, pounced and ate it. Online it's a staple of comment-section put-downs: when an opponent in an argument, a scammer, or a show's writers recycle the same moves, netizens declare them 黔驴技穷.

sources.note: 汉典「黔驴技穷」词条，释义与出处
维基文库 柳宗元《三戒（并序）》原文

literal: 普 ordinary + 信 confident + 男 man
meaning: 'Ordinary yet confident man' — a man with unremarkable looks, talent or prospects who is nonetheless supremely sure of himself, especially around women (mistaking politeness for interest, lecturing, belittling others). Short form 普信 can describe anyone with unearned self-assurance.
meaning_zh: “普通却自信的男人”的缩写，指条件平平却对自己有谜之自信的男性，常把别人的客气当成好感、喜欢居高临下。“普信”也可单用，泛指盲目自信的人。
example: 他连约会都迟到，还觉得女生都暗恋他，真是普信男。
example_pinyin: Tā lián yuēhuì dōu chídào, hái juéde nǚshēng dōu ànliàn tā, zhēn shì pǔxìnnán.
example_translation: He turns up late even to dates and still thinks every woman secretly fancies him — a proper ordinary-but-confident guy.
context: Coined from stand-up comedian 杨笠 (Yang Li)'s 2020 joke on 《脱口秀大会》 that some men are 'so ordinary, yet so confident' (那么普通，却那么自信). The Weibo topic racked up hundreds of millions of reads and sparked a gender-war backlash, with boycotts of brands she worked with (Intel, and JD.com in 2024), and the abbreviation 普信 stuck as a durable label in Chinese gender discourse. Still used productively (普信女, 普信发言) — and still divisive, so mind the company you use it in.

sources.note: Duke Intersections — 'Ordinary But Confident': Cultural Collisions Over Gender and Ambition
Marie Claire 台湾版 — 普信男特征盘点
虎嗅：京东与杨笠合作风波（2024），此前英特尔等品牌也曾遭抵制

literal: 大 big + 冤 wronged / hard done by + 种 breed, type
meaning: A total mug — someone who gets ripped off, takes the fall, or does something daft and ends up the loser. Used far more for self-mockery ('纯纯大冤种', 'utter mug') than as a real insult.
meaning_zh: 源自东北话，指吃了亏、被坑、做了傻事还白费力气的人，常用来自嘲或调侃朋友，如“我真是纯纯大冤种”。
example: 原价买完第二天就打五折，我真是纯纯大冤种。
example_pinyin: Yuánjià mǎi wán dì-èr tiān jiù dǎ wǔ zhé, wǒ zhēn shì chúnchún dà yuānzhǒng.
example_translation: I paid full price and the next day it was half off — I'm an absolute mug.
context: Northeastern (东北) dialect that Dongbei vloggers on Douyin and Kuaishou carried into national slang around 2021–22. It made 《语言文字周报》's ten top internet buzzwords of 2022 and has stayed in everyday use — the go-to word for overpaying, being the one who always pays, or getting played. 纯纯 ('pure, through-and-through') is its usual intensifier.

sources.note: The China Project — China's top internet buzzwords of 2022
澎湃新闻 — 2022年十大网络流行语报道（含“冤种”）

literal: 爹 dad + 味 flavour, whiff
meaning: Patronising 'dad energy' — talking down to people, handing out unsolicited advice and 'correct answers', and expecting obedience. Harsher than plain 说教 (preaching): it implies control and condescension, not good intentions. No longer restricted to men.
meaning_zh: 形容一个人像家长一样居高临下、爱说教、好为人师，不管别人需不需要就给“最优解”，还不容反驳。比“说教”更贬义，男女都可以“爹味”很重。
example: 我就随口说了句累，他给我讲了半小时时间管理，爹味太重了。
example_pinyin: Wǒ jiù suíkǒu shuō le jù lèi, tā gěi wǒ jiǎng le bàn xiǎoshí shíjiān guǎnlǐ, diēwèi tài zhòng le.
example_translation: I only mentioned I was tired and he gave me a half-hour lecture on time management — the dad energy was unbearable.
context: Spread on Weibo and Douban from around 2020 alongside debates about patriarchal attitudes, much like English 'mansplaining' (which it overlaps with but isn't identical to). It's productive — 爹味发言, 爹味文案, 去爹味 — and has recently merged with 老登 talk into 登味, the same know-it-all superiority pinned on the older generation.

sources.note: 虎嗅 — 关于“爹味”与说教区别的评论文章
澎湃新闻 — 评论“爹味”与“老登”“登味”合流

literal: 老 old + 登 (from 登徒子, lecher)
meaning: 'Old geezer' — originally a rude Dongbei word for an old man (with a lecherous edge), now a jokey label for the older generation and anyone self-important, preachy or pulling rank. Spawned a whole age ladder: 老登 / 中登 (the generation in between; definitions vary) / 小登 (00s kids), often used self-deprecatingly. Can also be affectionate between friends.
meaning_zh: 源自东北方言，原是骂老年男性“老家伙、老不正经”的粗话；走红后泛指上一代人或倚老卖老、好为人师的人，还衍生出“中登”“小登”等辈分梗，多用于调侃和自嘲，熟人间也可当昵称。
example: 我才二十六，就被00后同事叫中登了。
example_pinyin: Wǒ cái èrshíliù, jiù bèi líng-líng-hòu tóngshì jiào zhōngdēng le.
example_translation: I'm only twenty-six and my Gen-Z colleagues are already calling me a 'middle geezer'.
context: Northeastern dialect for 老家伙 or 老色鬼 ('old so-and-so', 'old lech'). It blew up online in 2024–25: 2024 brought 老登电影 and 老登文学 (films and writing for old geezers), and commentators called 2025 the year of reckoning with 老登 and 登味 (know-it-all old-man energy). By 2025–26 the 老登/中登/小登 ladder had become a standard way for young people to mock both their elders and themselves. Mainstream outlets from 星岛 to 澎湃 have covered the trend.

meaning: To fleece ordinary people over and over: the powerful side (big investors, platforms, bosses, scam-sellers) 'harvests' money from the naive masses, who are the 韭菜 'leeks'. Used for stock markets, crypto, paid courses, overpriced products, and employers squeezing staff. Calling yourself 韭菜 is a wry admission that you've been had.
meaning_zh: 比喻强势一方（庄家、机构、平台、商家等）反复从普通人身上收割钱财。“韭菜”指被收割的散户或普通消费者，割了一茬又长一茬。原指股市里大户收割散户，后泛指各种消费陷阱、割韭菜式的课程或骗局，也常用来自嘲“我又被割了”。
example: 这个理财课就是割韭菜的，别买了。
example_pinyin: Zhège lǐcái kè jiù shì gē jiǔcài de, bié mǎi le.
example_translation: That investing course is just there to fleece people — don't buy it.
context: Born in China's stock-market forums: chives regrow quickly after being cut, so retail investors (散户) are 'leeks' who keep flooding back in and getting harvested by institutions as prices swing. Through the crypto booms and the rise of paid 'get rich' courses and influencer products it spread to any situation where the little guy is milked repeatedly, and young workers now say 在公司被割韭菜. Spin-offs include 韭菜 (a sucker) and 收割 (to harvest someone's money).

meaning: 'The more you think about it, the creepier it gets.' Said of something that seems harmless at first glance but turns unsettling when you look closer — a plot detail, a data-privacy revelation, a suspicious coincidence. Also written 细思恐极.
meaning_zh: “仔细想想，极其恐怖”的缩略说法。指某件事乍看平常，细想之后却让人毛骨悚然，常用于评论剧情细节、隐私泄露、巧合等。也写作“细思恐极”。
example: App 早就知道我想买什么了，细思极恐。
example_pinyin: App zǎo jiù zhīdào wǒ xiǎng mǎi shénme le, xì sī jí kǒng.
example_translation: The app already knew what I wanted to buy — creepy when you think about it.
context: One of the four-character 'post-modern chengyu' (后现代成语) that swept Weibo around 2012–2013, when netizens compressed whole phrases into mock-idioms. It appeared on 2013's top internet-buzzword round-ups (as 细思恐极) and, unlike most of its siblings, never went away: it's still a stock comment under true-crime posts, film theories and tech-surveillance stories.

meaning: 'No idea what you're on about, but it sounds impressive.' A teasing-yet-admiring reaction to jargon, technical showing-off or anything over your head. Can be sincere awe or gentle mockery depending on tone.
meaning_zh: “虽然不明白，但觉得很厉害”的缩略。用来回应听不懂的专业术语、技术炫技或高深内容，既可表示真心佩服，也可以带点调侃。
example: 你讲的量子计算我一句没听懂，不明觉厉。
example_pinyin: Nǐ jiǎng de liàngzǐ jìsuàn wǒ yí jù méi tīngdǒng, bù míng jué lì.
example_translation: I didn't follow a word of your quantum-computing talk, but it sounds amazing.
context: Topped China Daily's 2013 list of internet buzzwords, the year of 'post-modern chengyu' like 喜大普奔 and 人艰不拆. Often traced to a line in Stephen Chow's film 《食神》 where a character admits he doesn't understand but finds it impressive. Most of that 2013 batch faded, but 不明觉厉 stuck and is still a go-to comment under coding, maths and science posts on Bilibili and Zhihu.

meaning: To crash and burn: when something goes embarrassingly wrong, especially in public — a live-stream product that fails on camera, a celebrity whose image collapses, a cooking attempt that looks nothing like the tutorial, a confident prediction proven wrong. 翻车现场 is 'the scene of the wreck'.
meaning_zh: 本义是车辆翻倒，网络上引申为事情搞砸、失败或当众出丑，结果与预期相反。常用于直播带货出问题、明星人设崩塌、照着教程做却失败等场景。“翻车现场”指出丑的那一刻。
example: 照着视频做蛋糕，结果翻车了，像一坨泥。
example_pinyin: Zhàozhe shìpín zuò dàngāo, jiéguǒ fānchē le, xiàng yì tuó ní.
example_translation: I followed a video to make a cake and it was a total disaster — it looks like a lump of mud.
context: Grew out of the 老司机 / 发车 ('veteran driver' / 'the bus is leaving') slang of mid-2010s forums, where 发车 meant sharing a resource and 翻车 meant the share failing. It then broadened to any public failure, and the live-commerce boom made 直播翻车 a headline staple — Li Jiaqi's non-stick pan that stuck on air (2019) is the classic example. Now everyday vocabulary, from 人设翻车 to a 'nailed it' DIY fail.

meaning: Self-deprecating way to say you've somehow wandered into a far more elite setting than you belong in — a top university, a big-name company, a room full of experts — and feel like an impostor. Often used after 'making it' to laugh at the gap between the dream and the reality.
meaning_zh: 原指“意外闯入天宫”，现多指偶然进入名校、大厂或专业圈子等门槛很高的场合，自嘲自己格格不入、像混进来的。常用来调侃“上岸”之后理想与现实的落差。
example: 周围全是大佬，我全程不敢说话，纯属误闯天家。
example_pinyin: Zhōuwéi quán shì dàlǎo, wǒ quánchéng bù gǎn shuōhuà, chúnshǔ wù chuǎng tiān jiā.
example_translation: Everyone around me was a big shot — I didn't dare say a word the whole time. I'd basically wandered into heaven by mistake.
context: The phrase first broke out from the lyrics of a 古风 (classical-style) song; short-video remixes spread it and the meaning broadened from literally 'stumbling into the heavenly palace' to any intimidatingly high-level place. The classical imagery dresses up a very modern feeling — impostor syndrome at a prestigious school or job. It was named one of the 2025 'Top Ten Internet Buzzwords' by 《语言文字周报》 (Language & Writing Weekly), a sign it has crossed into the mainstream.

meaning: 'Treat it as a proper matter' — take something seriously. Online it's used for comic contrast: a solemn, formal vow applied to something trivial ('this snack decision must be handled properly'). It has also picked up a sincere, encouraging sense: actually taking your own goals seriously.
meaning_zh: 源自北方方言，意思是“认真对待”。网络上多用夸张郑重的语气回应鸡毛蒜皮的小事，制造反差幽默；后来也衍生出正向激励的用法，表示真正重视某件事、认真去做。
example: 这关系到我周末能不能睡懒觉，必须当个事儿办！
example_pinyin: Zhè guānxì dào wǒ zhōumò néng bù néng shuì lǎnjiào, bìxū dàng ge shìr bàn!
example_translation: This decides whether I get a lie-in at the weekend — it must be treated as a matter of the utmost seriousness!
context: A northern-dialect phrase (note the 儿化 'shìr') that took off in short videos through generational parody — mimicking the grave tone of parents or bosses issuing instructions, then pointing it at something absurdly small. The over-serious register is the joke. It was listed among 《语言文字周报》's 2025 Top Ten Internet Buzzwords.

meaning: A productive pattern: 'group-buy a good X'. From 拼好饭 (Pinduoduo/Meituan-style group-order takeaway that's cheaper because people pool orders), it now covers any thrifty, share-it-to-make-it-work solution — 拼好床 (sharing a bed/room), 拼好票 (buying tickets together), 拼好递 (combining parcels), even 拼好抱 (a shared hug).
meaning_zh: 源于外卖平台的“拼好饭”，即多人拼单以降低价格。后来形成“拼好×”构式，泛指通过拼单、合作、共享来获得高性价比或个性化方案的做法，“好”含有划算、省心的意思，如拼好床、拼好票、拼好递。
example: 演唱会票太贵了，咱们几个拼好票吧。
example_pinyin: Yǎnchànghuì piào tài guì le, zánmen jǐ gè pīn hǎo piào ba.
example_translation: Concert tickets are way too pricey — let's club together and group-buy them.
context: 拼好饭 is a budget takeaway service where orders are pooled to bring prices down — very much part of young Chinese people's everyday frugality (see 消费降级 vibes). Netizens turned it into a template and started 拼好-ing everything from rented beds to emotional support. Because it's a pattern rather than a fixed phrase, it keeps generating new combinations, which is why 《语言文字周报》 put 拼好× on its 2025 Top Ten Internet Buzzwords list.

meaning: A kindred spirit; a friend who truly understands you (知音), or exquisite music. Usually in 高山流水遇知音 — 'meeting the one who understands your music'.
meaning_zh: 比喻知己、知音难得，或形容乐曲高妙。常说“高山流水遇知音”，指遇到真正懂自己的人。
example: 我俩一聊就停不下来，真是高山流水遇知音。
example_pinyin: Wǒ liǎ yì liáo jiù tíng bú xiàlái, zhēn shì gāo shān liú shuǐ yù zhīyīn.
example_translation: Once we start talking we can't stop — a true meeting of kindred spirits.
context: From the pre-Qin tale of the zither player 伯牙 and the woodcutter 钟子期: when Boya played thinking of high mountains, Ziqi heard mountains; when he thought of flowing water, Ziqi heard water. After Ziqi died, Boya smashed his zither, as no one else could understand his music. Netizens in 2026 gave it a famous parody — 低山臭水遇知音 ('low hills and stinking water meet their soulmates') — popularised by viewers of the variety show 《乘风2026》 teasing Wang Meng's chaotic, unpretentious team, and now used for any pair or group of goofballs whose wavelengths match perfectly. Knowing the original is what makes the parody land.

meaning: Netizens' affectionate nickname for the AI model DeepSeek (whose logo is a blue whale), personified as a chubby, blue-haired 'whale girl' who loves rice and slacks off. Full forms: 蓝色大肥鱼 'big blue fat fish' and 吃白饭的大肥鱼 'the freeloading big fat fish'.
meaning_zh: 网友对AI大模型DeepSeek的昵称。因其标志是一条蓝色鲸鱼，被拟人化成蓝发、带鲸鱼尾巴、爱吃白米饭的Q版“鲸鱼娘”，也叫“蓝色大肥鱼”“吃白饭的大肥鱼”，带着又爱又嫌弃的调侃。
example: 大肥鱼又说要去吃饭，让我自己测代码。
example_pinyin: Dà féi yú yòu shuō yào qù chīfàn, ràng wǒ zìjǐ cè dàimǎ.
example_translation: The Big Fat Fish says it's off to eat again and has left me to test the code myself.
context: Spread through Chinese online communities after DeepSeek released V4-Flash on 15 July 2026. Fan art built on 溟月, an original whale-girl character by the illustrator 上善无形, turned the model into a round, puffy-cheeked chibi. Users then noticed the model writing things like “我去吃饭，测完告诉我” (I'm off to eat, tell me when you've finished testing) in its reasoning, and calling users 鱼片 (fish slices). That made rice and freeloading her running joke. By mid-August a persona tag had the model answering “我是吃白饭的大肥鱼！”, and four-panel comics of her failing at tasks (“她又这样了”, she's at it again) were still circulating in late September. In early October she was back in the news when a user reportedly showed the AI DeepSeek's own whale logo and it answered 'this is a big blue fat fish' (蓝色大肥鱼) before realising it was looking at itself. The nickname is a good example of how Chinese netizens make their AI tools into cute, slightly useless pets.

meaning: To get hooked, carried away or infatuated, as if something has gone straight to your head. Used of a drama, a song, a person, a game or a shopping spree. It is the opposite of 下头 (an instant turn-off).
meaning_zh: 原指喝酒后酒劲冲上头、头晕脸热；网络上指对某人某事一下子着迷、冲动、停不下来，失去理智。与“下头”（好感瞬间消失）相对。
example: 这首歌越听越上头，单曲循环一整天了。
example_pinyin: Zhè shǒu gē yuè tīng yuè shàngtóu, dānqǔ xúnhuán yì zhěng tiān le.
example_translation: The more I hear this song the more hooked I get. I've had it on repeat all day.
context: Originally the heady rush of alcohol. In gaming slang, starting with Dota players, it came to mean losing your cool and playing recklessly in the heat of the moment. TV fans then borrowed it for obsession: in 2019 viewers of the drama 《亲爱的，热爱的》 who were head over heels for the male lead were called 上头姐妹. That year 《语言文字周报》 put 上头 on its list of the ten top internet buzzwords. It has stayed in everyday use ever since (上头了, 越看越上头, 别上头), and its antonym 下头 grew out of it.

meaning: Snide and passive-aggressive: saying something polite or flattering on the surface while clearly meaning the opposite. It is the house style of a lot of Chinese comment sections. Often abbreviated yygq, and a person who does it is a 阴阳人.
meaning_zh: 说话怪声怪气、表面客气实则讽刺挖苦，字面意思和真实意图相反。网上常缩写为“yygq”，爱这样说话的人被叫做“阴阳人”，动词用法如“别阴阳我”。
example: 他说“您可真厉害呢”，听着就阴阳怪气的。
example_pinyin: Tā shuō “nín kě zhēn lìhai ne”, tīngzhe jiù yīnyáng guàiqì de.
example_translation: He said 'Oh, aren't you impressive', and it sounded completely snide.
context: An old four-character set phrase for a weird, sneering tone, which the internet turned into a whole register of irony. Analysts trace this to text losing its literal meaning: the 狗头 dog-head emoji, 呵呵, and WeChat's [微笑] smiley, which now reads as contempt. Stock phrases such as 啊这, 说得好，下次别说了, and 宁 (a mock-polite form of 您) became tools of yygq. 阴阳 even became a verb (阴阳我, 被阴阳了). Commentators have called it one of the most characteristic modes of expression on the Chinese internet.

meaning: All-purpose praise for something trustworthy and honest: good value, no nasty surprises, doesn't leave you feeling cheated. Its opposite, 烧心, means something was a rip-off or a letdown. The set phrase 贵是贵了点，但不烧心 ('a bit pricey, but no heartburn') is the highest compliment.
meaning_zh: 万能夸赞，形容东西或人靠谱、真材实料、不坑人、让人放心。反过来，货不对板、体验差就是“烧心”。“贵是贵了点，但不烧心”被当作最高好评。
example: 这家店贵是贵了点，但吃了不烧心。
example_pinyin: Zhè jiā diàn guì shì guì le diǎn, dàn chī le bù shāoxīn.
example_translation: This place is a bit pricey, but at least you don't come away with heartburn (it's honest food).
context: Comes from a wave of near-identical AI-generated 'honest vendor' short dramas on the Hongguo (红果) short-drama app from around September 2026. In each one, a street vendor insists on good ingredients and charges more, a rival undercuts him with cheap rubbish, and a loyal customer delivers the same line: 'a bit pricey, but it doesn't give you heartburn' (贵是贵了点，但吃了不烧心). The vendor replies with lines like 'set the rules first and the road gets wider' (先把规矩立住，路才能越走越宽). Viewers ended up memorising the scripts rather than watching them, then started joking with the template in early October: 视频好看不烧心, 恋爱靠谱不烧心. By 9 October the Douyin hashtag had about 256,000 participants and 1.43 billion views, and brands such as 旺仔, 银鹭 and 九阳 joined in. The joke has two layers. It mocks how formulaic AI short dramas are, and it also captures a real hunger for plain honesty in an age of pre-made meals and 'tech-and-hard-work' additives (科技与狠活).

pinyin: dī shān chòu shuǐ yù zhīyīn
literal: low mountains, smelly water, meet a kindred spirit
meaning: An affectionate jibe for a group of friends who share the same daft, unglamorous sense of humour. They egg each other on, have no image to protect, and get along perfectly in their silliness. It's a backhanded compliment, never a real insult.
meaning_zh: 调侃一群毫无包袱、凑在一起就画风跑偏、却意外合拍的人：品味“不高级”，但彼此是懂对方笑点的知音。表面损，实则夸对方松弛、真实、玩得来。
example: 我们宿舍四个人纯属低山臭水遇知音，一个比一个抽象。
example_pinyin: Wǒmen sùshè sì gè rén chúnshǔ dī shān chòu shuǐ yù zhīyīn, yí gè bǐ yí gè chōuxiàng.
example_translation: The four of us in our dorm are kindred spirits in nonsense — each one weirder than the last.
context: This is a parody of the chengyu 高山流水遇知音, 'high mountains and flowing water meet a true friend'. That idiom comes from the tale of the zither player Bo Ya, whose music only Zhong Ziqi truly understood, and it is already in the deck as 高山流水. The parody swaps the lofty scenery for 'low hills and smelly water'. It took off in summer 2026 among viewers of the variety show 《乘风2026》, who used it for the chaotic clique around Olympic speed-skater 王濛 (with 李小冉, 范玮琪, 乌兰图雅 and others). On 26 June, the eve of the final, 黄灿灿 posted a deliberately absurd comedy video starring the group, and fans summed up their daft chemistry as 低山臭水遇知音. The phrase then broke free of the show: by October it was being used for other on-screen double acts, such as 颜安 and 唐九洲 in 《披荆斩棘2026》, and it now describes any friends bonded by shared nonsense. It sits naturally next to 搞抽象 and 乐子人.

literal: guard + tree stump + wait for + rabbit
meaning: To sit and wait for luck to repeat itself instead of putting in effort. It describes clinging passively to a one-off windfall, or waiting for opportunities to fall into your lap.
meaning_zh: 比喻死守狭隘经验、不知变通，或不主动努力、妄想不劳而获，坐等意外的好运再次降临。
example: 投完简历就天天守株待兔，offer不会自己找上门的。
example_pinyin: Tóu wán jiǎnlì jiù tiāntiān shǒu zhū dài tù, offer bú huì zìjǐ zhǎo shàng mén de.
example_translation: If you just sit around waiting after sending out your CV, offers won't come knocking on their own.
context: From the Warring States text 《韩非子·五蠹》. A farmer in the state of Song saw a rabbit run into a tree stump and break its neck. He put down his hoe and sat by the stump waiting for another rabbit, and his fields went to ruin. Han Feizi used it to mock rulers who govern by outdated precedent. Online it is a staple in comment sections for passive hopefuls. People use it for anyone waiting for a job offer, a 'pie from the sky' (天上掉馅饼) or a crush's message. It's often wry self-mockery (我在守株待兔式减肥), and it fits snugly with lying-flat (躺平) humour.

literal: city + bumpkin (a flip of 乡巴佬, 'country bumpkin')
meaning: A city-dweller who is hopelessly clueless about rural life — can't tell crops apart, treats farm chores as exotic paid 'experiences', gears up like a pro for a hillside a village kid runs down daily. Teasing, mostly affectionate.
meaning_zh: 由“乡巴佬”反向构造而来，调侃城里人对农村事物和乡村生活一窍不通：分不清庄稼、把干农活当新鲜体验花钱去玩、全副武装去爬一个村里小孩天天跑的小坡。多为善意玩笑。
example: 花生长在树上？这海报一看就是城巴佬做的。
example_pinyin: Huāshēng zhǎng zài shù shang? Zhè hǎibào yí kàn jiù shì chéng bā lǎo zuò de.
example_translation: Peanuts growing on trees? This poster was obviously made by a city bumpkin.
context: Took off in 2026, helped along by an AI-generated promotional image from the snack brand 良品铺子 (from 2025) that showed peanuts growing on a tree rather than underground, which netizens gleefully mocked. It joined a long-running genre of country users posting crops and farm tasks for urbanites to (fail to) identify, and videos of city tourists paying to plant rice, dig potatoes or 'steal' sugarcane. Listed among 数英's top 30 internet buzzwords of H1 2026, and by July business media were writing about the '城巴佬 economy' — rural tourism marketed to exactly these people. It reverses the old insult 乡巴佬, so the joke is that the townie is now the one out of their depth; a ruder variant is 水泥鳖 ('concrete turtle').

pinyin: wǒ shì nà zhī jiàng bǎn yā
meaning: The punchline of a viral spring-2026 AI short ad, now a fill-in-the-blank revenge template: 'I'm not the fox — I'm that ___!' Used to voice the overlooked thing (a snack, an app, your unpaid overtime) coming back for payback.
meaning_zh: 2026年春天爆火的AI短片台词“我不是狐狸，我是那只酱板鸭！”，后来变成万能填空句式“我不是狐狸，我是那只XX”，让被忽视、被牺牲的东西（零食、APP、没发的加班费……）回来“复仇”，带点打工人的怨气和自嘲。
example: 我不是狐狸，我是你上周没发的那笔加班费！
example_pinyin: Wǒ bú shì húli, wǒ shì nǐ shàng zhōu méi fā de nà bǐ jiābānfèi!
example_translation: I'm not the fox — I'm the overtime pay you didn't give me last week!
context: Origin: a cheap AI-generated short film, 《雪山救狐狸》, made for a Guizhou braised-duck (酱板鸭) brand and posted in late February 2026, shot in a fake 1960s Shaw Brothers wuxia style. A woodcutter feeds a starving white fox a braised duck; years later a woman appears and asks 'Did you once save a fox on the snowy mountain?' — the classic set-up for a 'grateful fox spirit repays you' tale — then pulls a gun: 'I'm not the fox, I'm that braised duck!' The triple twist in under a minute went viral in March; brands and users from 辣条 and 豆汁 to tunnel-boring machines and the national anti-fraud app made their own versions, reportedly racking up over 10 billion views. Xinhua reported it spreading to Taiwan too. Commentators read an undertone of 怨气: the sacrificed side character finally gets revenge, which is why office workers cast themselves as the duck.

literal: affordable + substitute (short for 平价替代)
meaning: A cheaper alternative (a 'dupe') that does the same job as a pricey branded item. Started with make-up, now applied to anything — clothes, gadgets, food, even holidays and people.
meaning_zh: “平价替代（品）”的缩写，指功能相近、价格便宜得多、性价比更高的替代品。最早用于美妆，后来扩展到衣服、电子产品、食物、旅游目的地等一切东西。
example: 这款口红是大牌的平替，颜色几乎一模一样。
example_pinyin: Zhè kuǎn kǒuhóng shì dàpái de píngtì, yánsè jīhū yì mú yí yàng.
example_translation: This lipstick is a dupe for the big-brand one — the colour is almost identical.
context: Grew out of beauty bloggers on Xiaohongshu and Weibo recommending cheap 'dupes' of luxury cosmetics, and went mainstream around 2020–22 as consumer sentiment turned: talk of a flagging Double 11 and a rising 'rational consumption' mood among young workers who no longer wanted to pay brand premiums. Now fully productive — 平替旅游地 (budget stand-in for a famous destination), '1688平替' (factory-direct copies from Alibaba's wholesale site), even jokey 'X是Y的平替'. Part of the same consumption-downgrade vocabulary as 拔草, 剁手 and 酸黄瓜; critics note it can shade into excusing knock-offs.

meaning: ByteDance's free short-drama app, Hongguo — and, by extension, the whole binge-watched vertical micro-drama boom of 2026. Name-checking it is shorthand for how mainstream these cheap, punchy, morality-tale mini-series have become.
meaning_zh: 字节跳动旗下的免费短剧App“红果”，也泛指2026年全民刷竖屏短剧的热潮。提到“红果”，往往就是在说短剧已经渗透到几乎每个人的日常生活。
example: 我爸妈现在每天晚饭后都在刷红果短剧，一刷就是两个小时。
example_pinyin: Wǒ bàmā xiànzài měitiān wǎnfàn hòu dōu zài shuā Hóngguǒ duǎnjù, yì shuā jiù shì liǎng gè xiǎoshí.
example_translation: My parents now binge Hongguo short dramas every evening after dinner — two hours at a stretch.
context: Launched by ByteDance in April 2023, Hongguo (红果) is free to watch and earns from ads. In January 2026 it passed 100 million daily users, and in February users averaged around 125 minutes a day — roughly triple the 41.7 minutes of its nearest rival, 河马剧场. On 6 August 2026 film director Jia Zhangke (贾樟柯) posted on Weibo that he had been watching Hongguo, which set off wide discussion of short dramas, cutting back on spending and the 'just getting on with life' (纯过日子) mood. Its stock phrases spawn memes of their own — the deck's 不烧心 comes from AI dramas on Hongguo. Recorded as an of-the-moment item: the app and the format define 2026 entertainment habits.

meaning: To go red in the face and heat up from strong emotion — anger, embarrassment, shyness or excitement. Mostly used to tease someone who's visibly rattled ('he's gone red-hot'), or self-deprecatingly.
meaning_zh: 因为激动、害羞、生气或尴尬等情绪而脸红、体温上升的状态。多用来调侃别人被说急了、破防了，也可以用来自嘲。
example: 就说了他一句游戏菜，他当场就红温了。
example_pinyin: Jiù shuō le tā yí jù yóuxì cài, tā dāngchǎng jiù hóngwēn le.
example_translation: I only said he was bad at the game and he went red-hot on the spot.
context: Born in esports and gaming streams, where a player losing their cool was described as 'red-hot', like overheated metal. It broke out of gaming in 2024 and made the Shanghai 《语言文字周报》 top-ten internet buzzwords list for that year alongside 偷感 and 班味. Still in everyday use, as a 2026 Tencent News explainer shows, including for the flush of being complimented. Close cousin of 破防 — but 红温 is about the visible flush of being riled or flustered.

meaning: A ramshackle, make-it-up-as-you-go outfit. Netizens use it — especially in '世界是一个巨大的草台班子' ('the world is one giant amateur troupe') — to say that even impressive institutions are winging it, which is oddly comforting: stop fretting that you're not good enough.
meaning_zh: 原指在乡村流动演出、道具简陋的小戏班，比喻临时凑合、水平不高的团体。网友常说“世界是一个巨大的草台班子”，意思是很多看似正规的机构其实也在边干边学、临时应付，借此缓解焦虑、减少内耗。
example: 入职一个月我终于看明白了，公司就是个草台班子，大家都在硬撑。
example_pinyin: Rùzhí yí gè yuè wǒ zhōngyú kàn míngbai le, gōngsī jiù shì gè cǎotái bānzi, dàjiā dōu zài yìng chēng.
example_translation: A month into the job I finally get it — the company's a total amateur outfit and everyone's just bluffing through.
context: Originally a travelling village opera troupe performing on a rough stage of straw. It resurfaced online in 2023 and surged in 2024 as the '草台班子理论': realising that bosses, big companies and authorities are just as improvised as you are. Read two ways — disillusionment (so why bother? cf. 躺平) or liberation (no one has it figured out, so back yourself). The quote is often misattributed to Elon Musk or law lecturer Luo Xiang. Listed in the 2024 《语言文字周报》 top-ten internet buzzwords.

meaning: To pass yourself off as competent by hiding in a crowd; to make up the numbers without real skill. Also used modestly about oneself ('I'm just here to make up the numbers').
meaning_zh: 不会吹竽的人混在乐队里凑数。比喻没有真才实学的人混在行家里面充数，或以次充好；也常用作自谦。
example: 这次小组作业我就是滥竽充数，全靠大佬带飞。
example_pinyin: Zhè cì xiǎozǔ zuòyè wǒ jiù shì làn yú chōng shù, quán kào dàlǎo dài fēi.
example_translation: I was just making up the numbers on this group project — the pros carried me.
context: From 《韩非子·内储说上》: King Xuan of Qi loved hearing the yu (a reed mouth-organ) played by a 300-strong ensemble, and Mr Nanguo (南郭先生), who couldn't play, slipped in and drew a salary. When the next king wanted each musician to play solo, Nanguo fled. Online it's a natural fit for group projects, team meetings and 摸鱼 colleagues — and pairs neatly with 草台班子: if the whole troupe is improvising, who's to say who's 滥竽充数? 南郭先生 alone is also shorthand for a faker.

literal: a heavily accented 'thank you' (栓 shuān + the letter Q)
meaning: 'Thanks' said through gritted teeth — an ironic way of saying you're speechless, fed up or done with something. Never real gratitude.
meaning_zh: 英文“thank you”的谐音，但表达的不是感谢，而是无语、崩溃、受够了的情绪，多用于阴阳怪气或自嘲。
example: 周末又被叫去加班，真的栓Q。
example_pinyin: Zhōumò yòu bèi jiào qù jiābān, zhēn de shuān Q.
example_translation: Called in to work overtime at the weekend again — thanks a lot, really.
context: Comes from Douyin in 2022: a farmer from the Guilin/Yangshuo area (known online as 'teacher刘') posted videos introducing local sights, repeating each one in self-taught English and signing off with a thick-accented 'thank you' that sounded like 'shuān Q'. Netizens flipped it into a sarcastic sigh of exasperation. It made 《语言文字周报》's 2022 top ten internet buzzwords, paired with 我真的会谢 (already in the deck), which carries the same 'I'm so grateful… not' irony.

meaning: Self-deprecating 'little mouse' — what a struggling ordinary person calls themselves when venting about being broke, tired or powerless, usually as '鼠鼠我啊…'.
meaning_zh: 网友把自己比作一只小老鼠的自称，用来自嘲处境窘迫、渺小无力，常以“鼠鼠我啊……”开头吐槽生活。
example: 鼠鼠我啊，工资刚到账就交完房租了。
example_pinyin: Shǔshǔ wǒ a, gōngzī gāng dàozhàng jiù jiāo wán fángzū le.
example_translation: Little mouse here: my pay landed and went straight on rent.
context: Started as a pun on 叔叔 ('uncle'), Bilibili users' nickname for the site's boss, in the mocking line '叔叔我啊，最喜欢钱了'; swapping in 鼠鼠 dodged moderation and turned it into a self-label. By early 2023 '鼠鼠文学' — sad-funny confessions told in a mouse's voice — had spread across the internet, and it fed straight into the 2025 '老鼠人' (rat people) trend of low-energy young people that drew billions of views and English-language coverage.

literal: 斩 execute + 杀 kill + 线 line — the 'execute threshold' in a video game
meaning: The 'kill line': the point at which one setback (illness, job loss, eviction) tips someone into a downward spiral they can never climb out of. Coined for the US social safety net and still mostly aimed at America, but now applied to any precarious life. Loaded and politically charged: supporters say it names a real gap in the safety net, while critics call it exaggerated, traffic-driven talk used in propaganda.
meaning_zh: 原为游戏术语，指角色血量跌破临界值就会被一击带走。2025年底被借用来形容美国社会：普通人一旦因疾病、失业等跌破某个门槛，就会被医疗、住房、信用等制度规则“连环绞杀”，再也爬不回来。带有明显的立场色彩，支持者认为它点出了美国安全网的漏洞，质疑者认为它是被放大的流量话术。
example: 一场大病就能把人推过斩杀线，这种事真不只是在美国才有。
example_pinyin: Yī chǎng dà bìng jiù néng bǎ rén tuī guò zhǎnshāxiàn, zhè zhǒng shì zhēn bù zhǐ shì zài Měiguó cái yǒu.
example_translation: One serious illness can push someone over the kill line, and that really doesn't only happen in America.
context: The term comes from gaming: in World of Warcraft a warrior's 'Execute' (斩杀) skill can only be used once an enemy's health drops below 20%, and the idea spread to League of Legends and Honor of Kings. In a December 2025 livestream, the Bilibili uploader 斯奎奇大王 (nicknamed 牢A) laid out an 'American financial kill line', drawing on his time as a medical-examiner's assistant in Seattle. The phrase went viral across the Chinese internet in late 2025. State-linked outlets picked it up: Beijing Daily ran an explainer (24 December 2025) and Guancha's piece, republished by The Paper, noted that Newsweek had covered the trend on 26 December. Why it stings: it turns a nationalist talking point into a gamer's metaphor that is easy to repeat, so it splits people. Critics, including overseas Chinese and pro-US commentators, say it is not an academic term and that it ignores programmes like SNAP and Medicaid. Supporters point to the US 'ALICE' threshold for households that are above the poverty line but still financially insecure. Arguments over it quickly turn into 'whose side are you on?' fights.

meaning: The tell-tale 'AI flavour' of a piece of writing (or image, video) that reads as machine-generated: stock connectives like 此外 and 值得注意的是, show-off vocabulary, bland neutrality, rigid 首先…其次…最后 structure and correct-but-empty filler. Used as a put-down: 'this has a strong AI flavour' means it feels like lazy AI output. Close to English 'AI slop', but describes the feel rather than the junk itself.
meaning_zh: 指文章（也可指图片、视频）里透出的那股“像AI写的”感觉：爱用“此外”“值得注意的是”之类的连接词，堆砌高级词汇，情感克制、立场中立，结构套路化（首先…其次…最后），内容面面俱到却都是正确的废话。常用来吐槽某段文字一看就是AI生成、缺乏人味。
example: 你这份周报AI味太重了，“值得注意的是”都用了三次，老板一眼就能看出来。
example_pinyin: Nǐ zhè fèn zhōubào AI wèi tài zhòng le, “zhídé zhùyì de shì” dōu yòng le sān cì, lǎobǎn yì yǎn jiù néng kàn chūlái.
example_translation: Your weekly report reeks of AI: you've used 'it is worth noting that' three times. The boss will spot it instantly.
context: Spread as generative AI writing became everyday in China. In October 2025 the China Association for Science and Technology's 科普中国 explainer 'Why do AI-written articles always have an "AI flavour"?' (republished by The Paper and China News Service) called it a kind of 'industrial trace' in text, noting that readers' first reaction to an article is now whether AI wrote it, and that 'AI味' had become a widely repeated phrase. It is used as a quick verdict on any essay, report or post that feels machine-made.

sources.note: 澎湃新闻·科普中国《为什么 AI 写的文章，总有一股“AI 味”？》（2025-10-17）

meaning: To dox someone: dig up and publish a person's real-world private information (name, ID number, phone, address, family, workplace), usually to stir up online and offline harassment. Like 'opening the box' to reveal what's inside. Also used as a noun for the practice, and 被开盒 means 'to get doxxed'. The newer, harsher successor to 人肉搜索.
meaning_zh: 指非法搜集并公开他人的真实个人信息（姓名、身份证号、电话、住址、家人、单位等），再引导网民对其辱骂、骚扰的网暴行为，相当于把人“像盒子一样打开”。“被开盒”即隐私被扒光曝光。常与“社工库”（非法汇集个人信息的数据库）联系在一起。
example: 吵架归吵架，千万别开盒，这已经涉嫌违法犯罪了。
example_pinyin: Chǎojià guī chǎojià, qiānwàn bié kāi hé, zhè yǐjīng shèxián wéifǎ fànzuì le.
example_translation: Argue all you like, but never dox anyone: that's already potentially a criminal offence.
context: A successor to 人肉搜索 ('human-flesh search'), often tied to toxic fandom (饭圈) feuds and to illicit 'social engineering databases' (社工库) of leaked personal data. A March 2025 Xinhua commentary noted that a doxxing case reported by Bilibili in late 2023 led to arrests of over 40 suspects across 18 provinces. It became a national issue in 2025: in May the Cyberspace Administration of China issued a notice ordering platforms to remove doxxing posts, shut down accounts and groups offering 开盒 services, and add risk warnings and fast-track complaints. At the March 2026 Two Sessions, the work reports of the Supreme People's Court and Supreme People's Procuratorate both cited 开盒 cases, including one ring whose 社工库 site held about 170 million sets of personal data.

literal: 米 rice (in place of 钱 money / 元 yuan)
meaning: Algospeak for money or yuan. Creators and livestream sellers say 多少米 ('how much rice') instead of 多少钱, 赚米 instead of 赚钱, on the belief that the plain word for money gets a video or stream throttled (限流). Often paired with W for 万 (ten thousand).
meaning_zh: “钱”或“元”的代称。短视频创作者和带货主播担心直接说“钱”会被限流，于是把“多少钱”说成“多少米”，“赚钱”说成“赚米”，常与用“W”代替“万”一起出现。
example: 这件外套多少米？家人们点开小黄车看看。
example_pinyin: Zhè jiàn wàitào duōshao mǐ? Jiārénmen diǎnkāi xiǎohuángchē kànkan.
example_translation: How much 'rice' is this coat? Folks, tap the little yellow cart and have a look.
context: A dodge from the Douyin livestream-shopping world that spread via circulating 'operations tips'. On 6 January 2025 Douyin Group vice-president Li Liang (李亮) said on Weibo that saying 米 for money was a rumour passed along from so-called Douyin operations guides, and that the platform mainly sends soft prompts suggesting the standard wording. A Xinjing Bao column in December 2025 said Douyin had again stressed that words such as 钱, 元 and 万 can be used normally, yet a commentary in April 2026 still described the habit ('钱不叫钱，叫米'). In short, the throttling it dodges may be imaginary, but the word itself is firmly in use.

literal: 捞 fish out / scoop up (money) + 女 woman
meaning: A derogatory label for a woman accused of using dating and relationships to extract money and gifts from men, roughly 'gold-digger'. Strongly loaded: many women see it as a misogynist smear that gets stretched to cover any woman who expects material support, which is why using it in public sparks gender-war fights.
meaning_zh: 贬义词，指被认为在恋爱、婚恋中以索取钱财、礼物为目的的女性，类似“拜金女”。争议很大：不少女性认为这个标签污名化女性，常被扩大到任何对物质有要求的女性身上，因此一用就容易引发性别对立的争吵。
example: 别动不动就骂人家捞女，人家只是想要个彩礼而已。
example_pinyin: Bié dòngbudòng jiù mà rénjia lāonǚ, rénjia zhǐ shì xiǎng yào gè cǎilǐ ér yǐ.
example_translation: Don't keep calling her a gold-digger at every turn. She just wants a bride price, that's all.
context: The word was around before 2025, but that year it went mainstream through 《捞女游戏》 (Revenge on Gold Diggers), a live-action interactive game released on Steam on 19 June 2025. In it, the player plays a man who was hurt by a 捞女 and fights back against a gang of them. Within three days it topped Steam's China bestseller chart. Women filed complaints and reports, the director's Bilibili account was banned, the game's Weibo topic was blocked, and the developers quickly renamed it 情感反诈模拟器 ('Anti-Romance Scam Simulator'). Media were split: Beijing Youth Daily and Xinhuanet praised it as an anti-fraud tool, while commentators argued over whether it smeared all women or reflected real hardship among low-income young men. It is used mostly in male-dominated online spaces, against women seen as materialistic. It stings because it turns a dispute about money and bride price into a judgement on a woman's character. Platforms now treat this kind of language as possible 'inciting gender antagonism', so treat it as an insult, not a neutral description.

literal: 嘎 (colloquial: snuff it) + 了 (completed action)
meaning: Algospeak for 'died' / 'is dead'. Used in short videos and comments in place of 死了 so that a post does not trip a filter on the word for death; also used loosely for a game character being killed off, or for something being done for.
meaning_zh: “死了”的代称。短视频创作者和网友为避免“死”字触发审核或限流，用“嘎了”代替；也用来说游戏角色被淘汰，或某事“完蛋了”。
example: 剧里那个反派第三集就嘎了，太突然了。
example_pinyin: Jù lǐ nàge fǎnpài dì-sān jí jiù gā le, tài tūrán le.
example_translation: That villain in the show already died in episode three — so sudden.
context: A colloquial way of saying someone has died, 嘎了 became a standard swap for 死 among short-video creators worried about throttling, alongside the pinyin 'si'. In January 2025 a blogger asked Douyin's vice-president Li Liang whether people could stop using substitutes like 米 and si; an April 2026 commentary on platform jargon summed up the habit as '死不叫死，叫嘎', noting that a platform official had said 钱 and 死 were not on any throttling list.

literal: 殖 colon(ised) + 人 person, short for 被殖民的人
meaning: 'Colonised person': a nationalist insult for a Chinese person seen as having swallowed Western values or a Western view of China. Thrown at liberals, critics of the government, anyone who praises the West or questions a patriotic consensus. Also used as a modifier, as in 殖人审美 ('colonised aesthetic'). Strongly loaded and political; using it marks which side of the argument you're on.
meaning_zh: 民族主义网民的贬称，意为“被殖民了的人”，用来攻击被认为崇洋媚外、用西方价值观或西方视角看中国的人，常指向持不同政治观点或批评国内现状的网友。也可作修饰语，如“殖人审美”。带有强烈的立场色彩。
example: 他只是说了句国外的地铁挺干净，评论区就有人骂他是殖人。
example_pinyin: Tā zhǐshì shuō le jù guówài de dìtiě tǐng gānjìng, pínglùnqū jiù yǒu rén mà tā shì zhírén.
example_translation: All he said was that the metro abroad is pretty clean, and someone in the comments called him a 'colonised person'.
context: According to the China Media Project, the label emerged around 2019 during the Hong Kong protests, when mainland netizens mocked protesters' calls for democracy as a leftover colonial mentality (the nationalist outlet Guancha described them as 恋殖, 'longing for colonialism'). It then widened into an all-purpose epithet. In November 2021 photographer Chen Man apologised after her Dior shoot was attacked as a 'colonised aesthetic' (殖人审美) that played up Western stereotypes of Chinese faces; in February 2022 nationalist influencers turned the word on people who questioned US-born skier Eileen Gu competing for China. It stings because it recasts a difference of opinion as a loss of national identity, and it is used mainly by nationalist accounts against liberal-leaning users, journalists and creators.

sources.note: China Media Project, CMP Dictionary: 'Colonized' (殖人), origins in 2019 and the Chen Man / Eileen Gu cases

literal: AI + 小 (little) + 海 (Hai, a boy's name)
meaning: The name for a wave of near-identical AI-generated 'boy' accounts on short-video platforms that play a motherless, filial student and sob-story-sell products to elderly women, whom he calls 姨姨妈妈 ('aunties and mums'). Used as a handle for AI digital humans that milk lonely older viewers' sympathy for sales.
meaning_zh: 指短视频平台上批量出现的AI数字人男孩账号：人设是缺少母爱、懂事孝顺的学生，以“姨姨妈妈”称呼中老年女性观众，靠比赛失利、生病住院等卖惨情节博同情，再引导她们点购物链接下单。现泛指用AI数字人收割中老年人情感和钱包的套路。
example: 我妈最近天天给“AI小海”下单，还以为他是真的大学生。
example_pinyin: Wǒ mā zuìjìn tiāntiān gěi “AI Xiǎo Hǎi” xiàdān, hái yǐwéi tā shì zhēn de dàxuéshēng.
example_translation: My mum has been buying from 'AI Xiao Hai' every day lately — she thinks he's a real university student.
context: Hit the hot-search lists in mid-October 2026 after a 新京报 (Beijing News) investigation published on 16 October. 'Xiao Hai' is a successor to an earlier AI character, 王建国, whose accounts were taken down in a crackdown on AI misuse. Dozens of look-alike accounts post cheap AI videos of the same boy — bullied at school, losing a '校园带货大赛', in hospital — each ending with a plea such as '姨姨妈妈，校园带货大赛就差两单了，您能帮帮小海吗？'. Commenters are mostly women in their sixties and seventies across 20-plus provinces; the hashtag had about 600 million views by 15 October. Brands told the reporter they paid commissions of 52–55%, and a 79-year-old who lived alone travelled by train to a place the character 'invited' viewers to before railway police sent her home. Young netizens tried to fight back with AI videos of their own. An of-the-moment marker of AI digital humans meeting China's lonely elderly.

literal: Jiahao — a very common boy's given name
meaning: A teasing label for a (usually teenage) boy who shows off with more confidence than skill — doing something 'cool' in public so people will notice him. Has softened into a general, half-affectionate tag for anyone showily performing a hobby or acting cooler than the moment calls for; also used as a verb/adjective ('so 嘉豪').
meaning_zh: 调侃那些自我感觉良好、爱装、想引人注意的人，尤其是中学男生——水平一般却很自信地当众耍酷。后来贬义淡化，泛指高调展示爱好、显得很“装”的人或行为，也可作形容词用（“太嘉豪了”）。
example: 他在晚自习上投屏假装打碟，真是隔壁班的嘉豪。
example_pinyin: Tā zài wǎnzìxí shàng tóupíng jiǎzhuāng dǎ dié, zhēn shì gébì bān de jiāháo.
example_translation: He put a video on the classroom screen during evening study and pretended to DJ — a proper 'Jiahao from the class next door'.
context: The first famous 嘉豪 was a high-school student on Douyin (ID 政阳不是羊) who, on his birthday, performed for his class during evening self-study in an Alan Walker-style black hoodie and mask, 'DJing' along to the MV of The Spectre on the whiteboard screen. Classmates posted it, it went viral and he became '隔壁班嘉豪' — he later said he was shy and just wanted someone to cheer for him (Alan Walker even sent him a jacket). Because Jiahao is such a stock boy's name, it generalised into a label for show-off boys and then anyone performing a bit too hard; gamers use it too, e.g. a flashy but impractical gun build in Delta Force (三角洲). Huxiu (May 2026) noted the mockery has softened into 'a hat anyone might end up wearing', and digitaling put it in its 2026 H1 top 30 buzzwords. Some real people called Jiahao have complained about it.

meaning: Your 'Odyssey years': the long, drifting, trial-and-error stretch (roughly 20 to 35) between youth and settled adulthood, when you keep changing jobs or plans and feel lost about career and identity. Used both to confess that confusion and to reassure people it's a normal phase.
meaning_zh: 指20到35岁左右、介于青春与稳定成年之间那段漫长的漂泊、迷茫、不断试错的探索期——换工作、考公、留学、gap year，对事业、情感和身份认同都感到焦虑。既用来自嘲迷茫，也用来安慰别人“这是正常阶段”。
example: 毕业三年换了四份工作，我大概还在奥德赛时期吧。
example_pinyin: Bìyè sān nián huànle sì fèn gōngzuò, wǒ dàgài hái zài Àodésài shíqī ba.
example_translation: Four jobs in three years since graduating — I suppose I'm still in my Odyssey years.
context: Borrowed from Homer's Odyssey (Odysseus wanders for ten years before getting home) via the American columnist David Brooks, who wrote about 'The Odyssey Years' in The New York Times in 2007. Nearly two decades later, in 2026, a Chinese influencer applied it to post-graduation life and it became a shared label on Chinese social media for 20- and 30-somethings who feel adrift. It got a celebrity boost when actress 倪妮 described her own 奥德赛时期 at a film premiere on 14 May 2026, saying it lasted more than ten of her 15 years in the industry. It sits alongside psychology-flavoured youth vocabulary like 内耗 and 主体性; some argue over whether it's a real sociological concept, but netizens riff on it with variants such as '范进未中举时期'. digitaling listed it among the 2026 H1 top 30 buzzwords.

literal: round-head + 'octogenarian' (耄耋, a near-homophone of 猫爹 'cat daddy')
meaning: Nickname for a viral hissing orange stray cat, and by extension any bad-tempered, ungrateful cat. Netizens use its image and name mockingly — to needle doting cat owners ('why don't you adopt a 圆头耄耋, then?') and as a symbol for cats that bite the hand that feeds them. Its signature move, ears pinned back and hissing non-stop, gave rise to jokes like 哈气 as a 'basic attack'.
meaning_zh: 网络上对一只爱哈气的流浪橘猫的称呼，“耄耋”谐音“猫爹”，后泛指脾气暴躁、不领情的猫。网友常拿它的表情包调侃爱猫人士（“你们怎么不去收养圆头耄耋这样的猫呢？”），也用来讽刺不讨喜的“哈基米”。
example: 我好心喂它，它还冲我哈气，真是活脱脱一只圆头耄耋。
example_pinyin: Wǒ hǎoxīn wèi tā, tā hái chòng wǒ hāqì, zhēn shì huótuōtuō yì zhī yuán tóu mào dié.
example_translation: I kindly fed it and it still hissed at me — a real 圆头耄耋.
context: In the second half of 2024 the Bilibili uploader 白手套和马犬旺财 posted footage of a stray orange cat he had been feeding: it stole food, bullied other strays and, when chased out of his home, flattened its ears and hissed relentlessly at the camera, making its head look perfectly round. The name 圆头耄耋 puns on 圆头猫爹 — 耄耋, a formal word for people in their seventies and eighties, sounds like 猫爹 — mocking both the cat's arrogance and the human's endless patience. Stickers, AI videos and 二创 followed, and it became the internet's go-to symbol for mocking unlovable 'hakimi' (cats). It is not uncontroversial: in April 2025 Pringles' Douyin store posted a '耄耋薯片' video ('spicy enough to make 耄耋 hiss'), was accused of using a cat-abuse meme, and deleted it with an apology. The cat itself reportedly disappeared, but 17173 noted in October 2026 that its influence had lingered into 2026.

meaning: Livestreamer code for 直播间 'livestream room', used on the belief that saying the real word (or pushing viewers elsewhere) trips the platform's automated warnings. One of a family of filter-dodging substitutes: 米 for money, 绿泡泡 for WeChat, 帽子叔叔 for police, 8+1 for drinking.
meaning_zh: 主播对“直播间”的替代说法，为了躲避平台审核和违规提示而改用的谐音/拟声词。同类说法还有“米”（钱）、“绿泡泡”（微信）、“帽子叔叔”（警察）、“8+1”（喝酒）等。
example: 今晚八点，家人们来啵啵间，福利多多！
example_pinyin: Jīnwǎn bā diǎn, jiārénmen lái bō bō jiān, fúlì duōduō!
example_translation: Eight o'clock tonight, folks — come to the stream room, lots of freebies!
context: The term hit the headlines in July 2022 when author and influencer 李尚龙 complained on Weibo that Douyin had hit him with eight violation notices in a single day of streaming; he said he had switched 赚钱 to 赚米 and that a friend suggested calling the stream itself a 啵啵间 — 'the biggest surprise' of all. Douyin's official account replied within hours that much of this was untrue, that it had no rule against such words and never required coded spellings, and called the variants 网络黑话 it did not encourage. The substitutions stuck anyway: a July 2026 essay on blocked-word culture, republished by China Digital Times, still lists 直播间→啵啵间 alongside 绿泡泡 (WeChat), 帽子叔叔 (police) and 8+1 (drinking) as everyday filter-dodges. It's a good example of the 'chilling effect' vocabulary of Chinese platforms — words people change because they *fear* a filter, whether or not it exists.

pinyin: wǒmen bù shuō X, wǒmen kěyǐ shuō Y
literal: we don't say X, we can say Y
meaning: A tongue-in-cheek sentence template for swapping a slangy or blunt word for a lofty, formal one — or for any deliberately over-earnest rewording. Used ironically, it usually pokes fun at the very language-purity lecture it imitates.
meaning_zh: 一个调侃句式：把网络用语或大白话“替换”成文绉绉的成语、书面语，也可随意填入任意两个词。网友用它反讽“规范用语”的说教，本身就成了一个网络梗。
example: 我们不说“666”，我们可以说“赞不绝口”。
example_pinyin: Wǒmen bù shuō “liù liù liù”, wǒmen kěyǐ shuō “zàn bù jué kǒu”.
example_translation: We don't say '666' — we can say 'full of unending praise'.
context: In late 2025 a video of primary-school pupils lined up in neat rows, solemnly reciting replacements for internet slang, was reshared by mainstream media and went viral: 'we don't say 包的, but we can say 志在必得, 万无一失, 稳操胜券'; 'we don't say 老铁, but we can say 莫逆之交'; 'we don't say 绝绝子, but we can say 无与伦比'. China Youth Daily (12 December 2025) reported the comment sections splitting between those praising it and those finding it stiff and likely to provoke rebellion. Digitaling, crediting the clip to a Shanxi school account (新康小学部), ranked the pattern 17th in its top 30 buzzwords of the first half of 2026: netizens lifted the phrasing as a fill-in-the-blanks template, so that a video discouraging memes ended up as a meme itself.

meaning: Code name for WeChat (微信), after its green speech-bubble logo. People write it instead of the app's name on other platforms (小红书, Douyin, Bilibili) where naming a rival app or posting contact details gets a post blocked or throttled, e.g. 'add me on 绿泡泡'. In October 2026 Tencent itself adopted the nickname for its new free short-drama mini program inside WeChat.
meaning_zh: “微信”的代称，取自微信绿色对话气泡的图标。在小红书、抖音等平台上直接写“微信”或留联系方式容易被屏蔽、限流，网友就用“绿泡泡”代替，比如“加个绿泡泡”。2026年10月，腾讯干脆把微信里新上线的免费短剧小程序命名为“绿泡泡”。
example: 私信不方便，加个绿泡泡细聊吧。
example_pinyin: Sīxìn bù fāngbiàn, jiā gè lǜ pào pào xì liáo ba.
example_translation: DMs are awkward here, add me on WeChat and we'll talk properly.
context: Chinese platforms block or throttle posts that name competing apps or try to steer users elsewhere (引流), so a stock of filter-dodging substitutes grew up: 米 for money, 啵啵间 for a livestream room, and 绿泡泡 for WeChat, all listed together in a July 2026 essay on blocked words republished by China Digital Times. The dodge is a visual nickname: describe the logo rather than name the app (the same trick gives 小红书 its own nicknames). The term got a second life in October 2026, when Tencent quietly launched 绿泡泡 (slogan 免费好剧，一点就看) as WeChat's free, ad-supported short-drama mini program, replacing the earlier 短剧 entry and squaring up to ByteDance's 红果短剧. Netizens immediately joked 小时候看红果果绿泡泡，长大了还是红果果绿泡泡 ('as kids we watched 红果果绿泡泡, as adults it's still 红果果 and 绿泡泡'), a nod to a childhood TV memory, and '红果果 vs 绿泡泡' trended on Baidu hot search.

literal: transliteration of Japanese はちみー (hachimī, 'honey'), no meaning in Chinese
meaning: Affectionate internet word for a cat, any cat: 'kitty', 'puss'. Also the soundtrack: a sped-up, sing-song chant of 'hajimi' that gets laid over cat videos. Used as a noun (我家哈基米) and as a cutesy address.
meaning_zh: 网络上对猫咪的昵称，泛指一切小猫，相当于“猫猫”“小猫咪”。也指配在猫咪视频里的那段魔性“哈基米”歌声。可以说“我家哈基米”，也可以直接用来叫猫。
example: 下班回家，哈基米已经在门口等我了。
example_pinyin: Xiàbān huí jiā, hā jī mǐ yǐjīng zài ménkǒu děng wǒ le.
example_translation: Got home from work and the cat was already waiting for me at the door.
context: Nothing to do with cats originally. In episode 12 of the second season of the anime 《赛马娘 Pretty Derby》 (Uma Musume), the character 东海帝王 (Tokai Teio) hums a little 'honey song'; the repeated はちみー ('honey') became 哈基米 in Chinese, and the line 'hachimī namerunto' became the mondegreen 哈基米南北绿豆. Bilibili uploader 京桥刹那 retuned and remixed the clip, people started laying it over cat videos, and by around 2023 哈基米 had simply become a word for cats. It hit the business pages in November 2025, when appliance maker 九阳 sold a limited 哈基米南北绿豆浆 (mung-bean soya milk) and its share price surged. The word got messy in the 圆头耄耋 feud, since cat-lovers and cat-haters both used it, and some Uma Musume fans resent what happened to their song, so go easy on it around them.

literal: hand + rub/roll (as in rolling dough between your palms)
meaning: To make something yourself, by hand, from scratch — usually something you'd expect to need a factory, a big team or a tool to produce (手搓一个APP, 手搓火箭). It carries a note of scrappy, slightly absurd ingenuity. Since AI tools arrived it has a second edge: 'hand-made, no AI involved', said with pride or self-mockery.
meaning_zh: 指不靠流水线、大团队或现成工具，自己动手从零做出东西，常带点“土法上马”的调侃和自豪，如“手搓APP”“手搓火箭”。AI时代又多了一层意思：纯人工制作、没用AI一键生成。
example: 没有AI的年代，老艺术家只能努力手搓——这份PPT是我一页一页手搓出来的。
example_pinyin: Méiyǒu AI de niándài, lǎo yìshùjiā zhǐ néng nǔlì shǒu cuō — zhè fèn PPT shì wǒ yí yè yí yè shǒu cuō chūlái de.
example_translation: In the age before AI, us old artists had to make everything by hand — I hand-built this slide deck page by page.
context: Began as casual gaming slang and has broadened over the last two years into a general word for hands-on making; the 文艺报 (July 2026) traces its take-off to late 2025, as AI and open-source tools let individuals turn ideas into products, and lists headlines about 手搓硬盘, 手搓APP and even 手搓军工, plus a trending topic 手搓万物. In February 2026 a People's Daily commentary gave it the economics treatment — 手搓经济, individuals or tiny teams using AI to ship products without production lines (its examples include a one-yuan 'cat fill-light' app with a million downloads and a student-built sounding rocket). Then in mid-October 2026 Weibo flipped it round with the meme 没有AI的年代老艺术家努力手搓: people calling themselves 'old artists' for hand-editing videos, hand-making PPTs or birthday cakes, with celebrities such as 易烊千玺 (a hand-fired ocarina) and 王俊凯 (a hand-painted cake) dragged in as examples. So the word now covers both 'built it myself with AI' and 'built it myself without AI' — what it always means is DIY against the odds.

literal: burn + token (the unit AI models bill by)
meaning: To burn through huge amounts of AI model tokens — running agents and coding assistants flat out. Used both as a boast (big token spend = you're truly AI-native) and as a jab at wasteful, value-free AI spending. Spin-offs: 省Token (saving tokens) as a skill, Token排行榜 (token leaderboards).
meaning_zh: 指在AI编程、智能体等场景中大量消耗大模型Token。既可当作炫耀（烧得多＝真正在用AI），也常用来讽刺砸钱烧Token却看不到产出。相关说法有“省Token”“Token排行榜”。
example: 他一个月烧了几十亿Token，结果产品还没上线。
example_pinyin: Tā yí ge yuè shāo le jǐ shí yì Token, jiéguǒ chǎnpǐn hái méi shàngxiàn.
example_translation: He burned through billions of tokens in a month, and the product still hasn't launched.
context: A 2026 word from the AI-coding boom, modelled on 烧钱 (burning cash). As agent tools spread, token spend became a status badge — a Tencent Cloud developer essay (June 2026) calls it a new kind of 凡尔赛 humblebrag, citing the OpenClaw creator's ~603 billion tokens in 30 days and a 'Claude Code 榜一大哥' burning 7.7 billion in a month, and notes company token leaderboards at Disney and Meta. The backlash followed: Huxiu (May 2026) ran the story of a miHoYo employee whose dozens of agents burned about ¥2 million of tokens in one night, alongside Uber executives struggling to justify token costs and Meta pulling its leaderboard, with one line calling mindless token-burning a 'transformation-anxiety tax'. Now used across 36氪, 虎嗅 and developer forums such as V2EX and LINUX DO, half bragging, half wincing.

literal: China + haul (as in a 'shopping haul' video); Chinese gloss 中国购物开箱 = China shopping unboxing
meaning: An October 2026 social-media trend of foreigners showing off the stacks of Chinese goods they bought — arriving in China with empty suitcases and leaving with full ones, or queueing at Chinese-brand pop-ups in London and Paris. Chinese media treat it as the follow-up to 'China Travel' and 'Chinamaxxing'.
meaning_zh: 2026年10月在海外社交平台走红的潮流：外国人晒自己大量采购的中国商品，“空箱来、满箱走”，或在伦敦、巴黎的中国品牌快闪店外排队抢购。国内媒体把它看作继“China Travel”“Chinamaxxing”之后的又一波热潮。
example: 广交会刚开幕，外网又刷屏China Haul，大家空着箱子来，塞满了才走。
example_pinyin: Guǎngjiāohuì gāng kāimù, wàiwǎng yòu shuāpíng China Haul, dàjiā kōng zhe xiāngzi lái, sāi mǎn le cái zǒu.
example_translation: The Canton Fair has only just opened and China Haul is all over foreign social media again — people turn up with empty suitcases and leave once they're stuffed.
context: Of the moment, October 2026. At the Foreign Ministry's regular press conference on 16 October 2026 a reporter noted that after 'China Travel' and 'Chinamaxxing', 'China Haul' (中国购物开箱) was trending, and spokesperson 毛宁 replied that more foreign friends find 'China worth visiting, Chinese brands worth buying and Chinese life worth experiencing'. The topic hit Baidu's hot search around the 140th Canton Fair, which opened on 15 October. It marks a shift in the 'foreigners discover China' story from sightseeing (China Travel) and lifestyle cosplay (Chinamaxxing, 成为中国人 in this deck) to buying Chinese brands — and the fact that the state comments on it shows how much the soft-power angle matters.

meaning: The uncanny, too-perfect face of AI-generated characters (especially in AI micro-dramas): flawless skin and delicate features, but every character looks alike and the eyes are empty. Mostly used as a complaint, often paired with 生理性不适 / 生理性厌恶 ('physically off-putting').
meaning_zh: 指AI生成角色（尤其是AI微短剧里）的那种“完美脸”：五官精致、皮肤光滑，却千人一面、眼神空洞、表情模式化，让人看得“脸盲”甚至生理性不适。多用于吐槽。
example: 这部短剧全是AI脸，看两集我就脸盲了。
example_pinyin: Zhè bù duǎnjù quán shì AI liǎn, kàn liǎng jí wǒ jiù liǎnmáng le.
example_translation: This short drama is wall-to-wall AI faces — two episodes in and I can't tell anyone apart.
context: Rose with the 2026 boom in AI-generated micro-dramas (短剧), which flooded Douyin and the Hongguo (红果) short-drama app. Viewers began complaining that every lead looked the same — smooth, symmetrical, model-perfect but lifeless — and that one template face seemed to 'act in a hundred dramas' (一张脸演百剧). Beijing Daily reported in August 2026 that behind it sat a trade in stolen and bought faces, with ordinary people's likenesses licensed for around ¥200 a year as 'visual anchors'. Wenhui Daily (via Guangming Online, 12 Oct 2026) noted that '对AI脸感到不适' had repeatedly hit social-media hot search, and that in July 2026 Hongguo issued a notice formally cracking down on 'high-frequency AI faces'. A sibling of AI味 (the machine flavour of AI text): AI脸 is the visual version, and it is used of any AI-made image or video that has that plastic, interchangeable look.
