meaning: Euphemism for a paid proxy/VPN provider used to get over the Great Firewall — usually a small outfit selling subscription links to proxy 'nodes'. Saying 'airport' instead of VPN keeps the talk innocuous; the people buying from them are 'taking off'.
meaning_zh: 翻墙服务商的代称，一般指出售订阅链接、提供代理“节点”的付费翻墙服务。用“机场”代替“VPN”“翻墙”，说起来更隐晦，不容易触发审查。
example: 我的机场又跑路了，得赶紧换一家。
example_pinyin: Wǒ de jīchǎng yòu pǎolù le, děi gǎnjǐn huàn yì jiā.
example_translation: My 'airport' has done a runner again — I need to find another one, fast.
context: Comes from Shadowsocks, the proxy tool that became the go-to way over the wall in the 2010s. China Digital Times records that its paper-plane logo became a byword for 翻墙 itself, so the services selling access were nicknamed 机场 — where the planes take off from. It sits in a family of coy euphemisms for getting round the firewall, alongside 科学上网 ('scientific internet use') and 魔法上网 ('magic internet use'). In 2026 the 机场 model is the mainstream way mainland users get out: subscription URLs from commercial airports, loaded into Clash or Shadowrocket, from about ¥2 a month, with an April 2026 crackdown forcing providers to raise prices or change protocols. A timely word: in October 2026 twenty Harbin students were disciplined for unauthorised VPN use after a classmate reportedly informed on them. CC-CEDICT now lists 'service provider for Shadowsocks or similar software' as a sense of 机场.

literal: buy the casket, return the pearl
meaning: To keep the packaging and throw away the substance; to value the trimmings over what actually matters. Online it is the stock quip for buying something only for the freebie, toy or tie-in merch that comes with it.
meaning_zh: 买下装珍珠的木匣，却把珍珠退还。比喻舍本逐末、取舍不当。网上常用来调侃为了赠品、周边、联名玩具而买单，正品反倒成了附带的。
example: 为了玩具点了三份套餐，饭全剩下了，真是买椟还珠。
example_pinyin: Wèile wánjù diǎn le sān fèn tàocān, fàn quán shèngxià le, zhēn shì mǎi dú huán zhū.
example_translation: Ordered three meal deals for the toys and left all the food — the casket bought, the pearl handed back.
context: From the Han Feizi (《韩非子·外储说左上》): a pearl seller from Chu made such a lavish scented case for his pearl that the buyer from Zheng kept the case and gave the pearl back. Han Feizi's own jab was at the seller — 'good at selling caskets, not at selling pearls' — but the idiom came to mock the buyer's poor judgement. In today's consumer culture of blind boxes, IP tie-ins and 谷子 merch it has found a natural second life: when KFC's Psyduck (可达鸭) toy sold out in 2022, Jiemian summed it up as 'buy a meal, get a toy has become buy a toy, get a meal — 买椟还珠, nothing more'. Netizens reach for it whenever the gift outshines the product, from milk-tea cup sleeves to snack-pack figurines, usually with self-mocking resignation.

sources.note: 界面新闻，2022-05-25：《肯德基的可达鸭，从赠品到商品》——“买套餐送玩具，变成了买玩具送套餐，买椟还珠，也不过如此。”

meaning: To ditch milk tea, coffee and sugary drinks and carry a huge 1.5–2 litre bottle of plain water around, glugging from it all day. Used as a self-care badge ('I've gone big-water'), often half-jokingly, with mock-heroic slogans attached.
meaning_zh: 放下奶茶、咖啡等含糖饮料，改为随身带1.5到2升的大瓶白水，大口大口地喝。年轻人把它当作一种低成本的自我照顾方式，常带点玩笑和“中二”口号。
example: 我戒了奶茶，现在每天上班都喝大水。
example_pinyin: Wǒ jièle nǎichá, xiànzài měitiān shàngbān dōu hē dà shuǐ.
example_translation: I've quit milk tea — now I do the big-water thing at work every day.
context: A Douyin trend that broke out in mid-October 2026: young people posted videos of themselves unscrewing 1.5- or even 2-litre bottles and tipping their heads back to gulp, with captions like 弱者喝饮料，强者喝大水 ('the weak drink soft drinks, the strong drink big water') and 小水解渴，大水解人生 ('small water quenches thirst, big water sorts out your life'). It travels in a trio with 睡大觉、练薄肌 ('sleep big, train lean muscle') as a cheap healthy-living pose. #喝大水# reached the trending lists, and by 13–14 October mainstream outlets were running doctors' warnings: drinking too much too fast can cause hyponatraemia (水中毒, 'water poisoning'), so sip steadily rather than chug.

literal: red + stone (a sound-alike for 吃屎 'eat shit')
meaning: Crude slang written politely: 'to eat shit', i.e. to sit through something dreadful — a terrible film, short drama, game plot or cringe video. Often used of yourself ('I ate the shit so you don't have to') or of the taste for deliberately watching trash online (赛博赤石). Vulgar in sense, though the spelling looks innocent.
meaning_zh: “吃屎”的谐音写法，把“屎”换成“石”，看上去像普通词。指硬着头皮看完/玩完特别烂的内容（烂片、短剧、烂剧情、审丑视频），也可指专门在网上找“屎”来品鉴的爱好（“赛博赤石”）。意思粗俗，写法隐晦。
example: 这部短剧我替大家赤石了，千万别看。
example_pinyin: Zhè bù duǎnjù wǒ tì dàjiā chìshí le, qiānwàn bié kàn.
example_translation: I ate the shit on this short drama for all of you — do not watch it.
context: A dodge-the-swearword homophone: 赤石 (chì shí, 'red stone') reads like 吃屎 (chī shǐ), so the insult survives while the text stays clean. It grew up in Bilibili and gaming circles around 审丑 (ironic appreciation of the awful): a February 2025 BB姬 essay on Tencent News, '为什么越来越多人喜欢赛博赤石', traces the 'cyber shit-eating' craze from livestreamer 岛市老八, who literally ate it on stream, to people bingeing junk short dramas and memes, and calls it a widespread 'spiritual need'. The word went far enough that in May 2025 Danganronpa creator Kazuma Kodaka (小高和刚), replying to a Chinese player's review of his game 百日战纪 on 小黑盒, asked what 赤石 meant because so many posts used it — to much amusement; he later replied on Xiaohongshu 'now I know'.

sources.note: 腾讯新闻·BB姬（2025-02-04）：《从奶龙到东北雨姐，为什么越来越多人喜欢“赛博赤石”了？》，释“赤石（吃屎）梗”
游民星空（2025-05-24）：小高和刚回复玩家时提问“请问赤石是什么”

meaning: 'Snitch journalism': a news outlet 'investigating' a story by asking the authorities whether someone has broken a rule, effectively reporting them. A derogatory label for reporters who act as informants rather than watchdogs.
meaning_zh: 带贬义的说法，指媒体以“采访”为名，向主管部门询问当事人是否违规、是否该罚，实际上等于替网友去举报。批评的是媒体成了告状的传声筒，而不是独立的监督者。
example: 这哪是新闻，分明是举报式采访。
example_pinyin: Zhè nǎ shì xīnwén, fēnmíng shì jǔbào shì cǎifǎng.
example_translation: That's not journalism — it's snitch journalism, plain and simple.
context: Born in late September 2026. On 26 September, at a concert in Chengdu, singer Na Ying (那英) briefly sang 《弯弯的月亮》 in tribute to Liu Huan (刘欢), who had died the day before. Some netizens asked whether the unapproved addition broke performance-licensing rules, and Hunan's 潇湘晨报 rang the organiser and the culture authorities to ask whether it had been approved and whether she faced a fine — and described its own piece as 举报式采访. On 29 September the Chengdu culture bureau ruled it a fragmentary sing-along that needed no re-approval; the paper's post was later removed. Commentators pounced: blogger 西坡 (reposted by Huxiu, 1 Oct) said the media had become mere 'relay passers' between netizens and officials, and Hu Xijin wrote that the approach 'lacks empathy'. China Media Project (20 Oct) glossed the phrase as 'informant-style reporting' — closer to 'snitch journalism' — and tied it to the shrinking room for watchdog reporting.

literal: 崩 (northern dialect: coax / fleece) + 老头 (old man)
meaning: Loaded 2026 label for a grey-zone online hustle: chatting up lonely, financially stable middle-aged men with flattery, sympathy and flirtation, then asking for small, frequent transfers (a milk tea, a taxi fare). Somewhere between begging, emotional labour and fraud; used mockingly of both the hustlers and the 'old men' who fall for it.
meaning_zh: 2026年走红的反讽黑话：通过陪聊、撒娇、嘘寒问暖等方式，与情感空虚但有稳定收入的中年男性搞暧昧，再以买奶茶、付车费等名义小额高频地要钱。介于乞讨、情绪陪伴和诈骗之间，既调侃“崩”人的一方，也调侃被“崩”的“老头”。
example: 他每天给网友转二十块买奶茶，大家都说他被崩老头了。
example_pinyin: Tā měitiān gěi wǎngyǒu zhuǎn èrshí kuài mǎi nǎichá, dàjiā dōu shuō tā bèi bēng lǎotóu le.
example_translation: He transfers twenty yuan to his online friend every day 'for a milk tea' — everyone says he's being fleeced in a 崩老头 scheme.
context: A tech-media piece (雷科技, May 2026) called 崩老头 'a recently popular online chat routine' aimed at lonely middle-aged, divorced or retired men, arguing they aren't stupid so much as starved of companionship. 崩 here is northern dialect for coaxing or fleecing money out of someone, 'the same idea as 爆金币' (making a game enemy drop coins), and 老头 isn't literally old: it means men born in the 1970s–90s with steady income and an empty emotional life. By September 2026 Huxiu was reporting that it had turned into an industry: a house rule of 三聊一崩 (chat three times, ask for money once), single operators juggling two or three hundred 'old men', 求崩 ('please fleece me') posts on 小红书, and AI personas writing the scripts. The term sits on the gender-war fault line: some read it as women exploiting lonely men, others as men buying cheap emotional comfort, which is why it starts arguments.

literal: 易 (新易盛) + 中 (中际旭创) + 天 (天孚通信), which spells the name of a famous historian
meaning: A-share investors' nickname for the three big optical-module (CPO) stocks driving China's AI hardware rally: 新易盛 (Eoptolink), 中际旭创 (Innolight) and 天孚通信 (TFC Optical). One character from each company happens to spell 易中天, the well-known historian, so headlines like '易中天集体下跌' read as a pun. It stands for the whole AI-compute trade.
meaning_zh: A股股民对三只CPO光模块龙头股的合称：新易盛、中际旭创、天孚通信，各取一字，恰好拼成历史学者易中天的名字。常用来指代整个AI算力硬件板块，“易中天集体大涨/下跌”成了财经新闻的固定说法，与易中天本人无关。
example: 今天大盘又被“易中天”带着走，光模块一跌全线飘绿。
example_pinyin: Jīntiān dàpán yòu bèi “Yì Zhōng Tiān” dàizhe zǒu, guāngmókuài yì diē quánxiàn piāo lǜ.
example_translation: The market got dragged around by 'Yi Zhongtian' again today — the moment optical modules fell, the whole board went green.
context: Born out of the AI boom: the optical modules that link GPUs in data centres made these three companies the darlings of the 2025–26 A-share market, and investors bundled them under a name that is also a household name: 易中天, the well-known historian (who has nothing to do with the stocks). By 2026 it had moved from stock forums into mainstream finance copy: Jiemian (July 2026) called them the CPO 'three giants' known to the market as 易中天, and China News Service ran the headline '“易中天”，集体回应“美国光模块禁令”' (August 2026) when the shares slumped on reports of a US import ban. On 22 October 2026 '“易中天”集体下跌' was on Baidu's hot-search list. Note that in Chinese stock markets red means up and green (飘绿) means down. It's part of a wider habit of nicknaming stock groups, and a good test of whether a learner can tell a pun from a person.

literal: use (以) the partial (偏) to sum up (概) the whole (全)
meaning: To generalise from a part to the whole; to take one case or one side and judge everything by it. Online it's the stock rebuttal in comment-section fights when someone turns one anecdote into a verdict on a whole group, city or generation.
meaning_zh: 用片面的观点或个别例子去推断整体，从而得出错误结论。网上吵架时常被用来反驳“拿一个例子否定一群人”的说法，例如“别以偏概全”。
example: 你遇到一个坏司机就说全城司机都没素质，这不是以偏概全吗？
example_pinyin: Nǐ yùdào yí gè huài sījī jiù shuō quán chéng sījī dōu méi sùzhì, zhè bú shì yǐ piān gài quán ma?
example_translation: You meet one bad driver and say every driver in the city has no manners — isn't that over-generalising?
context: A plain-spoken idiom rather than a story-idiom: there is no fable behind it, just the logic of its four characters (偏 'one-sided part' vs 全 'whole'). China Daily's translation column renders it 'take a part for the whole / over-generalise'. It's the chengyu people actually type in comment sections: under any viral story about one rude tourist, one bad landlord or one 'typical' Gen Z worker, a reply of '别以偏概全' (don't over-generalise) or '典型的以偏概全' is almost guaranteed.

meaning: To pamper your prefrontal cortex: a 2026 lifestyle trend of protecting your focus and self-control by cutting multitasking, decisions and brain-frying input. Goes with the half-joking self-diagnosis 前额叶受损 ('my prefrontal cortex is damaged') to explain away distraction, short temper or procrastination.
meaning_zh: “富养”自己的前额叶：2026年兴起的一种生活方式，年轻人为保护专注力和自控力，刻意减少多任务、减少决策、少接收消耗脑子的信息。常与半开玩笑的自我诊断“前额叶受损”连用，用来解释自己走神、易怒、拖延。
example: 今天不刷短视频了，我要富养前额叶。
example_pinyin: Jīntiān bù shuā duǎn shìpín le, wǒ yào fùyǎng qián'éyè.
example_translation: No short videos today — I'm pampering my prefrontal cortex.
context: 富养 ('raise in comfort') is borrowed from parenting talk and here applied to a brain region. The Paper (澎湃, April 2026) traces the craze to a short popular-science video by a computational-neuroscience PhD that unexpectedly turned the prefrontal cortex into a talking point: suddenly 'the streets were full of people with prefrontal damage', people sought '前额叶友好型' (prefrontal-friendly) jobs, and stopped doing several things at once. By Q2 2026 the #前额叶 topic on RedNote (小红书) had over 86 million views, with note interactions up 267%+ in 90 days, and brands piled in (Qwen ran a 'prefrontal check-up centre', HeyTea a 'brain-waking' drink). It's self-help with a wink — the 'damage' is not a medical diagnosis.

meaning: 'Digital patina': the blur, mosaic artefacts, stacked watermarks and green tint a meme image picks up from being saved and reposted again and again. Said fondly — a heavily 'patinated' reaction image is a vintage classic with provenance.
meaning_zh: 图片（尤其是表情包）经过反复保存、转发、压缩后变糊、出马赛克、叠满水印甚至发绿的样子。借用古玩“包浆”的说法，带调侃和珍视意味：包浆越厚，说明这张表情包越老、越经典。
example: 这张表情包的电子包浆太厚了，起码传了十年。
example_pinyin: Zhè zhāng biǎoqíngbāo de diànzǐ bāojiāng tài hòu le, qǐmǎ chuán le shí nián.
example_translation: The digital patina on this meme is so thick — it's been doing the rounds for at least ten years.
context: 包浆 is antique-collectors' jargon for the glossy patina an object gains from years of handling; netizens transplanted it to images worn down by endless re-saving. Gcores (机核, 2018) noted that QQ tended to make images blurry while Baidu Tieba turned them gradually green, and that only memes with 'electronic patina' count as true classics worth collecting. GeekPark (via 36氪, 2019) blamed the greening on an early Android image-compression bug, fixed only in Android 7.0. Related jabs: 图都绿了 ('the picture's gone green') for a repost that's ancient.

meaning: 'Bot' / 'NPC': a put-down for someone who plays, talks or replies like a computer — clumsy, mechanical, canned or cold. 你个人机 'you bot'; 回话跟人机一样 'replies like a bot'. Mildly insulting rather than affectionate.
meaning_zh: 原指游戏里由电脑控制的“人机”玩家，引申为骂人或调侃：说某人操作笨拙、反应呆板，或者聊天只会机械地回“嗯嗯”“哦哦”“好吧”，像个没感情的机器人。带贬义。
example: 我说了一大段，他就回个“哦哦”，像个人机。
example_pinyin: Wǒ shuō le yí dà duàn, tā jiù huí ge “ò ò”, xiàng ge rénjī.
example_translation: I wrote him a whole paragraph and he just replied 'oh, ok' — like a bot.
context: In Chinese games 人机 is the AI-controlled opponent or teammate, notorious for dumb, repetitive behaviour, so calling a human player 人机 mocks them as bot-level. It then leaked out of gaming into everyday chat: in a late-2024 China Youth Daily piece on the hot-search word 聊缩力 (the knack for killing a conversation), netizens' examples included people who answer everything with '哦哦''嗯嗯''好吧', 'like a bot' (像个人机). An English slang glossary (Fluentide) glosses it as 'NPC / bot' and notes it stings more than the English. It's the opposite of 活人感 (feeling like a real person).

meaning: An 'orphan car': a vehicle, usually an EV, whose maker has gone bust or stopped production and service, leaving owners with no after-sales support, software updates or parts supply. Used by owners, the press and repair shops for the stranded cars of failed EV start-ups.
meaning_zh: 指车企破产清算、停产停服后，失去售后保障、技术更新和配件供应的车辆，多指倒闭新势力品牌的新能源车。车主坏了没处修、配件难买、保险难赔，只能靠第三方修理厂和拆车件。
example: 厂家倒了，我这辆车一夜之间成了孤儿车，坏个空调都得去拆车件里找配件。
example_pinyin: Chǎngjiā dǎo le, wǒ zhè liàng chē yí yè zhī jiān chéng le gū'ér chē, huài ge kōngtiáo dōu děi qù chāichējiàn lǐ zhǎo pèijiàn.
example_translation: The carmaker went under and overnight my car became an orphan car. Even if the air-con breaks I have to hunt for salvaged parts.
context: The label grew up around the shake-out of China's EV start-ups: when brands such as 威马 (WM Motor), 哪吒 (Neta) and 高合 (HiPhi) collapsed, their owners found service centres shut and parts drying up. On 24 October 2026 People's Daily ran 'Carmakers gone: who repairs the hundreds of thousands of orphan cars?' (it trended on Baidu hot search the same day). It estimated conservatively that there are several hundred thousand 孤儿车, noted that the rules already require makers to keep parts and service available for at least 10 years after a model is dropped, and blamed encrypted battery systems and locked fault codes for keeping third-party garages out. The piece also covered a Ministry of Industry and Information Technology draft notice that, for the first time, would make repair economics part of approval for new models. Owners gather in rights-protection and mutual-aid groups to swap tips on which garages will touch their brand. The term is a handy window on the price war and consolidation in China's car industry.

literal: 假装 pretend + 上班 go to work
meaning: 'Pretending to go to work': unemployed people keeping up the look of a job, leaving home at nine and coming back after six, spending the day in libraries, cafés or a rented desk. It also names the 假装上班公司, businesses that rent desks by the day so people can sit in an office. English coverage calls it 'mockupation'. Self-mocking, with an edge of social commentary about youth unemployment and saving face.
meaning_zh: 指失业或待业的人为了面子、为了不让家人担心，照样按点出门“上班”，在图书馆、咖啡馆或付费工位里待一整天。也指专门出租工位的“假装上班公司”。带自嘲意味，折射就业压力和“空窗期”焦虑。
example: 被裁三个月了，我还没敢告诉爸妈，每天照样九点出门假装上班。
example_pinyin: Bèi cái sān gè yuè le, wǒ hái méi gǎn gàosu bà mā, měi tiān zhàoyàng jiǔ diǎn chūmén jiǎzhuāng shàngbān.
example_translation: It's been three months since I was laid off and I still haven't dared tell my parents, so I leave home at nine every day and pretend to go to work.
context: Videos of people documenting their 'mock jobs' started spreading on Chinese social media in late 2024, and by 2025 real 假装上班公司 were renting out spare desks, some with staged 'interviews' and a 'boss' patrolling the floor (RealTime Mandarin, April 2026). The Hangzhou '假装上班无限公司', which went viral in July 2025, charged 30 yuan a day or 300 a month, with an 'overtime' fee after 18:00. By April 2026 local press reported that about a thousand people had passed through, and that most were now start-up founders and people between jobs rather than true pretenders. The phrase came back into the news on 20 October 2026, when Reuters profiled 'pretend-workers' hiding layoffs from their families. It cited posts with 610 million views on Douyin, more than 70 million on RedNote and up to 320 million on Weibo, and quoted a Cornell scholar saying the habit helps people save face. It is a sharper cousin of 摸鱼 and 精神下班: those people still have a job, but these people have lost theirs.

literal: I + Chovy (a League of Legends pro's name) / I + super + mighty
meaning: A 'platform-safe' exclamation standing in for the swear word 我操 / 卧槽 ('holy f***', 'WTF'). Used for shock, awe or exasperation, often at the start of a rant: 我Chovy，你们都在干嘛呢? It works as a sound-alike dodge, so the post or stream doesn't trip profanity rules, and many people using it have no idea who Chovy is.
meaning_zh: “我操/卧槽”的谐音替代说法，用来表达惊讶、赞叹、无语或暴躁。把粗口换成英雄联盟选手Chovy的名字或“我超威”，既保留了语气，又能避开平台对脏话的限制，现在已成万能口头禅，很多人用它时并不知道Chovy是谁。
example: 我Chovy，这题怎么又是我不会的？
example_pinyin: Wǒ Chovy, zhè tí zěnme yòu shì wǒ bú huì de?
example_translation: Holy cr*p, how is this another question I can't do?
context: Started as remixes of a livestream by actor 谢孟伟 ('嘎子', of 《小兵张嘎》 fame). In a milk-selling stream he drank several bottles of expired, soured milk his assistant had handed him, thinking it was yogurt, then threw the carton down and ranted, '我Chovy，你们都在干嘛呢?'. The clip circulated widely as GIFs and screenshots over the 2026 May Day holiday (Ali213, 11 May 2026), and the 'accident' was later reported to be scripted. Remixers turned his expletive into the sound-alikes 我超威 and 我Chovy, borrowing the League of Legends player's name. By August a Sina esports column called it perhaps 2026's biggest esports meme to break out beyond gaming, now 'a universal catchphrase' (万能口头禅). A Zhihu thread asks why Chovy has become the 'compliant' (合规) replacement for a traditional Chinese interjection. It's a textbook censorship workaround: same sound, cleaner surface.

meaning: A 'thin layer of muscle': the currently fashionable lean, defined physique, with visible lines and a hint of abs but no gym-bro bulk. The ideal is 穿衣显瘦，脱衣显壮 ('looks slim dressed, toned undressed'). Used as a body-type label (薄肌男, 薄肌身材) and as a goal (练薄肌), usually set against 'greasy' bodybuilder mass or 脂包肌 (muscle under fat).
meaning_zh: 指练出一层薄薄的肌肉线条、点到为止的身材：线条清晰、体脂适中、腹肌若隐若现，但不追求夸张的大块头，即“穿衣显瘦，脱衣显壮”。常说“薄肌男”“练薄肌”，与健美式大肌肉、“脂包肌”相对。
example: 我不想练成大块头，练个薄肌就够了。
example_pinyin: Wǒ bù xiǎng liàn chéng dà kuàitóu, liàn gè bójī jiù gòu le.
example_translation: I don't want to get massive. A lean, toned build is all I'm after.
context: A fitness-circle term that went mainstream on social media, especially Xiaohongshu, where #薄肌 became a prized label. A 2024 piece (精练GymSquare, republished by 虎嗅) called it the new 'refined' body ideal, displacing both 白幼瘦 (pale, young, thin) and bulky hypertrophy, and read it as a signal of self-discipline and control over one's time. In October 2026 it is back on hot-search boards as part of the wellness triad 喝大水、睡大觉、练薄肌 ('drink big water, sleep big sleeps, train thin muscle'), the companion of 喝大水. A 虎嗅 / 酷玩实验室 article (15 Oct 2026) says 练薄肌 'has long since gone from a gym term to an internet must-know', with English-teaching blogger 邵艾伦 styling himself the '薄肌教主' and running a '薄肌俱乐部'.

meaning: A TV drama that is 'carried by its cast': the script and plotting are weak, and the show survives on the stars' popularity, looks or on-screen chemistry. Usually a criticism of the show (and a backhanded compliment to the actors). Its mirror image is 剧抬人 ('the drama lifts the actor'): a strong script and role make a so-so or unknown performer look better than they are, so much so that 'a replacement could have played it better'.
meaning_zh: 指剧本、剧情本身薄弱，全靠演员的人气、颜值或CP感撑起热度的剧，多含批评意味。反义说法是“剧抬人”：剧本和角色出色，把演技或人气一般的演员“抬”了起来，换个人演甚至可能更好。
example: 这剧就是典型的人抬剧，剧情一塌糊涂，全靠男女主的脸撑着。
example_pinyin: Zhè jù jiù shì diǎnxíng de rén tái jù, jùqíng yì tā hú tú, quán kào nánnǚzhǔ de liǎn chēngzhe.
example_translation: This show's a classic case of the cast carrying it: the plot's a mess and it's propped up entirely by the leads' faces.
context: A pair of terms from drama-fan and review culture (Douban, Weibo), part of the endless argument over whether a hit made the star or the star made the hit. A 2023 Douban/NetEase review roundup of '剧抬人' dramas held up 《苍兰诀》 as the textbook case, defining it as 'not just replaceable, but replaceable by someone who'd do it better', and called 《镇魂》 a 人抬剧. The pair is back in the spotlight in October 2026: the costume drama 《尚公主》 (starring 孟子义 and 李昀锐, premiered around 23 October) hit Weibo hot search as '尚公主被指人抬剧', with viewers complaining that its court-intrigue plot is thin and only the leads' chemistry holds it up, while the rival 《嫁金钗》 was held up as the 剧抬人 counterexample.

meaning: As a verb: to gossip about someone quietly behind their back, to bitch about or badmouth them in whispers (蛐蛐领导, 有人在背后蛐蛐你). It has softened in wider use to cover general grumbling or teasing, and is often used self-mockingly ('let's have a little 蛐蛐 about the boss').
meaning_zh: 原指蟋蟀，网络用语中作动词，意为小声在背后议论别人，说闲话、坏话或八卦，如“蛐蛐领导”“有人蛐蛐你”。后来含义泛化，也可指吐槽、调侃。
example: 你俩在那蛐蛐啥呢？是不是又在蛐蛐领导？
example_pinyin: Nǐ liǎ zài nà qūqu shá ne? Shì bu shì yòu zài qūqu lǐngdǎo?
example_translation: What are you two whispering about over there? Slagging off the boss again?
context: From Northeastern (东北) dialect, where the faint, continuous chirping of crickets became a word for people murmuring about others. Baidu Baike credits Douyin comedy skits by Northeastern creators, with lines like '咱俩蛐蛐领导' ('let's gossip about the boss'), for spreading it nationwide, saying related Douyin topics passed 500 million views in 2022. Dazhong News put it on its 2024 roundup of internet buzzwords, and it is still everyday currency: on 23 October 2026 '别在背后蛐蛐任何人' ('don't gossip about anyone behind their back') was on Weibo hot search.

literal: seize + dwelling (i.e. take over another's body)
meaning: Literally a soul seizing someone else's body. Netizens say someone was 被夺舍了 ('body-snatched') when they suddenly act completely out of character: a shy friend turning chatty, a celebrity whose look or personality changes overnight, or yourself after an outburst you can't explain ('I was possessed yesterday'). Also used of people slipping back into an old self (被二十年前的自己夺舍).
meaning_zh: 原指灵魂占据他人的身体（借尸还魂）。网络上常说某人“被夺舍了”，形容其性格、言行或风格突然大变，像换了一个人；也用于明星形象突变，或自嘲一时失控的言行。
example: 他平时话都不说一句，今天在群里狂发消息，是被夺舍了吧？
example_pinyin: Tā píngshí huà dōu bù shuō yí jù, jīntiān zài qún lǐ kuáng fā xiāoxi, shì bèi duóshè le ba?
example_translation: He never says a word normally, and today he's spamming the group chat. Has he been body-snatched?
context: A staple of Chinese cultivation (修仙) and fantasy web novels, where a powerful soul takes over another person's body to live again (also called 借尸还魂 or 夺魂附体). From there it became the internet's go-to word for 'not themselves'. A 2022 Tencent News piece, '为什么娱乐圈总有人被夺舍？', traced the celebrity version: long-running rumours that stars from Avril Lavigne to Jay Chou were quietly 'replaced' by look-alikes. It is in constant everyday use: on 25 October 2026 Weibo hot search ran '厉娜许飞随时被20年前的自己夺舍', about two singers reunited on the variety show 《再见朋友》 and slipping straight back into an old feud from 20 years earlier.

meaning: 'Yellow-hair thinking' (also 黄毛理论): the tongue-in-cheek self-help idea that you should date and live like the cocky blond rival of romance stories — keep your own life, boundaries and pace, say what you want, and shrug off rejection — instead of grovelling and agonising over every unanswered message. Mocked as a licence to be a cad, defended as a jokey name for having self-respect. One of the autumn 2026 '邪修理论' alongside 大水理论 and 薄肌理论.
meaning_zh: “黄毛思维”（又称“黄毛理论”）：网友戏称的恋爱/人生“邪修理论”之一。借用恋爱故事里截胡男主心上人的“黄毛”形象，主张在关系里保留自己的生活、边界、节奏和选择权，想认识就开口，被拒绝也无所谓，不卑微、不讨好、不内耗。有人嘲讽它是教人当渣男，也有人认为它讲的是主体性。
example: 别再秒回了，学学黄毛思维：想约就约，被拒绝，无所谓。
example_pinyin: Bié zài miǎo huí le, xuéxue huáng máo sī wéi: xiǎng yuē jiù yuē, bèi jùjué, wúsuǒwèi.
example_translation: Stop replying instantly — try a bit of yellow-hair thinking: if you want to ask them out, ask; if they say no, who cares.
context: 黄毛 ('yellow hair') is an old anime and web-novel trope: the bleached-blond, devil-may-care guy who swoops in at the crucial moment and steals the hero's sweetheart, making him public enemy number one for 'pure-love warriors' (纯爱战士). In September–October 2026 the figure was flipped into a 'theory'. A Huxiu-republished essay (13 Oct 2026, from the WeChat account 缸中之脑cybernetics) grouped 黄毛思维 with 薄肌思维 and 大水理论 as the 'heretical-cultivation theories' (邪修理论) everyone was mocking, and quoted its defenders: it is 'not about actually dyeing your hair yellow or learning pick-up tricks, but building your own life, boundaries, rhythm, choices and goals', summed up as 'want to meet them, speak up; want a chance, go for it; rejected — no big deal'. A Xin Zhoukan (新周刊) piece on 26 Oct 2026 listed 黄毛理论 among the 'grand theories' of 2026, describing the 黄毛 as a stereotype who may not be richer or better educated than you but is bolder and more decisive — a jab at the anxious exam-cramming 'test-taker' (做题家) who loses out in love. Expect it said half-ironically.

meaning: To pick a fight with an enemy who isn't there: arguing against things nobody said, reading hostility into neutral or kind comments, or 'replying' to an imagined opponent. Used to mock someone for being paranoid, thin-skinned or shadow-boxing in an online argument.
meaning_zh: 原为《英雄联盟》英雄卡莎W技能的名字，网友借来形容“假想敌”式对线：对方根本没说过的话也要反驳，把别人的善意或中性言论脑补成恶意，自己跟空气吵架。多带嘲讽意味。
example: 人家只是说了句菜咸了，你别虚空索敌好吗？
example_pinyin: Rénjia zhǐshì shuōle jù cài xián le, nǐ bié xū kōng suǒ dí hǎo ma?
example_translation: They only said the food was a bit salty — can you stop fighting enemies who aren't there?
context: Lifted from League of Legends (英雄联盟): 虚空索敌 is the Chinese name of Kai'Sa's W ability ('Void Seeker'), a long-range beam that reveals the first enemy it hits. Because so many Chinese skill names sound like four-character idioms, players started using it as a 'new internet chengyu' — a 2024 Douban thread asking whether it is LoL's most famous skill has replies saying they use it all the time when trading barbs. The online sense has little to do with the skill: it describes picking a fight with an imagined opponent — inventing what the other side 'must' think, or treating goodwill as an attack. A 17173 commentary (July 2025) applied it to a blogger who, in the author's view, misread netizens' kindness as malice. Gaming slang that has fully crossed over into comment-section arguments.

meaning: A celebrity whose popularity has faded — a has-been or flop. Disparaging when outsiders say it, though fans sometimes call their own idol a 糊咖 pre-emptively to stay out of popularity comparisons. Cruder variant: 糊逼.
meaning_zh: 饭圈、娱乐圈用语，指人气下滑、“糊了”的艺人，带贬义。“糊”指不红、过气，“咖”源自闽南语，指某一类人物（如大咖、咖位）。粉丝有时也自称“我家是糊咖”来避免被拉去比较数据。
example: 他现在就是个糊咖，综艺都没人请了。
example_pinyin: Tā xiànzài jiù shì gè hú kā, zōngyì dōu méi rén qǐng le.
example_translation: He's a total has-been now — not even variety shows invite him any more.
context: Built from two pieces of fandom (饭圈) slang. 糊 ('burnt, mushy') for 'flopped' began on Baidu Tieba, where a post with hardly any replies 'flopped'; it then shifted to celebrities losing popularity and became a staple of fan wars comparing stars' numbers — exaggerated as 糊穿地心, 'flopped through the earth's core', and used in headlines about 糊电影 (box-office flops). 咖 comes from Southern Min, where it means 'a somebody' and, after another word, 'that kind of person' — the same 咖 as in 大咖 and 咖位. Put together, 糊咖 is 'one of the flopped ones'. Fans are touchy about it: an outsider calling their idol a 糊咖 can set off reporting campaigns and pile-ons, yet fans also say '我们家XX是糊咖，勿cue' ('our XX is a nobody, leave him out of it') to dodge comparisons.

sources.note: UBC Wiki, ASIA319 course entry on fandom slang 糊 'flop' (糊了, 糊穿地心, 糊咖, 糊逼, 咖 from Southern Min)

pinyin: qīng zhōu yǐ guò wàn chóng shān
literal: light boat · already · passed · ten thousand · layers of · mountains
meaning: 'The light boat has already sailed past ten thousand mountains': a triumphant line for having come through a long, hard struggle — above all Chinese tech breaking through sanctions or blockades (Huawei, home-grown chips), but also anyone who has finally 'landed' after a gruelling exam or ordeal.
meaning_zh: 借用李白诗句，表示历经重重困难之后终于闯过难关、扬眉吐气。网上最常用于形容国产科技（如华为手机、国产芯片）在封锁和制裁下实现突破，也用来形容考研、考公等熬过艰难后终于上岸。
example: 新芯片跑分出来了，评论区一片“轻舟已过万重山”。
example_pinyin: Xīn xīnpiàn pǎofēn chūlái le, pínglùnqū yí piàn “qīng zhōu yǐ guò wàn chóng shān”.
example_translation: The new chip's benchmark scores are out, and the comments are a wall of 'the light boat has passed ten thousand mountains'.
context: The closing line of Li Bai's poem 《早发白帝城》. At Huawei's developer conference in August 2023, consumer-business chief 余承东 (Richard Yu) said HarmonyOS had come through 'four hard years… 轻舟已过万重山, Huawei's flagship phones are on their way back'. When the Mate 60 Pro went on sale without warning on 29 August 2023 with a home-made Kirin chip, netizens flooded comment sections with the line, pairing it with Huawei's 2020 Weibo post '除了胜利，我们已经无路可走'; IT之家 put it in the headline of its hands-on review and People's Daily quoted it in a commentary. It has stuck as the stock cheer for any Chinese tech breakthrough under pressure — on 27 October 2026 '极客湾谈韬芯片轻舟已过万重山' was on Weibo hot search — and Xinmin Evening News noted people also use it for hard-won success such as passing the civil-service or postgraduate exams. Sits alongside 遥遥领先 in the patriotic-tech register; it can be sincere or mildly ironic.

literal: milk · green · wave (a misreading of the baijiu brand 明绿液)
meaning: A traffic-jam meme: drivers stuck on Anhui's expressways over Spring Festival 2026 misread the calligraphic billboard for the baijiu 明绿液 as '奶绿波' — and since they crawled past it all morning, 'still haven't got past 奶绿波' became the joke for being hopelessly stuck in holiday traffic.
meaning_zh: 2026年春节返程高峰，安徽宁洛高速严重堵车，司机们盯着路边“明绿液”白酒的书法广告牌，把字看成了“奶绿波”。“开了一上午，还没开出奶绿波”在抖音走红，成了调侃假期堵车、寸步难行的梗。
example: 国庆返程又堵死了，三个小时还没开出奶绿波。
example_pinyin: Guóqìng fǎnchéng yòu dǔ sǐ le, sān gè xiǎoshí hái méi kāi chū nǎi lǜ bō.
example_translation: The National Day drive home is gridlocked again — three hours and we still haven't got past 奶绿波.
context: During the Spring Festival 2026 return rush, the 宁洛高速 (Ningluo Expressway) in Anhui jammed into a car park. Bored drivers kept staring at a huge billboard for 明绿液, the premium baijiu of 安徽明光酒业 (majority-owned by 古井贡酒 since 2021), whose calligraphic lettering (by the late calligrapher 谢德萍) is hard to read; Douyin filled with guesses and one quip went viral: '开了一上午，还没开出奶绿波！' The brand leaned in: on 1 March its Douyin account thanked netizens '感谢网友赐名奶绿波', it registered the trademark the next day, and on 6 March opened a shop at the distillery selling 奶绿波 milk tea, while local tourism bureaux issued 200,000 coupons. Months later it still turns up in 2026 meme round-ups as shorthand for holiday gridlock — a textbook 'wild meme' a brand caught and monetised.

meaning: Big-tech code for the mid-2026 layoff wave: 30 June, the end of the second quarter, which became the common 'last day' for staff let go as Chinese internet companies cut jobs amid the AI push. 'Survived 630?' / '630 lastday'.
meaning_zh: 指2026年年中互联网大厂集中裁员的时间节点——6月30日，即二季度末。AI大规模进入职场后，许多公司把这天定为被裁员工的“last day”，“630”于是成了裁员潮的代称。
example: 我们组好几个人都是630走的，现在谁也不敢说AI用不上。
example_pinyin: Wǒmen zǔ hǎo jǐ gè rén dōu shì liù sān líng zǒu de, xiànzài shéi yě bù gǎn shuō AI yòng bù shàng.
example_translation: Several people on our team went in the 630 cuts — nobody dares say AI is useless now.
context: In mid-June 2026 rumours of '630大厂裁员' flew around Xiaohongshu and X; a V2EX thread asking for confirmation (15 June) explained '630 就是 6 月 30 号，Q2 结束就走', with one reply noting that 630 and 1230 used to be project milestones and had 'now become lastday'. In July 36氪 (republished on ifeng) wrote that '630' had become a social-media buzzword: the end of the first quarter in which AI truly entered China's internet workplaces at scale, with late June to mid-July the usual turnover point and the widely set last day of the wave; 虎嗅 reported staggered mid-year cuts at Meituan and Alibaba. Whether AI was the cause or the scapegoat is still argued. A time-stamped marker of 2026's AI-and-jobs anxiety.

meaning: 'Soft layoffs' (quiet firing): instead of formally dismissing someone and paying statutory severance, a company squeezes them until they 'choose' to resign — pointless transfers, pay cuts, piling on impossible work, digging up old expense claims, cutting off system access or kicking them out of work group chats. Used both by workers complaining and in media coverage of workplace rights.
meaning_zh: 公司不走正常解雇程序、不付或少付经济补偿，而是通过无理调岗、降薪、加压工作、翻旧账、收回权限、踢出工作群等手段逼员工“主动”辞职，就叫“软裁员”。多用于打工人吐槽和职场维权报道。
example: 又是调岗又是降薪，这不就是软裁员吗？
example_pinyin: Yòu shì diàogǎng yòu shì jiàngxīn, zhè bú jiù shì ruǎn cáiyuán ma?
example_translation: First a transfer, now a pay cut — isn't this just a soft layoff?
context: A term from HR and workers rather than the law: as a 凤凰网 feature reposted by 虎嗅 on 15 October 2026 puts it, there is no standard legal definition, but forcing staff out at below the cost of a proper dismissal (or at zero cost) is 'usually called 软裁员'. The incentive is money: an employee who resigns normally gets no compensation, so firms make staying unbearable instead. The piece's headline case is 小古 in Chongqing, who after six and a half years refused an unexplained transfer, had her computer removed and was dropped from 845 work group chats, was paid 55 yuan for her last half-month, and won about 67,000 yuan after arbitration and two court rounds. HR staff describe tactics like auditing old receipts for flaws and demanding dozens of rounds of PPT revisions. On 29 October 2026 '职场“软裁员”引争议' was on Baidu's real-time hot search, with experts calling for tighter rules. It's the Chinese counterpart of 'quiet firing' and sits naturally next to deck words like 牛马 and 打工人.

meaning: Someone who talks in riddles: hints, insinuates and refers to things obliquely instead of just saying them. Used to complain ('谜语人滚出去' — Riddler, get out!) or to describe a whole conversation where nobody will name the thing — often because it is sensitive and naming it outright could get a post removed.
meaning_zh: 指说话不直说、故弄玄虚、只给暗示让别人猜的人。网友常用“谜语人滚出哥谭”吐槽这种人；遇到敏感话题大家都不敢明说、只能拐弯抹角时，也会调侃“全员谜语人”。
example: 能不能别当谜语人了，到底发生了什么直接说！
example_pinyin: Néng bu néng bié dāng míyǔrén le, dàodǐ fāshēng le shénme zhíjiē shuō!
example_translation: Can you stop being the Riddler? Just tell me straight what happened!
context: 谜语人 is the Chinese name of Batman's villain the Riddler (Edward Nygma), who leaves puzzles at every crime. The meme came out of the game Batman: Arkham Knight, where catching him means solving 273 of his riddles scattered through Gotham's sewers and tunnels — players' shared verdict was '谜语人滚出哥谭' ('Riddler, get out of Gotham'), according to Moegirlpedia. From gaming circles it became general slang for anyone being cryptic. A timely example: when French footballer Mbappé was boycotted in China in October 2026 over 'inappropriate China-related remarks', domestic reports never said what he actually said; China Digital Times (27 October 2026) quoted a netizen complaining that those who didn't know couldn't get an answer, while 'those in the know are all 谜语人' (全员谜语人), referring to the remark only by hints. That censorship-adjacent use is where the word earns its keep.

meaning: Starting with a bang and ending with a whimper: a grand, impressive beginning followed by a weak, half-hearted finish. Online it is the stock verdict on TV dramas that open brilliantly and then fumble the ending, and on projects or plans that fizzle out.
meaning_zh: 开头声势浩大，结尾草草收场，比喻做事有始无终、前紧后松。网上常用来吐槽开局惊艳、结局拉胯的电视剧（即“烂尾”），也用来形容半途泄气的计划。
example: 前十集封神，后面越拍越水，典型的虎头蛇尾。
example_pinyin: Qián shí jí fēngshén, hòumiàn yuè pāi yuè shuǐ, diǎnxíng de hǔ tóu shé wěi.
example_translation: The first ten episodes were legendary, then it got thinner and thinner — classic tiger's head, snake's tail.
context: A classic chengyu: a tiger's mighty head on the body of a snake that tapers off to nothing. Taiwan's Ministry of Education idiom dictionary traces it to the Yuan-dynasty zaju play 《李逵负荆》 by 康进之, with the earlier form 龙头蛇尾 ('dragon's head, snake's tail') common in Chan Buddhist records. Today it lives in drama comment sections and review pieces about 烂尾 (botched endings): a 36氪 article (November 2024) on 《永夜星河》 and other shows that '高开低走' complained that even ordinary youth, romance and modern dramas had become '虎头蛇尾', leaving domestic drama stuck in a 虎头蛇尾 rut. Pair it with 高开低走 (opens high, goes low) and 烂尾 for the full vocabulary of disappointment.
